<p><b>Ethiopia</b>,<sup id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-14">&#91;a&#93;</a></sup> officially the <b>Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia</b>, is a <a href="/wiki/Landlocked_country" title="Landlocked country">landlocked country</a><sup id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-15">&#91;14&#93;</a></sup> located in the <a href="/wiki/Horn_of_Africa" title="Horn of Africa">Horn of Africa</a> region of <a href="/wiki/East_Africa" title="East Africa">East Africa</a>. It shares borders with <a href="/wiki/Eritrea" title="Eritrea">Eritrea</a> to the <a href="/wiki/Eritrea%E2%80%93Ethiopia_border" title="Eritrea–Ethiopia border">north</a>, <a href="/wiki/Djibouti" title="Djibouti">Djibouti</a> to the <a href="/wiki/Djibouti%E2%80%93Ethiopia_border" title="Djibouti–Ethiopia border">northeast</a>, <a href="/wiki/Somalia" title="Somalia">Somalia</a> to the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia%E2%80%93Somalia_border" title="Ethiopia–Somalia border">east and southeast</a>, <a href="/wiki/Kenya" title="Kenya">Kenya</a> to the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia%E2%80%93Kenya_border" title="Ethiopia–Kenya border">south</a>, <a href="/wiki/South_Sudan" title="South Sudan">South Sudan</a> to the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia%E2%80%93South_Sudan_border" title="Ethiopia–South Sudan border">west</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Sudan" title="Sudan">Sudan</a> to the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia%E2%80%93Sudan_border" title="Ethiopia–Sudan border">northwest</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16">&#91;b&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-17">&#91;15&#93;</a></sup> Ethiopia covers land area of 1,112,000 square kilometres (472,000 sq. miles).<sup id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-18">&#91;16&#93;</a></sup> As of 2023<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>, it is home to around 116.5 million inhabitants, making it the <a href="/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population" title="List of countries and dependencies by population">13th-most populous</a> country in the world, the <a href="/wiki/List_of_African_countries_by_population" title="List of African countries by population">2nd-most populous in Africa</a> after <a href="/wiki/Nigeria" title="Nigeria">Nigeria</a>, and the most populated landlocked country on Earth.<sup id="cite_ref-csa2_19-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-csa2-19">&#91;17&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-ReferenceB_20-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ReferenceB-20">&#91;18&#93;</a></sup> The national capital and largest city, <a href="/wiki/Addis_Ababa" title="Addis Ababa">Addis Ababa</a>, lies several kilometres west of the <a href="/wiki/East_African_Rift" title="East African Rift">East African Rift</a> that splits the country into the <a href="/wiki/African_Plate" title="African Plate">African</a> and <a href="/wiki/Somali_Plate" title="Somali Plate">Somali</a> <a href="/wiki/Plate_tectonics" title="Plate tectonics">tectonic plates.</a><sup id="cite_ref-CIA2_21-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CIA2-21">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Early_modern_human" title="Early modern human">Anatomically modern humans</a> emerged from modern-day Ethiopia and set out to the <a href="/wiki/Near_East" title="Near East">Near East</a> and elsewhere in the <a href="/wiki/Middle_Paleolithic" title="Middle Paleolithic">Middle Paleolithic</a> period.<sup id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22">&#91;20&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-23">&#91;21&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24">&#91;22&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-25">&#91;23&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-26">&#91;24&#93;</a></sup> Southwestern Ethiopia has been proposed as a possible <a href="/wiki/Afroasiatic_homeland" class="mw-redirect" title="Afroasiatic homeland">homeland of the Afroasiatic language family</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Blench2006_27-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Blench2006-27">&#91;25&#93;</a></sup> In 980 BCE, the Kingdom of <a href="/wiki/D%CA%BFmt" title="Dʿmt">D'mt</a> extended its realm over Eritrea and the northern region of Ethiopia, while the <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum" title="Kingdom of Aksum">Kingdom of Aksum</a> maintained a unified civilization in the region for 900 years. Christianity was embraced by the kingdom in 330,<sup id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-28">&#91;26&#93;</a></sup> and Islam arrived by the <a href="/wiki/Migration_to_Abyssinia" title="Migration to Abyssinia">first Hijra</a> in 615.<sup id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-29">&#91;27&#93;</a></sup> After the collapse of Aksum in 960, a variety of kingdoms, largely tribal confederations, existed in the land of Ethiopia. The <a href="/wiki/Zagwe_dynasty" title="Zagwe dynasty">Zagwe dynasty</a> ruled the north-central parts until being overthrown by <a href="/wiki/Yekuno_Amlak" title="Yekuno Amlak">Yekuno Amlak</a> in 1270, inaugurating the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Empire" title="Ethiopian Empire">Ethiopian Empire</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Solomonic_dynasty" title="Solomonic dynasty">Solomonic dynasty</a>, claimed descent from the biblical <a href="/wiki/Solomon" title="Solomon">Solomon</a> and <a href="/wiki/Queen_of_Sheba" title="Queen of Sheba">Queen of Sheba</a> under their son <a href="/wiki/Menelik_I" title="Menelik I">Menelik I</a>. By the 14th century, the empire grew in prestige through territorial expansion and fighting against adjacent territories; most notably, the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian%E2%80%93Adal_War" title="Ethiopian–Adal War">Ethiopian–Adal War</a> (1529–1543) contributed to fragmentation of the empire, which ultimately fell under a decentralization known as <i><a href="/wiki/Zemene_Mesafint" title="Zemene Mesafint">Zemene Mesafint</a></i> in the mid-18th century. <a href="/wiki/Emperor_of_Ethiopia" title="Emperor of Ethiopia">Emperor</a> <a href="/wiki/Tewodros_II" title="Tewodros II">Tewodros II</a> ended <i>Zemene Mesafint</i> at the beginning of his reign in 1855, marking the reunification and modernization of Ethiopia.<sup id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-30">&#91;28&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>From 1878 onwards, Emperor <a href="/wiki/Menelik_II" title="Menelik II">Menelik II</a> launched a series of conquests known as <a href="/wiki/Menelik%27s_Expansions" title="Menelik&#39;s Expansions">Menelik's Expansions</a>, which resulted in the formation of Ethiopia's current border. Externally, during the late 19th century, Ethiopia defended itself against foreign invasions, including from <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian%E2%80%93Egyptian_War" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethiopian–Egyptian War">Egypt</a> and <a href="/wiki/First_Italo-Ethiopian_War" title="First Italo-Ethiopian War">Italy</a>; as a result, Ethiopia and <a href="/wiki/Liberia" title="Liberia">Liberia</a> preserved their sovereignty during the <a href="/wiki/Scramble_for_Africa" title="Scramble for Africa">Scramble for Africa</a>. In 1935, Ethiopia was occupied by <a href="/wiki/Fascist_Italy_(1922%E2%80%931943)" title="Fascist Italy (1922–1943)">Fascist Italy</a> and annexed with Italian-possessed <a href="/wiki/Italian_Eritrea" title="Italian Eritrea">Eritrea</a> and <a href="/wiki/Italian_Somaliland" title="Italian Somaliland">Somaliland</a>, later forming <a href="/wiki/Italian_East_Africa" title="Italian East Africa">Italian East Africa</a>. In 1941, during <a href="/wiki/World_War_II" title="World War II">World War II</a>, it was <a href="/wiki/East_African_campaign_(World_War_II)" title="East African campaign (World War II)">occupied by the British Army</a>, and its full sovereignty was <a href="/wiki/Anglo-Ethiopian_Agreement#Negotiating_a_new_agreement" title="Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement">restored in 1944</a> after a period of <a href="/wiki/Occupied_Enemy_Territory_Administration_(Ethiopia)" title="Occupied Enemy Territory Administration (Ethiopia)">military administration</a>. The <a href="/wiki/Derg" title="Derg">Derg</a>, a Soviet-backed military junta, took power in 1974 after <a href="/wiki/1974_Ethiopian_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat" title="1974 Ethiopian coup d&#39;état">deposing</a> Emperor <a href="/wiki/Haile_Selassie" title="Haile Selassie">Haile Selassie</a> and the Solomonic dynasty, and ruled the country for nearly 17 years amidst the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Civil_War" title="Ethiopian Civil War">Ethiopian Civil War</a>. Following the <a href="/wiki/Fall_of_the_Derg" title="Fall of the Derg">dissolution of the Derg</a> in 1991, the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_People%27s_Revolutionary_Democratic_Front" title="Ethiopian People&#39;s Revolutionary Democratic Front">Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front</a> (EPRDF) dominated the country with a <a href="/wiki/1995_Constitution_of_Ethiopia" title="1995 Constitution of Ethiopia">new constitution</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ethnic_federalism#Ethiopia" title="Ethnic federalism">ethnic-based federalism</a>. Since then, Ethiopia has suffered from prolonged and unsolved <a href="/wiki/Ethnic_discrimination_in_Ethiopia" title="Ethnic discrimination in Ethiopia">inter-ethnic clashes</a> and political instability marked by <a href="/wiki/Democratic_backsliding" title="Democratic backsliding">democratic backsliding</a>. From 2018, regional and ethnically based factions carried out armed attacks in <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_civil_conflict_(2018%E2%80%93present)" title="Ethiopian civil conflict (2018–present)">multiple ongoing wars throughout Ethiopia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-BBC1120_31-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC1120-31">&#91;29&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Ethiopia is a <a href="/wiki/Multinational_state" title="Multinational state">multi-ethnic state</a> with over 80 different <a href="/wiki/List_of_ethnic_groups_in_Ethiopia" title="List of ethnic groups in Ethiopia">ethnic groups</a>. <a href="/wiki/Christianity" title="Christianity">Christianity</a> is the most widely professed faith in the country, with significant minorities of the adherents of <a href="/wiki/Islam" title="Islam">Islam</a> and a small percentage to <a href="/wiki/Traditional_African_religion" class="mw-redirect" title="Traditional African religion">traditional faiths</a>. This <a href="/wiki/Sovereign_state" title="Sovereign state">sovereign state</a> is a founding member of the UN, the <a href="/wiki/Group_of_24" title="Group of 24">Group of 24</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement" title="Non-Aligned Movement">Non-Aligned Movement</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Group_of_77" title="Group of 77">Group of 77</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Organisation_of_African_Unity" title="Organisation of African Unity">Organisation of African Unity</a>. Addis Ababa is the headquarters of the <a href="/wiki/African_Union" title="African Union">African Union</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Pan_African_Chamber_of_Commerce_and_Industry" title="Pan African Chamber of Commerce and Industry">Pan African Chamber of Commerce and Industry</a>, the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_Economic_Commission_for_Africa" title="United Nations Economic Commission for Africa">United Nations Economic Commission for Africa</a>, the <a href="/wiki/African_Standby_Force" title="African Standby Force">African Standby Force</a> and many of the global <a href="/wiki/Non-governmental_organization" title="Non-governmental organization">non-governmental organizations</a> focused on Africa. Ethiopia has been invited to join <a href="/wiki/BRICS" title="BRICS">BRICS</a> and will become a full member starting January 1, 2024.<sup id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-32">&#91;30&#93;</a></sup> Ethiopia is one of the <a href="/wiki/Least_developed_countries" title="Least developed countries">least developed countries</a> but is sometimes considered an <a href="/wiki/Emerging_power" title="Emerging power">emerging power</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-33">&#91;31&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-34">&#91;32&#93;</a></sup> having the <a href="/wiki/List_of_African_countries_by_GDP_growth" title="List of African countries by GDP growth">fastest economic growth</a> in <a href="/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa" title="Sub-Saharan Africa">Sub-Saharan African</a> countries because of <a href="/wiki/Foreign_direct_investment" title="Foreign direct investment">foreign direct investment</a> in expansion of agricultural and manufacturing industries.<sup id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-35">&#91;33&#93;</a></sup> However, in terms of <a href="/wiki/Per_capita_income" title="Per capita income">per capita income</a> and the <a href="/wiki/List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index" title="List of countries by Human Development Index">Human Development Index</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-36">&#91;34&#93;</a></sup> the country is regarded as poor with high rates of <a href="/wiki/Poverty_in_Ethiopia" title="Poverty in Ethiopia">poverty</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-37">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup> poor respect for <a href="/wiki/Human_rights_in_Ethiopia" title="Human rights in Ethiopia">human rights</a>, and a literacy rate of only 49%.<sup id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-38">&#91;36&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Agriculture_in_Ethiopia" title="Agriculture in Ethiopia">Agriculture</a> is the largest economic sector in Ethiopia, accounting for 36% of the country's <a href="/wiki/Gross_domestic_product" title="Gross domestic product">gross domestic product</a> as of 2020.<sup id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-39">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-40">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Etymology">Etymology</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=1" title="Edit section: Etymology">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Aethiopia" title="Aethiopia">Aethiopia</a></div>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Greek_language" title="Greek language">Greek</a> name <a href="/wiki/Aethiopia" title="Aethiopia">Αἰθιοπία</a> (from <span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text"><span lang="grc">Αἰθίοψ</span></span>, <i>Aithiops</i>, "an Ethiopian") is a compound word, later explained as derived from the Greek words <span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text"><span lang="grc">αἴθω</span></span> and <span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text"><span lang="grc">ὤψ</span></span> (<i>aithō</i> "I burn" + <i>ōps</i> "face"). According to the <a href="/wiki/A_Greek%E2%80%93English_Lexicon" title="A Greek–English Lexicon">Liddell-Scott Jones Greek-English Lexicon</a>, the designation properly translates as <i>burnt-face</i> in noun form and <i>red-brown</i> in adjectival form.<sup id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-41">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> The historian <a href="/wiki/Herodotus" title="Herodotus">Herodotus</a> used the appellation to denote those parts of Africa south of the <a href="/wiki/Sahara" title="Sahara">Sahara</a> that were then known within the <a href="/wiki/Ecumene" title="Ecumene">Ecumene</a> (habitable world).<sup id="cite_ref-Herodotus1_42-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Herodotus1-42">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup> Since the Greeks understood the term as "dark-faced", they divided the Ethiopians into two, those in Africa and those to the east from eastern Turkey to India.<sup id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-43">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> This Greek name was borrowed into <a href="/wiki/Amharic" title="Amharic">Amharic</a> as ኢትዮጵያ, <i>ʾĪtyōṗṗyā</i>. More likely <a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%CE%91%E1%BC%B0%CE%B8%CE%AF%CE%BF%CF%88#Etymology" class="extiw" title="wikt:Αἰθίοψ">Αἰθιοπία</a> was derived from a native word <i><a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E1%8B%95%E1%8C%A3%E1%8A%95#Ge&#39;ez" class="extiw" title="wikt:ዕጣን">ዕጣን</a></i> (ʿəṭan, incense), of which Ethiopia was an important source.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (April 2023)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p>In <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Greece" title="Ancient Greece">Greco</a>-<a href="/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire">Roman</a> epigraphs, <i>Aethiopia</i> was a specific toponym for ancient <a href="/wiki/Nubia" title="Nubia">Nubia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Hatke_44-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Hatke-44">&#91;42&#93;</a></sup> At least as early as <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;">&#8201;850</span>,<sup id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-45">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup> the name <i>Aethiopia</i> also occurs in many translations of the <a href="/wiki/Old_Testament" title="Old Testament">Old Testament</a> in allusion to Nubia. The ancient <a href="/wiki/Hebrew_language" title="Hebrew language">Hebrew</a> texts identify Nubia instead as <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Kush" title="Kingdom of Kush">Kush</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-46">&#91;44&#93;</a></sup> However, in the <a href="/wiki/New_Testament" title="New Testament">New Testament</a>, the Greek term Aithiops does occur, referring to a servant of the <a href="/wiki/Kandake" title="Kandake">Kandake</a>, the queen of Kush.<sup id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-47">&#91;45&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Following the Hellenic and biblical traditions, the <a href="/wiki/Monumentum_Adulitanum" title="Monumentum Adulitanum">Monumentum Adulitanum</a>, a 3rd-century inscription belonging to the <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum" title="Kingdom of Aksum">Aksumite Empire</a>, indicates that Aksum's ruler governed an area which was flanked to the west by the territory of Ethiopia and Sasu. The Aksumite King <a href="/wiki/Ezana_of_Axum" title="Ezana of Axum">Ezana</a> eventually conquered Nubia the following century, and the Aksumites thereafter appropriated the designation "Ethiopians" for their own kingdom. In the <a href="/wiki/Ge%CA%BDez" title="Geʽez">Ge'ez</a> version of the Ezana inscription, Aἰθίοπες is equated with the unvocalized <i>Ḥbšt</i> and <i>Ḥbśt</i> (Ḥabashat), and denotes for the first time the highland inhabitants of Aksum. This new <a href="/wiki/Demonym" title="Demonym">demonym</a> was subsequently rendered as <i>ḥbs</i> ('Aḥbāsh) in <a href="/wiki/Sabaean_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Sabaean language">Sabaic</a> and as <i>Ḥabasha</i> in <a href="/wiki/Arabic" title="Arabic">Arabic</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Hatke_44-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Hatke-44">&#91;42&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In the 15th-century Ge'ez <i><a href="/wiki/Book_of_Axum" title="Book of Axum">Book of Axum</a></i>, the name is ascribed to a legendary individual called <i><a href="/wiki/Ethiopis" title="Ethiopis">Ityopp'is</a></i>. He was an extra-biblical son of <a href="/wiki/Cush_(Bible)" title="Cush (Bible)">Cush, son of Ham</a>, said to have founded the city of <a href="/wiki/Axum" title="Axum">Axum</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Agrvt_48-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Agrvt-48">&#91;46&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In English, and generally outside of Ethiopia, the country was historically known as Abyssinia. This toponym was derived from the Latinized form of the ancient <i>Habash</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-49">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="History">History</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: History">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/History_of_Ethiopia" title="History of Ethiopia">History of Ethiopia</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_historiography" title="Ethiopian historiography">Ethiopian historiography</a></div>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Prehistory">Prehistory</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Prehistory">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Prehistoric_Ethiopia" title="Prehistoric Ethiopia">Prehistoric Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Homo_Sapiens_Idaltu.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Homo_Sapiens_Idaltu.JPG/220px-Homo_Sapiens_Idaltu.JPG" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Homo_Sapiens_Idaltu.JPG/330px-Homo_Sapiens_Idaltu.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Homo_Sapiens_Idaltu.JPG/440px-Homo_Sapiens_Idaltu.JPG 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="3000" /></a><figcaption>A <i><a href="/wiki/Herto_Man" title="Herto Man">Homo sapiens idaltu</a></i> hominid skull</figcaption></figure>
<p>Several important finds have propelled Ethiopia and the surrounding region to the forefront of&#160;<a href="/wiki/Paleontology" title="Paleontology">palaeontology</a>. The oldest <a href="/wiki/Hominidae" title="Hominidae">hominid</a> discovered to date in Ethiopia is the 4.2&#160;million-year-old <i><a href="/wiki/Ardipithecus" title="Ardipithecus">Ardipithecus ramidus</a></i> (<a href="/wiki/Ardi" title="Ardi">Ardi</a>) found by <a href="/wiki/Tim_D._White" title="Tim D. White">Tim D. White</a> in 1994.<sup id="cite_ref-OldestHuman_50-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-OldestHuman-50">&#91;48&#93;</a></sup> The most well-known hominid discovery is <i><a href="/wiki/Australopithecus_afarensis" title="Australopithecus afarensis">Australopithecus afarensis</a></i> (<a href="/wiki/Lucy_(Australopithecus)" title="Lucy (Australopithecus)">Lucy</a>). Known locally as <i>Dinkinesh</i>, the specimen was found in the <a href="/wiki/Awash_Valley" class="mw-redirect" title="Awash Valley">Awash Valley</a> of <a href="/wiki/Afar_Region" title="Afar Region">Afar Region</a> in 1974 by <a href="/wiki/Donald_Johanson" title="Donald Johanson">Donald Johanson</a>, and is one of the most complete and best preserved adult <a href="/wiki/Australopithecus" title="Australopithecus">Australopithecine</a> fossils ever uncovered. Lucy's taxonomic name refers to the region where the discovery was made. This hominid is estimated to have lived 3.2&#160;million years ago.<sup id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-51">&#91;49&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Dinkinesh_52-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Dinkinesh-52">&#91;50&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-iho1_53-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-iho1-53">&#91;51&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Ethiopia is also considered one of the earliest sites of the emergence of <a href="/wiki/Early_modern_human" title="Early modern human">anatomically modern humans</a>, <i><a href="/wiki/Human" title="Human">Homo sapiens</a></i>. The oldest of these local fossil finds, the <a href="/wiki/Omo_remains" title="Omo remains">Omo remains</a>, were excavated in the southwestern <a href="/wiki/Omo_Kibish_Formation" title="Omo Kibish Formation">Omo Kibish</a> area and have been dated to the <a href="/wiki/Middle_Paleolithic" title="Middle Paleolithic">Middle Paleolithic</a>, around 200,000 years ago.<sup id="cite_ref-Mcdougall2005_54-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Mcdougall2005-54">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup> Additionally, skeletons of <i><a href="/wiki/Herto_Man" title="Herto Man">Homo sapiens idaltu</a></i> were found at a site in the <a href="/wiki/Middle_Awash" title="Middle Awash">Middle Awash</a> valley. Dated to approximately 160,000 years ago, they may represent an extinct subspecies of <i>Homo sapiens</i>, or the immediate ancestors of anatomically modern humans.<sup id="cite_ref-55" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-55">&#91;53&#93;</a></sup> Archaic <i>Homo sapiens</i> fossils excavated at the <a href="/wiki/Jebel_Irhoud" title="Jebel Irhoud">Jebel Irhoud</a> site in Morocco have since been dated to an earlier period, about 300,000 years ago,<sup id="cite_ref-56" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-56">&#91;54&#93;</a></sup> while Omo-Kibish I (Omo I) from southern Ethiopia is the oldest anatomically modern Homo sapiens skeleton currently known (196 ± 5 ka).<sup id="cite_ref-57" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-57">&#91;55&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>According to some linguists, the first <a href="/wiki/Afroasiatic_languages" title="Afroasiatic languages">Afroasiatic</a>-speaking populations arrived in the region during the ensuing <a href="/wiki/Neolithic" title="Neolithic">Neolithic</a> era from the family's proposed <a href="/wiki/Afroasiatic_homeland" class="mw-redirect" title="Afroasiatic homeland">urheimat</a> ("original homeland") in the <a href="/wiki/Nile" title="Nile">Nile Valley</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-Zarins_58-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Zarins-58">&#91;56&#93;</a></sup> or the <a href="/wiki/Near_East" title="Near East">Near East</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Aane_59-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Aane-59">&#91;57&#93;</a></sup> The majority of scholars today propose that the Afroasiatic family developed in northeast Africa because of the higher diversity of lineages in that region, a telltale sign of linguistic origin.<sup id="cite_ref-Blench143144_60-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Blench143144-60">&#91;58&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-61">&#91;59&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-62">&#91;60&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2019, archaeologists discovered a 30,000-year-old <a href="/wiki/Middle_Stone_Age" title="Middle Stone Age">Middle Stone Age</a> rock shelter at the <a href="/wiki/Fincha_Habera,_Ethiopia" title="Fincha Habera, Ethiopia">Fincha Habera</a> site in <a href="/wiki/Bale_Mountains" title="Bale Mountains">Bale Mountains</a> at an elevation of 3,469 metres (11,381 feet) above sea level. At this high altitude humans are susceptible both to <a href="/wiki/Hypoxemia#Environmental_oxygen" title="Hypoxemia">hypoxia</a> and to extreme weather. According to a study published in the journal <i><a href="/wiki/Science_(journal)" title="Science (journal)">Science</a></i>, this dwelling is proof of the earliest permanent human occupation at high altitude yet discovered. Thousands of animal bones, hundreds of stone tools, and ancient fireplaces were discovered, revealing a diet that featured giant <a href="/wiki/Spalacidae" title="Spalacidae">mole rats</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-63" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-63">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-64">&#91;62&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-65">&#91;63&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-66" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-66">&#91;64&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-67">&#91;65&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-68">&#91;66&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-69">&#91;67&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Evidence of some of the earliest known stone-tipped projectile weapons (a characteristic tool of <i>Homo sapiens</i>), the stone tips of javelins or throwing spears, were discovered in 2013 at the Ethiopian site of <a href="/wiki/Gademotta" title="Gademotta">Gademotta</a>, which date to around 279,000 years ago.<sup id="cite_ref-SahlePLOS1_70-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SahlePLOS1-70">&#91;68&#93;</a></sup> In 2019, additional Middle Stone Age projectile weapons were found at Aduma, dated 100,000–80,000 years ago, in the form of points considered likely to belong to darts delivered by spear throwers.<sup id="cite_ref-Sahle_71-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Sahle-71">&#91;69&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Antiquity">Antiquity</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=4" title="Edit section: Antiquity">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/D%CA%BFmt" title="Dʿmt">Dʿmt</a> and <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum" title="Kingdom of Aksum">Kingdom of Aksum</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:KingEndybisEthiopia227-235CE.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/KingEndybisEthiopia227-235CE.jpg/220px-KingEndybisEthiopia227-235CE.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="112" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/KingEndybisEthiopia227-235CE.jpg/330px-KingEndybisEthiopia227-235CE.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/KingEndybisEthiopia227-235CE.jpg/440px-KingEndybisEthiopia227-235CE.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1283" data-file-height="652" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Aksumite_currency" title="Aksumite currency">Aksumite currency</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Axumite_kings" class="mw-redirect" title="Axumite kings">Aksumite king</a> called <a href="/wiki/Endubis" title="Endubis">Endubis</a>, 227–35, at the <a href="/wiki/British_Museum" title="British Museum">British Museum</a>. The inscriptions in <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Greek" title="Ancient Greek">Ancient Greek</a> read "ΑΧΩΜΙΤΩ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΣ" ("King of Axum") and "ΕΝΔΥΒΙΣ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΣ" ("King Endubis"), the Greek language was the <a href="/wiki/Lingua_franca" title="Lingua franca">lingua franca</a> by that time so its use in coins simplified foreign trade.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 980 BCE, <a href="/wiki/D%CA%BFmt" title="Dʿmt">Dʿmt</a> was established in present-day <a href="/wiki/Eritrea" title="Eritrea">Eritrea</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Tigray_Region" title="Tigray Region">Tigray Region</a> of Ethiopia and is widely believed to be the successor state to <a href="/wiki/Land_of_Punt" title="Land of Punt">Punt</a>. This polity's capital was located at <a href="/wiki/Yeha" title="Yeha">Yeha</a> in what is now northern Ethiopia. Most modern historians consider this civilization to be a native Ethiopian one, although in earlier times many suggested it was <a href="/wiki/Sabaeans" title="Sabaeans">Sabaean</a>-influenced because of the latter's hegemony of the <a href="/wiki/Red_Sea" title="Red Sea">Red Sea</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Munro-Hay57_72-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Munro-Hay57-72">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Other scholars regard Dʿmt as the result of a union of Afroasiatic-speaking cultures of the Cushitic and Semitic branches; namely, local <a href="/wiki/Agaw_people" title="Agaw people">Agaw peoples</a> and Sabaeans from Southern Arabia. However, <a href="/wiki/Ge%CA%BDez" title="Geʽez">Ge'ez</a>, the ancient Semitic language of Ethiopia, is thought to have developed independently from the <a href="/wiki/Sabaean_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Sabaean language">Sabaean language</a>. As early as 2000 BCE, other Semitic speakers were living in Ethiopia and Eritrea where Ge'ez developed.<sup id="cite_ref-73" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-73">&#91;71&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-74">&#91;72&#93;</a></sup> Sabaean influence is now thought to have been minor, limited to a few localities, and disappearing after a few decades or a century. It may have been a trading or military colony in alliance with the Ethiopian civilization of Dʿmt or some other proto-Axumite state.<sup id="cite_ref-Munro-Hay57_72-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Munro-Hay57-72">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Kingdom_of_Aksum.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/The_Kingdom_of_Aksum.png/220px-The_Kingdom_of_Aksum.png" decoding="async" width="220" height="246" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/The_Kingdom_of_Aksum.png/330px-The_Kingdom_of_Aksum.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/The_Kingdom_of_Aksum.png/440px-The_Kingdom_of_Aksum.png 2x" data-file-width="17877" data-file-height="20000" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum" title="Kingdom of Aksum">Empire of Axum</a> at its peak in the 6th century.</figcaption></figure>
<p>After the fall of Dʿmt during the 4th century BCE, the Ethiopian plateau came to be dominated by smaller successor kingdoms. In the 1st century CE, the <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum" title="Kingdom of Aksum">Kingdom of Aksum</a> emerged in what is now Tigray Region and Eritrea. According to the medieval <i><a href="/wiki/Book_of_Axum" title="Book of Axum">Book of Axum</a></i>, the kingdom's first capital, Mazaber, was built by Itiyopis, son of Cush.<sup id="cite_ref-Agrvt_48-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Agrvt-48">&#91;46&#93;</a></sup> Aksum would later at times extend its rule into Yemen on the other side of the Red Sea.<sup id="cite_ref-75" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-75">&#91;73&#93;</a></sup> The Persian prophet <a href="/wiki/Mani_(prophet)" title="Mani (prophet)">Mani</a> listed Axum with Rome, Persia, and China as one of the four great powers of his era, during the 3rd century.<sup id="cite_ref-76" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-76">&#91;74&#93;</a></sup> It is also believed that there was a connection between Egyptian and Ethiopian churches. There is diminutive evidence that the Aksumites were associated with the <a href="/wiki/Queen_of_Sheba" title="Queen of Sheba">Queen of Sheba</a>, via their royal inscription.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_77-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-77">&#91;75&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Around 316 CE, <a href="/wiki/Frumentius" title="Frumentius">Frumentius</a> and his brother Edesius from <a href="/wiki/Tyre,_Lebanon" title="Tyre, Lebanon">Tyre</a> accompanied their uncle on a voyage to Ethiopia. When the vessel stopped at a Red Sea port, the natives killed all the travellers except the two brothers, who were taken to the court as <a href="/wiki/Slavery_in_Ethiopia" title="Slavery in Ethiopia">slaves</a>. They were given positions of trust by the monarch, and they converted members of the royal court to Christianity. Frumentius became the first bishop of Aksum.<sup id="cite_ref-isbn0-313-32273-2_78-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-isbn0-313-32273-2-78">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup> A coin dated to 324 shows that Ethiopia was the second country to officially adopt Christianity (after Armenia did so in 301), although the religion may have been at first confined to court circles; it was the first major power to do so. The Aksumites were accustomed to the Greco-Roman sphere of influence, but embarked on significant cultural ties and trade connections between the <a href="/wiki/Indian_subcontinent" title="Indian subcontinent">Indian subcontinent</a> and the Roman Empire via the <a href="/wiki/Silk_Road" title="Silk Road">Silk Road</a>, primarily exporting <a href="/wiki/Ivory_trade" title="Ivory trade">ivory</a>, tortoise shell, gold and emeralds, and importing silk and spices.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_77-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-77">&#91;75&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-britishmuseum.org_79-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-britishmuseum.org-79">&#91;77&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Middle_Ages">Middle Ages</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=5" title="Edit section: Middle Ages">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia_in_the_Middle_Ages" title="Ethiopia in the Middle Ages">Ethiopia in the Middle Ages</a></div>
<p>The kingdom adopted the name "Ethiopia" during the reign of <a href="/wiki/Ezana_of_Axum" title="Ezana of Axum">Ezana</a> in the 4th century. After the conquest of <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Kush" title="Kingdom of Kush">Kingdom of Kush</a> in 330, the Aksumite territory reached its peak between the 5th and 6th centuries.<sup id="cite_ref-Munro-Hay57_72-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Munro-Hay57-72">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup> This period was interrupted by several incursions into the South Arabian protectorate, including <a href="/wiki/Jews" title="Jews">Jewish</a> <a href="/wiki/Dhu_Nuwas" title="Dhu Nuwas">Dhu Nuwas</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Himyarite_Kingdom" title="Himyarite Kingdom">Himyarite Kingdom</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Aksumite%E2%80%93Persian_wars" title="Aksumite–Persian wars">Aksumite–Persian wars</a>. In 575, the Aksumites <a href="/wiki/Sasanian_reconquest_of_Yemen" title="Sasanian reconquest of Yemen">besieged and retook Sana'a</a> following the assassination of its governor <a href="/wiki/Sayf_ibn_Dhi_Yazan" title="Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan">Sayf ibn Dhī Yazan</a>. The port city of <a href="/wiki/Adulis" title="Adulis">Adulis</a> was plundered by Arab Muslims in the 8th century; along with irrevocable <a href="/wiki/Land_degradation" title="Land degradation">land degradation</a>, claimed <a href="/wiki/Climate_change_(general_concept)" class="mw-redirect" title="Climate change (general concept)">climate change</a> and sporadic rainfall precipitation from 730 to 760,<sup id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-80">&#91;78&#93;</a></sup> the kingdom likely said to decline its power and important trade route, and Red Sea was left to the <a href="/wiki/Rashidun_Caliphate" title="Rashidun Caliphate">Rashidun Caliphate</a> in 646.<sup id="cite_ref-Munro-Hay57_72-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Munro-Hay57-72">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-:12_81-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:12-81">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup> Aksum came to an end in 960 when <a href="/wiki/Gudit" title="Gudit">Queen Gudit</a> defeated the last king of Aksum.<sup id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-82">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup> In response, the remnant of the Aksumite population to shift into the southern region and establish the <a href="/wiki/Zagwe_dynasty" title="Zagwe dynasty">Zagwe dynasty</a>, changing its capital to <a href="/wiki/Lalibela" title="Lalibela">Lalibela</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-83" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-83">&#91;81&#93;</a></sup> Zagwe's rule ended when an <a href="/wiki/Amhara_people" title="Amhara people">Amhara</a> noble man <a href="/wiki/Yekuno_Amlak" title="Yekuno Amlak">Yekuno Amlak</a> revolted against King <a href="/wiki/Yetbarak" title="Yetbarak">Yetbarak</a> and established the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Empire" title="Ethiopian Empire">Ethiopian Empire</a> (known by exonym "Abyssinia").
</p>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Map_of_the_Ethiopian_empire_under_Amda_Seyon.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Map_of_the_Ethiopian_empire_under_Amda_Seyon.jpg/201px-Map_of_the_Ethiopian_empire_under_Amda_Seyon.jpg" decoding="async" width="201" height="270" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Map_of_the_Ethiopian_empire_under_Amda_Seyon.jpg/301px-Map_of_the_Ethiopian_empire_under_Amda_Seyon.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Map_of_the_Ethiopian_empire_under_Amda_Seyon.jpg/401px-Map_of_the_Ethiopian_empire_under_Amda_Seyon.jpg 2x" data-file-width="645" data-file-height="868" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Empire" title="Ethiopian Empire">Ethiopian Empire</a> under Emperor <a href="/wiki/Amda_Seyon_I" title="Amda Seyon I">Amda Seyon I</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>The Ethiopian Empire initiated territorial expansion under the leadership of <a href="/wiki/Amda_Seyon_I" title="Amda Seyon I">Amda Seyon I</a>. He launched campaigns against his Muslim adversaries to the east, resulting in a significant shift in the balance of power in favor of the Christians for the next two centuries. After Amda Seyon's successful eastern campaigns, a most of the Muslim principalities in the <a href="/wiki/Horn_of_Africa" title="Horn of Africa">Horn of Africa</a> came under the suzerainty of the Ethiopian Empire. Among these Muslim entities was the <a href="/wiki/Sultanate_of_Ifat" title="Sultanate of Ifat">Sultanate of Ifat</a>. During the reign of Emperor <a href="/wiki/Zara_Yaqob" title="Zara Yaqob">Zara Yaqob</a>, the Ethiopian Empire reached its pinnacle. His rule was marked by the consolidation of territorial acquisitions from earlier rulers, the oversight of the construction of numerous churches and monasteries, the active promotion of literature and art, and the strengthening of central imperial authority.<sup id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-84">&#91;82&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-:3b_85-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:3b-85">&#91;83&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEConnelKillion2011160_86-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEConnelKillion2011160-86">&#91;84&#93;</a></sup> Ifat's successor, the <a href="/wiki/Adal_Sultanate" title="Adal Sultanate">Adal Sultanate</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-87">&#91;85&#93;</a></sup> tried to conquer Ethiopia during the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian%E2%80%93Adal_War" title="Ethiopian–Adal War">Ethiopian–Adal War</a>, but was ultimately defeated at the 1543 <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Wayna_Daga" title="Battle of Wayna Daga">Battle of Wayna Daga</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-88" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-88">&#91;86&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>By the 16th century, an influx of migration by ethnic <a href="/wiki/Oromo_people" title="Oromo people">Oromo</a> into northern parts of the region fragmented the empire's power. Embarking from present-day <a href="/wiki/Guji_Zone" title="Guji Zone">Guji</a> and <a href="/wiki/Borena_Zone" title="Borena Zone">Borena Zone</a>, the Oromos were largely motivated by several folkloric conceptions—beginning with <i>Moggaasaa</i><sup id="cite_ref-89" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-89">&#91;87&#93;</a></sup> and <i>Liqimssa</i>—many of whom related to their raids. This persisted until <i>gada</i> of Meslé.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPankhurst1997301_90-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPankhurst1997301-90">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-:8_91-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:8-91">&#91;89&#93;</a></sup> According to <a href="/wiki/Bahrey" title="Bahrey">Abba Bahrey</a>, the earliest expansion occurred under Emperor Dawit II (<i>luba</i> Melbah), when they encroached to <a href="/wiki/Bale_Province,_Ethiopia" title="Bale Province, Ethiopia">Bale</a> before invading Adal Sultanate.<sup id="cite_ref-Reference_92-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Reference-92">&#91;90&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Ethiopia saw major diplomatic contact with Portugal from the 17th century, mainly related to religion. Beginning in 1555,<sup id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-93">&#91;91&#93;</a></sup> Portuguese Jesuits attempted to develop Roman Catholicism as the state religion. After several failures, they sent several missionaries in 1603, including the most influential, Spanish Jesuit <a href="/wiki/Pedro_P%C3%A1ez" title="Pedro Páez">Pedro Paez</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-94" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-94">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup> Under Emperor <a href="/wiki/Susenyos_I" title="Susenyos I">Susenyos I</a>, Roman Catholicism became the state religion of the Ethiopian Empire in 1622.<sup id="cite_ref-Parfitt2019_95-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Parfitt2019-95">&#91;93&#93;</a></sup> This decision caused an uprising by the Orthodox populace.<sup id="cite_ref-berndl2005_96-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-berndl2005-96">&#91;94&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Gondarine_period_.281632.E2.80.931769.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Gondarine_period_(1632–1769)">Gondarine period (1632–1769)</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=6" title="Edit section: Gondarine period (1632–1769)">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Gondarine_period" title="Gondarine period">Gondarine period</a></div>
<p>In 1632, Emperor <a href="/wiki/Fasilides" title="Fasilides">Fasilides</a> successfully halted Roman Catholic state administration and restored <a href="/wiki/Orthodox_Tewahedo" title="Orthodox Tewahedo">Orthodox Tewahedo</a> as the state religion.<sup id="cite_ref-Parfitt2019_95-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Parfitt2019-95">&#91;93&#93;</a></sup> Fasilides' reign sparked solidification of imperial power and moved the capital to <a href="/wiki/Gondar" title="Gondar">Gondar</a> in 1636, commencing a period of transition known as "<a href="/wiki/Gondarine_period" title="Gondarine period">Gondarine period</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-97" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-97">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup>  He expelled Jesuits by reclaiming possessed lands and relegating them to <a href="/wiki/Fremona" title="Fremona">Fremona</a>. During his reign, he built one of the most iconic royal fortress, <a href="/wiki/Fasil_Ghebbi" title="Fasil Ghebbi">Fasil Ghebbi</a>, forty-four churches were built<sup id="cite_ref-98" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-98">&#91;96&#93;</a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_art" title="Ethiopian art">Ethiopian art</a> was revived. He also credited with constructing seven stone bridges over <a href="/wiki/Blue_Nile_River" class="mw-redirect" title="Blue Nile River">Blue Nile River</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-99" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-99">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Fasil_Ghebbi_IV_(23869587160).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Fasil_Ghebbi_IV_%2823869587160%29.jpg/220px-Fasil_Ghebbi_IV_%2823869587160%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Fasil_Ghebbi_IV_%2823869587160%29.jpg/330px-Fasil_Ghebbi_IV_%2823869587160%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Fasil_Ghebbi_IV_%2823869587160%29.jpg/440px-Fasil_Ghebbi_IV_%2823869587160%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4231" data-file-height="2819" /></a><figcaption>Fasil Ghebbi one of the most important castles of the <a href="/wiki/Gondarine_period" title="Gondarine period">Gondarine period</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Rebellion of the Agaw population in <a href="/wiki/Lasta" title="Lasta">Lasta</a> endured the reformation. Fasilides conducted <a href="/wiki/Punitive_expedition" title="Punitive expedition">punitive expeditions</a> to Lasta and successfully suppress it, which was described by the Scottish traveler <a href="/wiki/James_Bruce" title="James Bruce">James Bruce</a>, "almost the whole army perished amidst the mountains; great part from famine, but a greater still from cold, a very remarkable circumstance in these latitudes."<sup id="cite_ref-100" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-100">&#91;98&#93;</a></sup> Fasilides tried to establish firm relations with Yemeni Imam <a href="/wiki/Al-Mutawakkil_Isma%27il" title="Al-Mutawakkil Isma&#39;il">Al-Mutawakkil Isma'il</a> between 1642 and 1647 to discuss a trade route through Ottoman-held Massawa, which was unsuccessful.<sup id="cite_ref-101" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-101">&#91;99&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Gondar's power and reputation decayed following the death of <a href="/wiki/Iyasu_I" title="Iyasu I">Iyasu I</a> in 1706 because most emperors preferred to enjoy luxurious life rather than spending in politics. After <a href="/wiki/Iyasu_II" title="Iyasu II">Iyasu II</a> death in 1755, Empress <a href="/wiki/Mentewab" title="Mentewab">Mentewab</a> brought her brother, <a href="/wiki/Ras_(title)" title="Ras (title)">Ras</a> Wolde Leul, to Gondar and made him Ras Bitwaded, resulted in regnal conflict between Mentewab's <i>Quaregnoch</i> and Wollo group led by Wubit. In 1767, Ras <a href="/wiki/Mikael_Sehul" title="Mikael Sehul">Mikael Sehul</a>, a regent in <a href="/wiki/Tigray_Province" title="Tigray Province">Tigray Province</a>, seized Gondar and murdered the child <a href="/wiki/Iyoas_I" title="Iyoas I">Iyoas I</a> in 1769, who was emperor at the time, and installed 70-year-old <a href="/wiki/Yohannes_II" title="Yohannes II">Yohannes II</a>, marking the beginning of the decentralized Zemene Mesafint era.<sup id="cite_ref-102" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-102">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Zemene_Mesafint_.281769.E2.80.931889.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Zemene_Mesafint_(1769–1889)">Zemene Mesafint (1769–1889)</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=7" title="Edit section: Zemene Mesafint (1769–1889)">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Zemene_Mesafint" title="Zemene Mesafint">Zemene Mesafint</a></div><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:T%C3%A9wodros_II_-_2.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/T%C3%A9wodros_II_-_2.jpg/170px-T%C3%A9wodros_II_-_2.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="227" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/T%C3%A9wodros_II_-_2.jpg/255px-T%C3%A9wodros_II_-_2.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/T%C3%A9wodros_II_-_2.jpg/340px-T%C3%A9wodros_II_-_2.jpg 2x" data-file-width="377" data-file-height="504" /></a><figcaption>Emperor <a href="/wiki/Tewodros_II" title="Tewodros II">Tewodros II</a> (<span style="white-space:nowrap;"><abbr title="reigned">r.</abbr>&#8201;1855–1868</span>) brought an end of <i>Zemene Mesafint</i></figcaption></figure>
<p>Between 1769 and 1855, Ethiopia experienced a period of isolation referred to as the Zemene Mesafint or "Age of Princes". The emperors became figureheads, controlled by regional lords and noblemen like <i>Ras</i> Mikael Sehul, Ras <a href="/wiki/Wolde_Selassie" title="Wolde Selassie">Wolde Selassie</a> of Tigray, and by the <a href="/wiki/Yejju" title="Yejju">Yejju</a> Oromo dynasty of the <a href="/wiki/Zemene_Mesafint#Wara_Sheh_rulers_(Yejju)_(1784–1855)" title="Zemene Mesafint">Wara Sheh</a>, such as Ras <a href="/wiki/Gugsa_of_Yejju" title="Gugsa of Yejju">Gugsa of Yejju</a>. Prior to the Zemene Mesafint, Emperor Iyoas I had introduced the Oromo language (<i>Afaan Oromo</i>) at court, instead of Amharic.<sup id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103">&#91;101&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-104">&#91;102&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Ethiopian isolationism ended following a British mission that concluded with an alliance between the two nations, but it was not until 1855 that the Amhara kingdoms of northern Ethiopia (Gondar, <a href="/wiki/Gojjam" title="Gojjam">Gojjam</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Shewa" title="Shewa">Shewa</a>) were briefly united after the power of the emperor was restored beginning with the reign of <a href="/wiki/Tewodros_II" title="Tewodros II">Tewodros II</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Middleton2015_105-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Middleton2015-105">&#91;103&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-106">&#91;104&#93;</a></sup> Tewodros II began a process of consolidation, centralisation, and state-building that would be continued by succeeding emperors. This process reduced the power of regional rulers, restructured the empire's administration, and created a professional army. These changes created the basis for establishing the effective sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Ethiopian state.<sup id="cite_ref-107" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-107">&#91;105&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1875 and 1876, Ottoman and Egyptian forces, accompanied by many European and American advisors, twice <a href="/wiki/Egyptian%E2%80%93Ethiopian_War" title="Egyptian–Ethiopian War">invaded Abyssinia</a> but were initially defeated: once at the Battle of Gundit losing 800 men, and then in the second invasion, they were decisively defeated at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Gura" title="Battle of Gura">Battle of Gura</a> on 7<span class="nowrap">&#160;</span>March 1875, where the invading forces lost at least 3,000 men by death or capture.<sup id="cite_ref-108" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-108">&#91;106&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>From 1885 to 1889 (under <a href="/wiki/Yohannes_IV" title="Yohannes IV">Yohannes IV</a>), Ethiopia joined the <a href="/wiki/Mahdist_War" title="Mahdist War">Mahdist War</a> allied to Britain, Turkey, and Egypt against the Sudanese Mahdist State. In 1887, <a href="/wiki/Menelik_II" title="Menelik II">Menelik II</a>, king of <a href="/wiki/Shewa" title="Shewa">Shewa</a>, invaded the <a href="/wiki/Emirate_of_Harar" title="Emirate of Harar">Emirate of Harar</a> after his victory at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Chelenqo" title="Battle of Chelenqo">Battle of Chelenqo</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-109" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-109">&#91;107&#93;</a></sup> On 10 March 1889, Yohannes IV was killed by the Sudanese Khalifah Abdullah's army whilst leading his army in the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Gallabat" title="Battle of Gallabat">Battle of Gallabat</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-110" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-110">&#91;108&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="From_Menelik_II_to_Adwa_.281889.E2.80.931913.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="From_Menelik_II_to_Adwa_(1889–1913)">From Menelik II to Adwa (1889–1913)</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=8" title="Edit section: From Menelik II to Adwa (1889–1913)">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/First_Italo-Ethiopian_War" title="First Italo-Ethiopian War">First Italo-Ethiopian War</a> and <a href="/wiki/Menelik%27s_Expansions" title="Menelik&#39;s Expansions">Menelik's Expansions</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Emperor_Menelik_II.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Emperor_Menelik_II.png/220px-Emperor_Menelik_II.png" decoding="async" width="220" height="274" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Emperor_Menelik_II.png/330px-Emperor_Menelik_II.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Emperor_Menelik_II.png/440px-Emperor_Menelik_II.png 2x" data-file-width="4371" data-file-height="5445" /></a><figcaption>Menelik II in Coronation Garms and Tunic after the battle of Adwa</figcaption></figure>
<p>Ethiopia in roughly its current form began under the reign of Menelik II, who was Emperor from 1889 until his death in 1913. From his base in the central province of Shewa, Menelik set out to annex territories to the south, east, and west<sup id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_111-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-111">&#91;109&#93;</a></sup> — areas inhabited by the Oromo, <a href="/wiki/Sidama_people" title="Sidama people">Sidama</a>, Gurage, <a href="/wiki/Welayta_people" title="Welayta people">Welayta</a>, and other peoples.<sup id="cite_ref-igg_112-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-igg-112">&#91;110&#93;</a></sup> He achieved this with the help of <i>Ras</i> <a href="/wiki/Gobana_Dacche" title="Gobana Dacche">Gobana Dacche</a>'s Shewan Oromo militia, which occupied lands that had not been held since Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi's war, as well as other areas that had never been under Ethiopian rule.<sup id="cite_ref-113" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-113">&#91;111&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>For his leadership, despite opposition from more traditional elements of society, Menelik II was heralded as a national hero. He had signed the <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Wuchale" title="Treaty of Wuchale">Treaty of Wuchale</a> with Italy in May 1889, by which Italy would recognize Ethiopia's sovereignty so long as Italy could control an area north of Ethiopia (now part of modern Eritrea). In return, Italy was to provide Menelik with weapons and support him as emperor. The Italians used the time between the signing of the treaty and its ratification by the Italian government to expand their territorial claims. This <a href="/wiki/First_Italo%E2%80%93Ethiopian_War" class="mw-redirect" title="First Italo–Ethiopian War">First Italo–Ethiopian War</a> culminated in the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Adwa" title="Battle of Adwa">Battle of Adwa</a> on 1 March 1896, in which Italy's colonial forces were defeated by the Ethiopians.<sup id="cite_ref-igg_112-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-igg-112">&#91;110&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-114" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-114">&#91;112&#93;</a></sup> In 1896, the <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Addis_Ababa" title="Treaty of Addis Ababa">Treaty of Addis Ababa</a> was signed, replacing the Treaty of Wuchale with conditions more favorable to Ethiopia.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (August 2023)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> During this time, about a third of the population died in the <a href="/wiki/Famines_in_Ethiopia" title="Famines in Ethiopia">Great Ethiopian Famine</a> (1888 to 1892).<sup id="cite_ref-115" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-115">&#91;113&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-116" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-116">&#91;114&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Haile_Selassie_I_era_.281916.E2.80.931974.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Haile_Selassie_I_era_(1916–1974)">Haile Selassie I era (1916–1974)</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=9" title="Edit section: Haile Selassie I era (1916–1974)">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Haile_Selassie" title="Haile Selassie">Haile Selassie</a> and <a href="/wiki/Modernization_under_Haile_Selassie" title="Modernization under Haile Selassie">Modernization under Haile Selassie</a></div><p>The early 20th century was marked by the reign of Emperor <a href="/wiki/Haile_Selassie" title="Haile Selassie">Haile Selassie</a> <i>(Ras Tafari)</i>. Haile Selassie I was born to parents with ethnic links to three Afroasiatic-speaking populations of Ethiopia: the Oromo and Amhara, the country's two largest ethnic groups, as well as the <a href="/wiki/Gurage_people" title="Gurage people">Gurage</a>. He came to power after <a href="/wiki/Lij_Iyasu" title="Lij Iyasu">Lij Iyasu</a> was deposed, and undertook <a href="/wiki/Modernization_under_Haile_Selassie_I" class="mw-redirect" title="Modernization under Haile Selassie I">a nationwide modernization campaign</a> from 1916 when he was made a <i>Ras</i> and Regent (<i>Inderase</i>) for the <a href="/wiki/Queen_regnant" title="Queen regnant">Empress Regnant</a> <a href="/wiki/Zewditu" title="Zewditu">Zewditu</a>, and became the <i>de facto</i> ruler of the Ethiopian Empire. Following Zewditu's death, on 2 November 1930, he succeeded her as emperor.<sup id="cite_ref-117" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-117">&#91;115&#93;</a></sup> In 1931, Haile Selassie endowed Ethiopia with its first-ever <a href="/wiki/1931_Constitution_of_Ethiopia" title="1931 Constitution of Ethiopia">Constitution</a> in emulation of Imperial Japan's <a href="/wiki/Meiji_Constitution" title="Meiji Constitution">1890 Constitution</a>, through which the <a href="/wiki/Central_Europe" title="Central Europe">Central Europe</a> a model of unitary and homogeneous ethnolinguistic <a href="/wiki/Nation_state" title="Nation state">nation-state</a> was adopted for the Ethiopian Empire.<sup id="cite_ref-118" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-118">&#91;116&#93;</a></sup>
</p><h4><span id="Fascist_Italy_occupation_.281936.E2.80.931941.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Fascist_Italy_occupation_(1936–1941)">Fascist Italy occupation (1936–1941)</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=10" title="Edit section: Fascist Italy occupation (1936–1941)">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Second_Italo-Ethiopian_War" title="Second Italo-Ethiopian War">Second Italo-Ethiopian War</a>, <a href="/wiki/Italian_Ethiopia" title="Italian Ethiopia">Italian Ethiopia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Italian_East_Africa" title="Italian East Africa">Italian East Africa</a>, <a href="/wiki/Arbegnoch" title="Arbegnoch">Arbegnoch</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Black_Lions" title="Black Lions">Black Lions</a></div>
<p>The independence of Ethiopia was interrupted by the <a href="/wiki/Second_Italo-Ethiopian_War" title="Second Italo-Ethiopian War">Second Italo-Ethiopian War</a>, beginning when it was invaded by <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy#Fascist_regime_(1922–1943)" title="Kingdom of Italy">Fascist Italy</a> in early October 1935, and by subsequent Italian rule of the country (1936–1941) after Italian victory in the war.<sup id="cite_ref-119" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-119">&#91;117&#93;</a></sup> During this time, Haile Selassie exiled and appealed to the <a href="/wiki/League_of_Nations" title="League of Nations">League of Nations</a> in 1935, delivering an address that made him a worldwide figure, and the 1935 <a href="/wiki/Time_Person_of_the_Year" title="Time Person of the Year"><i>Time</i> Man of the Year</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-120" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-120">&#91;118&#93;</a></sup> As the majority of the Ethiopian population lived in rural towns, Italy faced continued resistance and ambushes in urban centers throughout its rule over Ethiopia. Haile Selassie fled into exile in <a href="/wiki/Fairfield_House,_Bath" title="Fairfield House, Bath">Fairfield House, Bath</a>, England. Mussolini was able to proclaim <a href="/wiki/Italian_Ethiopia" title="Italian Ethiopia">Italian Ethiopia</a> and the assumption of the imperial title by the Italian King <a href="/wiki/Vittorio_Emanuele_III" class="mw-redirect" title="Vittorio Emanuele III">Vittorio Emanuele III</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-121" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-121">&#91;119&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Abyssinian-soldiers-1936-142348340618.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Abyssinian-soldiers-1936-142348340618.jpg/220px-Abyssinian-soldiers-1936-142348340618.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Abyssinian-soldiers-1936-142348340618.jpg/330px-Abyssinian-soldiers-1936-142348340618.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Abyssinian-soldiers-1936-142348340618.jpg/440px-Abyssinian-soldiers-1936-142348340618.jpg 2x" data-file-width="949" data-file-height="722" /></a><figcaption>Ethiopian troops during the <a href="/wiki/Second_Italo-Ethiopian_War" title="Second Italo-Ethiopian War">Second Italo-Ethiopian War</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>In 1937, the Italian massacre of <a href="/wiki/Yekatit_12" title="Yekatit 12">Yekatit 12</a> took place, in which between 1,400 and 30,000 civilians were killed and many others imprisoned.<sup id="cite_ref-:02_122-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:02-122">&#91;120&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-123" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-123">&#91;121&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-124" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-124">&#91;122&#93;</a></sup> This massacre was a reprisal for the attempted assassination of <a href="/wiki/Rodolfo_Graziani" title="Rodolfo Graziani">Rodolfo Graziani</a>, the viceroy of <a href="/wiki/Italian_East_Africa" title="Italian East Africa">Italian East Africa</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-125" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-125">&#91;123&#93;</a></sup> The Italians employed the use of asphyxiating chemical weapons in their Ethiopian invasion. They regularly dropped bombs throughout Ethiopia that carried <a href="/wiki/Mustard_gas" title="Mustard gas">mustard gas</a> and debilitated the Ethiopian forces. On the whole, the Italians dropped about 300 tons of mustard gas as well as thousands of other artillery. This use of chemical weapons amounted to egregious war crimes.<sup id="cite_ref-126" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-126">&#91;124&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Following the entry of Italy into <a href="/wiki/World_War_II" title="World War II">World War II</a>, <a href="/wiki/British_Empire" title="British Empire">British Empire</a> forces, together with the <i><a href="/wiki/Arbegnoch" title="Arbegnoch">Arbegnoch</a></i> (literally, "patriots", referring to armed resistance soldiers) liberated Ethiopia in the course of the <a href="/wiki/East_African_Campaign_(World_War_II)" class="mw-redirect" title="East African Campaign (World War II)">East African Campaign</a> in 1941. An <a href="/wiki/Italian_guerrilla_war_in_Ethiopia" title="Italian guerrilla war in Ethiopia">Italian guerrilla warfare campaign</a> continued until 1943. The country was placed under <a href="/wiki/Occupied_Enemy_Territory_Administration_(Ethiopia)" title="Occupied Enemy Territory Administration (Ethiopia)">British military administration</a>. This was followed by British recognition of Ethiopia's full <a href="/wiki/Sovereignty" title="Sovereignty">sovereignty</a>, without any special British privileges, when the <a href="/wiki/Anglo-Ethiopian_Agreement" title="Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement">Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement</a> was signed in December 1944,<sup id="cite_ref-127" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-127">&#91;125&#93;</a></sup> although <a href="/wiki/Anglo-Ethiopian_Agreement#British_Ogaden" title="Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement">some regions</a> remained under British control for more years. Under the peace treaty of 1947, Italy recognized the sovereignty and independence of Ethiopia.
</p>
<h4><span id="Post-World_War_II_.281941.E2.80.931974.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Post-World_War_II_(1941–1974)">Post-World War II (1941–1974)</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=11" title="Edit section: Post-World War II (1941–1974)">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/1960_Ethiopian_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempt" class="mw-redirect" title="1960 Ethiopian coup d&#39;état attempt">1960 Ethiopian coup d'état attempt</a>, <a href="/wiki/Federation_of_Ethiopia_and_Eritrea" title="Federation of Ethiopia and Eritrea">Federation of Ethiopia and Eritrea</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Eritrean_War_of_Independence" title="Eritrean War of Independence">Eritrean War of Independence</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Emperor_Haile_Selassie_I_with_President_FDR.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Emperor_Haile_Selassie_I_with_President_FDR.jpg/220px-Emperor_Haile_Selassie_I_with_President_FDR.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="174" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Emperor_Haile_Selassie_I_with_President_FDR.jpg/330px-Emperor_Haile_Selassie_I_with_President_FDR.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Emperor_Haile_Selassie_I_with_President_FDR.jpg/440px-Emperor_Haile_Selassie_I_with_President_FDR.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1200" data-file-height="951" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Haile_Selassie" title="Haile Selassie">Emperor Haile Selassie I</a> with U.S. <a href="/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt" title="Franklin D. Roosevelt">President Franklin Delano Roosevelt</a> on February 13, 1945, in Egypt inside a <a href="/wiki/USS_Quincy_(CA-71)" title="USS Quincy (CA-71)">U.S Navy Battleship.</a> Which in addition hosted <a href="/wiki/Farouk_of_Egypt" title="Farouk of Egypt">King Farouk of Egypt</a>, and the King of <a href="/wiki/Saudi_Arabia" title="Saudi Arabia">Saudi Arabia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ibn_Saud" title="Ibn Saud">Abdul Aziz al-Saud</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>On 24 October 1945, Ethiopia became a founding member of the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations" title="United Nations">United Nations</a>. Ethiopia participated in the <a href="/wiki/Korean_War" title="Korean War">Korean War</a> as part of combined forces of the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_Command" title="United Nations Command">United Nations Command</a>. The <a href="/wiki/Kagnew_Battalion" title="Kagnew Battalion">Kagnew Battalion</a> saw action in fewer significant battles, including the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Pork_Chop_Hill" title="Battle of Pork Chop Hill">Battle of Pork Chop Hill</a>. In 1952, Haile Selassie orchestrated a <a href="/wiki/Federation_of_Ethiopia_and_Eritrea" title="Federation of Ethiopia and Eritrea">federation with Eritrea</a>. He dissolved this in 1962 and <a href="/wiki/Annexation" title="Annexation">annexed</a> Eritrea, resulting in the <a href="/wiki/Eritrean_War_of_Independence" title="Eritrean War of Independence">Eritrean War of Independence</a>.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (July 2023)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p>Haile Selassie was nearly deposed in a <a href="/wiki/1960_Ethiopian_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempt" class="mw-redirect" title="1960 Ethiopian coup d&#39;état attempt">1960 coup attempt</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-128" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-128">&#91;126&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Clapham-497_129-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Clapham-497-129">&#91;127&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-130" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-130">&#91;128&#93;</a></sup> The coup considered one of serious threat to Haile Selassie until 1974 <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Revolution" title="Ethiopian Revolution">Ethiopian Revolution</a>. In 1963, Haile Selassie played a leading role in the formation of the <a href="/wiki/Organisation_of_African_Unity" title="Organisation of African Unity">Organisation of African Unity</a> (OAU).<sup id="cite_ref-131" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-131">&#91;129&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Opinion within Ethiopia turned against Haile Selassie, owing to the worldwide <a href="/wiki/1973_oil_crisis" title="1973 oil crisis">1973 oil crisis</a> causing a sharp increase in gasoline prices starting on 13 February 1974. Students and workers in Addis Ababa began demonstrating against the government on 20 February 1974.<sup id="cite_ref-132" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-132">&#91;130&#93;</a></sup> There were resulting food shortages, uncertainty regarding the succession, border wars, and discontent in the middle class created through modernization.<sup id="cite_ref-Black_Book2_133-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Black_Book2-133">&#91;131&#93;</a></sup> The feudal oligarchical cabinet of <a href="/wiki/Aklilu_Habte-Wold" title="Aklilu Habte-Wold">Aklilu Habte-Wold</a> was toppled, and a new government was formed with <a href="/wiki/Endelkachew_Makonnen" title="Endelkachew Makonnen">Endelkachew Makonnen</a> serving as Prime Minister.<sup id="cite_ref-134" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-134">&#91;132&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="The_Derg_era_.281974.E2.80.931991.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="The_Derg_era_(1974–1991)">The Derg era (1974–1991)</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=12" title="Edit section: The Derg era (1974–1991)">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Revolution" title="Ethiopian Revolution">Ethiopian Revolution</a>, <a href="/wiki/Derg" title="Derg">Derg</a>, <a href="/wiki/People%27s_Democratic_Republic_of_Ethiopia" title="People&#39;s Democratic Republic of Ethiopia">People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Civil_War" title="Ethiopian Civil War">Ethiopian Civil War</a>, <a href="/wiki/Eritrean_War_of_Independence" title="Eritrean War of Independence">Eritrean War of Independence</a>, and <a href="/wiki/1983%E2%80%9385_famine_in_Ethiopia" class="mw-redirect" title="1983–85 famine in Ethiopia">1983–85 famine in Ethiopia</a></div>
<p>Haile Selassie's rule ended on 12 September 1974, when he was <a href="/wiki/1974_Ethiopian_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat" title="1974 Ethiopian coup d&#39;état">deposed</a> by the <a href="/wiki/Derg" title="Derg">Derg</a>, a non-ideological committee made up of military and police officers led by <a href="/wiki/Aman_Andom" title="Aman Andom">Aman Andom</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-135" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-135">&#91;133&#93;</a></sup> After the execution of <a href="/wiki/Massacre_of_the_Sixty" title="Massacre of the Sixty">60 former government and military officials</a> including Aman in November 1974,<sup id="cite_ref-136" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-136">&#91;134&#93;</a></sup> the new <a href="/wiki/Provisional_Military_Administrative_Council" class="mw-redirect" title="Provisional Military Administrative Council">Provisional Military Administrative Council</a> abolished the monarchy in March 1975 and established Ethiopia as a <a href="/wiki/Marxist-Leninist_state" class="mw-redirect" title="Marxist-Leninist state">Marxist-Leninist state</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-137" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-137">&#91;135&#93;</a></sup> The abolition of <a href="/wiki/Feudalism" title="Feudalism">feudalism</a>, increased <a href="/wiki/Literacy" title="Literacy">literacy</a>, <a href="/wiki/Nationalization" title="Nationalization">nationalization</a>, and sweeping <a href="/wiki/Land_reform" title="Land reform">land reform</a> including the <a href="/wiki/Resettlement_and_villagization_in_Ethiopia" title="Resettlement and villagization in Ethiopia">resettlement and villagization</a> from the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Highlands" title="Ethiopian Highlands">Ethiopian Highlands</a> became priorities.<sup id="cite_ref-138" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-138">&#91;136&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Derg.gif" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Derg.gif/220px-Derg.gif" decoding="async" width="220" height="150" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Derg.gif/330px-Derg.gif 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/53/Derg.gif 2x" data-file-width="400" data-file-height="273" /></a><figcaption>Ethiopian leader <a href="/wiki/Mengistu_Haile_Mariam" title="Mengistu Haile Mariam">Mengistu Haile Mariam</a> (left) with fellow Derg members <a href="/wiki/Tafari_Benti" title="Tafari Benti">Tafari Benti</a> (middle) and <a href="/wiki/Atnafu_Abate" title="Atnafu Abate">Atnafu Abate</a> (right). Mengistu was sentenced to death in Ethiopia for <a href="/wiki/Red_Terror_(Ethiopia)" title="Red Terror (Ethiopia)">crimes</a> committed during his government, which killed up to 500,000 people;<sup id="cite_ref-BBC_139-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC-139">&#91;137&#93;</a></sup> he lived in exile in Zimbabwe as of 2018.</figcaption></figure>
<p>After internal conflicts that resulted in the execution of <a href="/wiki/Tafari_Benti" title="Tafari Benti">Tafari Benti</a> and <a href="/wiki/Atnafu_Abate" title="Atnafu Abate">Atnafu Abate</a> in 1977, <a href="/wiki/Mengistu_Haile_Mariam" title="Mengistu Haile Mariam">Mengistu Halie Mariam</a> gained undisputed leadership of the Derg.<sup id="cite_ref-140" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-140">&#91;138&#93;</a></sup> The Derg suffered several coups, uprisings, wide-scale drought, and a huge refugee problem. In 1977, Somalia, which had previously been receiving assistance and arms from the <a href="/wiki/USSR" class="mw-redirect" title="USSR">USSR</a>, invaded Ethiopia in the <a href="/wiki/Ogaden_War" title="Ogaden War">Ogaden War</a>, capturing part of the <a href="/wiki/Ogaden" title="Ogaden">Ogaden</a> region.
