Ethiopia recovered it after it began receiving massive military aid from the Soviet bloc countries of the USSR, <a href="/wiki/Cuba" title="Cuba">Cuba</a>, <a href="/wiki/South_Yemen" title="South Yemen">South Yemen</a>, <a href="/wiki/East_Germany" title="East Germany">East Germany</a>, and <a href="/wiki/North_Korea" title="North Korea">North Korea</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-141" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-141">&#91;139&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-142" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-142">&#91;140&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-143" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-143">&#91;141&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1976–78, up to 500,000 were killed as a result of the <a href="/wiki/Red_Terror_(Ethiopia)" title="Red Terror (Ethiopia)">Red Terror</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-BBC_139-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC-139">&#91;137&#93;</a></sup> a violent <a href="/wiki/Political_repression" title="Political repression">political repression</a> campaign by the Derg against various opposition groups, most notably the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_People%27s_Revolutionary_Party" title="Ethiopian People&#39;s Revolutionary Party">Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Party</a> (EPRP).<sup id="cite_ref-Black_Book2_133-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Black_Book2-133">&#91;131&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-144" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-144">&#91;142&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-145" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-145">&#91;143&#93;</a></sup> In 1987, the Derg dissolved itself and established the <a href="/wiki/People%27s_Democratic_Republic_of_Ethiopia" title="People&#39;s Democratic Republic of Ethiopia">People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia</a> (PDRE) upon the adoption of the <a href="/wiki/1987_Constitution_of_Ethiopia" title="1987 Constitution of Ethiopia">1987 Constitution of Ethiopia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-146" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-146">&#91;144&#93;</a></sup> A <a href="/wiki/1983%E2%80%931985_famine_in_Ethiopia" title="1983–1985 famine in Ethiopia">1983–85 famine</a> affected around 8 million people, resulting in 1 million dead. Insurrections against <a href="/wiki/Authoritarianism" title="Authoritarianism">authoritarian</a> rule sprang up, particularly in the northern regions of Eritrea and Tigray. The <a href="/wiki/Tigray_People%27s_Liberation_Front" title="Tigray People&#39;s Liberation Front">Tigray People's Liberation Front</a> (TPLF) merged with other ethnically based opposition movements in 1989, to form the coalition known as the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_People%27s_Revolutionary_Democratic_Front" title="Ethiopian People&#39;s Revolutionary Democratic Front">Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front</a> (EPRDF).<sup id="cite_ref-147" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-147">&#91;145&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The collapse of Marxism–Leninism in general, and in <a href="/wiki/Eastern_Europe" title="Eastern Europe">Eastern Europe</a> during the <a href="/wiki/Revolutions_of_1989" title="Revolutions of 1989">revolutions of 1989</a>, coincided with the Soviet Union stopping aid to Ethiopia altogether in 1990. To garner international support Mengistu embraced a <a href="/wiki/Mixed_economy" title="Mixed economy">mixed economy</a> and an end to one party rule but it was too late to save his regime.<sup id="cite_ref-148" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-148">&#91;146&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-149" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-149">&#91;147&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-150" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-150">&#91;148&#93;</a></sup> EPRDF forces advanced on Addis Ababa in May 1991, and Mengistu fled the country and was granted asylum in Zimbabwe, where he still resides.<sup id="cite_ref-151" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-151">&#91;149&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-152" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-152">&#91;150&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Federal_Democratic_Republic_.281991.E2.80.93present.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Federal_Democratic_Republic_(1991–present)"><span id="AnchorFederal">Federal Democratic Republic (1991–present)</span></span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=13" title="Edit section: Federal Democratic Republic (1991–present)">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia_under_federal_republic" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethiopia under federal republic">Ethiopia under federal republic</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Eritrean_independence_referendum,_1993" class="mw-redirect" title="Eritrean independence referendum, 1993">Eritrean independence referendum, 1993</a></div>
<h4><span id="EPRDF_leadership_.281991.E2.80.932018.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="EPRDF_leadership_(1991–2018)">EPRDF leadership <span id="AnchorFederal">(1991–2018)</span></span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=14" title="Edit section: EPRDF leadership (1991–2018)">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:P092409PS-0663_(3993804373).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/P092409PS-0663_%283993804373%29.jpg/220px-P092409PS-0663_%283993804373%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/P092409PS-0663_%283993804373%29.jpg/330px-P092409PS-0663_%283993804373%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/P092409PS-0663_%283993804373%29.jpg/440px-P092409PS-0663_%283993804373%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3500" data-file-height="2333" /></a><figcaption>Late Former Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Meles_Zenawi" title="Meles Zenawi">Meles Zenawi</a> meeting with then US President <a href="/wiki/Barack_Obama" title="Barack Obama">Barack Obama</a> in 2009</figcaption></figure>
<p>In July 1991, the EPRDF convened a National Conference to establish the <a href="/wiki/Transitional_Government_of_Ethiopia" title="Transitional Government of Ethiopia">Transitional Government of Ethiopia</a> composed of an 87-member Council of Representatives and guided by a national charter that functioned as a transitional constitution.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELyons1996121–23_153-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELyons1996121–23-153">&#91;151&#93;</a></sup> In 1994, a new constitution was written that established a parliamentary republic with a bicameral legislature and a judicial system.<sup id="cite_ref-Constitution2_154-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Constitution2-154">&#91;152&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_general_election,_1995" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethiopian general election, 1995">first multiparty election</a> took place in May 1995, which was won by the EPRDF.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELyons1996142_155-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELyons1996142-155">&#91;153&#93;</a></sup> The president of the transitional government, EPRDF leader <a href="/wiki/Meles_Zenawi" title="Meles Zenawi">Meles Zenawi</a>, became the first <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Ethiopia" title="Prime Minister of Ethiopia">Prime Minister</a> of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, and <a href="/wiki/Negasso_Gidada" title="Negasso Gidada">Negasso Gidada</a> was elected its president.<sup id="cite_ref-156" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-156">&#91;154&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In April 1993, <a href="/wiki/Eritrea" title="Eritrea">Eritrea</a> gained independence from Ethiopia after a <a href="/wiki/1993_Eritrean_independence_referendum" title="1993 Eritrean independence referendum">national referendum</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-157" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-157">&#91;155&#93;</a></sup> In May 1998, a border dispute with Eritrea led to the <a href="/wiki/Eritrean%E2%80%93Ethiopian_War" title="Eritrean–Ethiopian War">Eritrean–Ethiopian War</a>, which lasted until June 2000 and cost both countries an estimated $1&#160;million a day.<sup id="cite_ref-158" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-158">&#91;156&#93;</a></sup> This had a negative effect on Ethiopia's economy.<sup id="cite_ref-159" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-159">&#91;157&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Meles died on 20 August 2012 in Brussels, where he was being treated for an unspecified illness.<sup id="cite_ref-160" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-160">&#91;158&#93;</a></sup> Deputy Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Hailemariam_Desalegn" title="Hailemariam Desalegn">Hailemariam Desalegn</a> was appointed as a new prime minister until the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_general_election,_2015" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethiopian general election, 2015">2015 elections</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-161" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-161">&#91;159&#93;</a></sup> and remained so afterwards with his party in control of every parliamentary seat.<sup id="cite_ref-AJE_HD_holds_162-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AJE_HD_holds-162">&#91;160&#93;</a></sup> On 15 February 2018, Hailemariam <a href="/wiki/Resignation_of_Hailemariam_Desalegn" title="Resignation of Hailemariam Desalegn">resigned</a> as Prime Minister, following <a href="/wiki/2014%E2%80%932016_Oromo_protests" title="2014–2016 Oromo protests">years of protests</a> and a <a href="/wiki/2016%E2%80%932018_Ethiopian_state_of_emergency" title="2016–2018 Ethiopian state of emergency">state of emergency</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Reuters1_163-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Reuters1-163">&#91;161&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-164" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-164">&#91;162&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-165" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-165">&#91;163&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span id="Abiy_Ahmed_and_the_Prosperity_Party_.282018.E2.80.93present.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Abiy_Ahmed_and_the_Prosperity_Party_(2018–present)">Abiy Ahmed and the Prosperity Party (2018–present)</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=15" title="Edit section: Abiy Ahmed and the Prosperity Party (2018–present)">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h4>
<p><span class="anchor" id="Government_reforms_(2018–present)"></span>
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_civil_conflict_(2018%E2%80%93present)" title="Ethiopian civil conflict (2018–present)">Ethiopian civil conflict</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tigray_War" title="Tigray War">Tigray War</a>, and <a href="/wiki/War_in_Amhara" title="War in Amhara">War in Amhara</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Abiy_Ahmed_receiving_the_Nobel_Peace_Prize_in_Oslo_2019.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Abiy_Ahmed_receiving_the_Nobel_Peace_Prize_in_Oslo_2019.jpg/220px-Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Abiy_Ahmed_receiving_the_Nobel_Peace_Prize_in_Oslo_2019.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Abiy_Ahmed_receiving_the_Nobel_Peace_Prize_in_Oslo_2019.jpg/330px-Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Abiy_Ahmed_receiving_the_Nobel_Peace_Prize_in_Oslo_2019.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Abiy_Ahmed_receiving_the_Nobel_Peace_Prize_in_Oslo_2019.jpg/440px-Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Abiy_Ahmed_receiving_the_Nobel_Peace_Prize_in_Oslo_2019.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5472" data-file-height="3648" /></a><figcaption>Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Abiy_Ahmed" title="Abiy Ahmed">Abiy Ahmed</a> receiving the <a href="/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize" title="Nobel Peace Prize">Nobel Peace Prize</a> in Oslo in 2019</figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="/wiki/Abiy_Ahmed" title="Abiy Ahmed">Abiy Ahmed</a> became prime minister following Hailemariam's resignation. He made a <a href="/wiki/2018_Eritrea%E2%80%93Ethiopia_summit" title="2018 Eritrea–Ethiopia summit">historic visit to Eritrea in 2018</a>, ending the <a href="/wiki/Eritrean%E2%80%93Ethiopian_border_conflict" title="Eritrean–Ethiopian border conflict">state of conflict between the two countries</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-166" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-166">&#91;164&#93;</a></sup> and was awarded the Nobel prize for peace in 2019.<sup id="cite_ref-167" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-167">&#91;165&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Human_rights_in_Ethiopia#Ethnic_violence" title="Human rights in Ethiopia">Ethnic violence rose</a> during the late 2010s and early 2020s,<sup id="cite_ref-168" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-168">&#91;166&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-169" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-169">&#91;167&#93;</a></sup> with various clashes and conflicts leading to millions of Ethiopians being displaced.<sup id="cite_ref-irinnews_170-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-irinnews-170">&#91;168&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-171" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-171">&#91;169&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-172" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-172">&#91;170&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The federal government that elections for election in 2020 (later being <a href="/wiki/2021_Ethiopian_general_election" title="2021 Ethiopian general election">rescheduled to 2021</a>) be cancelled, due to health and safety concerns about <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Ethiopia" title="COVID-19 pandemic in Ethiopia">COVID-19</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-173" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-173">&#91;171&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Tigray_Region" title="Tigray Region">Tigray Region</a>'s TPLF opposed this, and <a href="/wiki/2020_Tigray_regional_election" title="2020 Tigray regional election">proceeded to hold elections</a> anyway on 9 September 2020.<sup id="cite_ref-174" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-174">&#91;172&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-175" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-175">&#91;173&#93;</a></sup> Relations between the federal government and Tigray deteriorated rapidly,<sup id="cite_ref-176" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-176">&#91;174&#93;</a></sup> and on 4 November 2020, Ethiopia began a military offensive in Tigray in response to <a href="/wiki/Northern_Command_attacks_(Ethiopia)" title="Northern Command attacks (Ethiopia)">attacks on army units stationed</a> there, marking the beginning of the <a href="/wiki/Tigray_War" title="Tigray War">Tigray War</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-177" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-177">&#91;175&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-178" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-178">&#91;176&#93;</a></sup> By March 2022, as many as 500,000 people had died as a result of <a href="/wiki/War_crimes_in_the_Tigray_War" title="War crimes in the Tigray War">violence</a> and <a href="/wiki/Famine_in_northern_Ethiopia_(2020%E2%80%93present)" title="Famine in northern Ethiopia (2020–present)">famine</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-179" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-179">&#91;177&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-180" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-180">&#91;178&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-181" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-181">&#91;179&#93;</a></sup> After a number of <a href="/wiki/Tigrayan_peace_process" title="Tigrayan peace process">peace and mediation proposals</a> in the intervening years, Ethiopia and the Tigrayan rebel forces agreed to a <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia%E2%80%93Tigray_peace_agreement" title="Ethiopia–Tigray peace agreement">cessation of hostilities on 2 November 2022</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-182" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-182">&#91;180&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>By April 2023, <a href="/wiki/War_in_Amhara" title="War in Amhara">War in Amhara</a> began in the Amhara region of Ethiopia between the ENDF and Fano militia. 
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Government_and_politics">Government and politics</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=16" title="Edit section: Government and politics">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Politics_of_Ethiopia" title="Politics of Ethiopia">Politics of Ethiopia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Law_of_Ethiopia" title="Law of Ethiopia">Law of Ethiopia</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Judiciary_of_Ethiopia" title="Judiciary of Ethiopia">Judiciary of Ethiopia</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Rulers_and_Heads_of_State_of_Ethiopia" class="mw-redirect" title="Rulers and Heads of State of Ethiopia">Rulers and Heads of State of Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ethiopian_Parliament.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Ethiopian_Parliament.jpg/220px-Ethiopian_Parliament.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="124" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Ethiopian_Parliament.jpg/330px-Ethiopian_Parliament.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Ethiopian_Parliament.jpg/440px-Ethiopian_Parliament.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1280" data-file-height="720" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/House_of_People%27s_Representatives" class="mw-redirect" title="House of People&#39;s Representatives">House of People's Representatives</a> is the lower house of the Ethiopian <a href="/wiki/Federal_Parliamentary_Assembly" title="Federal Parliamentary Assembly">Federal Parliamentary Assembly</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Ethiopia is a <a href="/wiki/Federalism" title="Federalism">federal</a> <a href="/wiki/Parliamentary_republic" title="Parliamentary republic">parliamentary republic</a>, wherein the <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Ethiopia" title="Prime Minister of Ethiopia">Prime Minister</a> is the <a href="/wiki/Head_of_government" title="Head of government">head of government</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/President_of_Ethiopia" title="President of Ethiopia">President</a> is the <a href="/wiki/Head_of_state" title="Head of state">head of state</a> but with largely ceremonial powers. <a href="/wiki/Executive_power" class="mw-redirect" title="Executive power">Executive power</a> is exercised by the government and federal <a href="/wiki/Legislative_power" class="mw-redirect" title="Legislative power">legislative power</a> vested in both the government and the two chambers of parliament. The <a href="/wiki/House_of_Federation" title="House of Federation">House of Federation</a> is the upper chamber of the bicameral legislature with 108 seats, and the lower chamber is the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Peoples%27_Representatives" title="House of Peoples&#39; Representatives">House of Peoples' Representatives</a> (HoPR) with 547 seats. The House of Federation is chosen by the regional councils whereas MPs of the HoPR are elected directly, in turn, they elect the president for a six-year term and the prime minister for a 5-year term.
</p><p>The Ethiopian <a href="/wiki/Judiciary_of_Ethiopia" title="Judiciary of Ethiopia">judiciary</a> consists of dual system with two court structures: the federal and state courts. The FDRE Constitution vested federal judicial authority to the <a href="/wiki/Federal_Supreme_Court_of_Ethiopia" title="Federal Supreme Court of Ethiopia">Federal Supreme Court</a> which can overturn and review decisions of subordinate federal courts; itself has regular division assigned for fundamental <a href="/wiki/Error_(law)" title="Error (law)">errors of law</a>. In addition, the Supreme Court can perform <a href="/wiki/Circuit_court" title="Circuit court">circuit hearings</a> in established five states at any states of federal levels or "area designated for its jurisdiction" if deemed "necessary for the efficient rendering of justice".<sup id="cite_ref-183" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-183">&#91;181&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-184" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-184">&#91;182&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Federal Supreme Proclamation granted three subject matter principles: laws, parties and place to federal court jurisdiction, first "cases arising under the <a href="/wiki/1995_Constitution_of_Ethiopia" title="1995 Constitution of Ethiopia">Constitution</a>, <a href="/wiki/Federal_law" title="Federal law">federal laws</a> and <a href="/wiki/International_treaties" class="mw-redirect" title="International treaties">international treaties</a>", second over "parties specified by federal laws".<sup id="cite_ref-185" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-185">&#91;183&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On the basis of Article 78 of the 1994 Ethiopian Constitution, the judiciary is completely independent of the executive and the legislature.<sup id="cite_ref-186" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-186">&#91;184&#93;</a></sup> To ensure this, the vice-president and President of the Supreme Court appointed by Parliament on the nomination of Prime Minister. Once elected, the executive power has no authority to remove from office. Other judges are nominated by the <a href="/wiki/Federal_Judicial_Administration_Council" title="Federal Judicial Administration Council">Federal Judicial Administration Council</a> (FJAC) on the basis of transparent criteria and the Prime Minister's recommendation for appointment in the HoPR. In all cases, judges cannot be removed from their duty unless they retired, violated disciplinary rules, gross incompatibility, or inefficiency to unfit due to ill health. Contrary, the majority vote of HoPR have the right to sanction removal in federal judiciary level or state council in cases of state judges.<sup id="cite_ref-:7_187-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:7-187">&#91;185&#93;</a></sup> In 2015, the realities of this provision were questioned in a report prepared by <a href="/wiki/Freedom_House" title="Freedom House">Freedom House</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-188" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-188">&#91;186&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>According to the <a href="/wiki/Democracy_Index" class="mw-redirect" title="Democracy Index">Democracy Index</a> published by the United Kingdom-based <a href="/wiki/Economist_Intelligence_Unit" title="Economist Intelligence Unit">Economist Intelligence Unit</a> in late 2010, Ethiopia was an "authoritarian regime", ranking as the 118th-most democratic out of 167 countries.<sup id="cite_ref-189" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-189">&#91;187&#93;</a></sup> Ethiopia had dropped 13 places on the list since 2008, and the 2010 report attributed the drop to the government's crackdown on opposition activities, media, and civil society before the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_general_election,_2010" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethiopian general election, 2010">2010 parliamentary election</a>, which the report argued had made Ethiopia a <a href="/wiki/Dominant-party_system" title="Dominant-party system"><i>de facto</i> one-party state</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-190" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-190">&#91;188&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Governance">Governance</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=17" title="Edit section: Governance">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Government_of_Ethiopia" title="Government of Ethiopia">Government of Ethiopia</a></div>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti">.mw-parser-output .tmulti .multiimageinner{display:flex;flex-direction:column}.mw-parser-output .tmulti Zewde</a></div></div></div></div></div>
<p>In post-1995 regime, Ethiopia's politics has been liberalized which promotes all-encompassing reforms to the country. Today, its economy is based on <a href="/wiki/Mixed_economy" title="Mixed economy">mixed</a>, <a href="/wiki/Market_economy" title="Market economy">market-oriented</a> principles.<sup id="cite_ref-:7_187-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:7-187">&#91;185&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The first <a href="/wiki/1994_Ethiopian_Constituent_Assembly_election" title="1994 Ethiopian Constituent Assembly election">election</a> of 547-member constituent assembly was held in June 1994. This assembly adopted the <a href="/wiki/Constitution_of_Ethiopia" class="mw-redirect" title="Constitution of Ethiopia">constitution of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia</a> in December 1994. The elections for Ethiopia's first popularly chosen national parliament and regional legislatures were held in May and June 1995. Most opposition parties chose to boycott these elections. There was a landslide victory for the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_People%27s_Revolutionary_Democratic_Front" title="Ethiopian People&#39;s Revolutionary Democratic Front">Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front</a> (EPRDF). International and non-governmental observers concluded that opposition parties would have been able to participate had they chosen to do so.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2020)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> The first government of Ethiopia under the new constitution was installed in August 1995 with <a href="/wiki/Negasso_Gidada" title="Negasso Gidada">Negasso Gidada</a> as president. The EPRDF-led government of Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Meles_Zenawi" title="Meles Zenawi">Meles Zenawi</a> promoted a policy of <a href="/wiki/Ethnic_federalism" title="Ethnic federalism">ethnic federalism</a>, devolving significant powers to regional, ethnically based authorities. Ethiopia today has eleven semi-autonomous administrative regions that have the power to raise and spend their own revenues. Under past governments, some fundamental freedoms, including <a href="/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press" title="Freedom of the press">freedom of the press</a>, were circumscribed.<sup id="cite_ref-FH_Ethiopia_191-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FH_Ethiopia-191">&#91;189&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Citizens had little access to media other than the state-owned networks, and most private newspapers struggled to remain open and suffered periodic harassment from the government.<sup id="cite_ref-FH_Ethiopia_191-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FH_Ethiopia-191">&#91;189&#93;</a></sup> Starting from the 2005 elections, at least 18 journalists who had written articles critical of the government, were arrested on genocide and treason charges. The government used press laws governing libel to intimidate journalists who were critical of its policies.<sup id="cite_ref-HRW_Ethiopia_192-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-HRW_Ethiopia-192">&#91;190&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Meles' government was elected in 2000 in the first-ever multiparty elections; however, the results were heavily criticized by international observers and denounced by the opposition as fraudulent. The EPRDF also won the 2005 election returning Meles to power. Although the opposition vote increased in the election, both the opposition and observers from the European Union and elsewhere stated that the vote did not meet international standards for fair and free elections.<sup id="cite_ref-FH_Ethiopia_191-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FH_Ethiopia-191">&#91;189&#93;</a></sup> Ethiopian police are said to have massacred 193 protesters, mostly in the capital <a href="/wiki/Addis_Ababa" title="Addis Ababa">Addis Ababa</a>, in the violence following the May 2005 elections in the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_police_massacre" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethiopian police massacre">Ethiopian police massacre</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-193" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-193">&#91;191&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Israeli_PM_with_Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Ahmed.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/Israeli_PM_with_Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Ahmed.jpg/220px-Israeli_PM_with_Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Ahmed.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="138" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/Israeli_PM_with_Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Ahmed.jpg/330px-Israeli_PM_with_Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Ahmed.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/Israeli_PM_with_Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Ahmed.jpg/440px-Israeli_PM_with_Ethiopian_Prime_Minister_Ahmed.jpg 2x" data-file-width="640" data-file-height="400" /></a><figcaption>Ethiopian Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Abiy_Ahmed" title="Abiy Ahmed">Ali</a> with Israeli Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Benjamin_Netanyahu" title="Benjamin Netanyahu">Netanyahu</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>The government initiated a crackdown in the provinces as well; in Oromia Region, the authorities used concerns over insurgency and terrorism to use torture, imprisonment, and other repressive methods to silence critics following the election, particularly people sympathetic to the registered opposition party <a href="/wiki/Oromo_National_Congress" class="mw-redirect" title="Oromo National Congress">Oromo National Congress</a> (ONC).<sup id="cite_ref-HRW_Ethiopia_192-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-HRW_Ethiopia-192">&#91;190&#93;</a></sup> The government has been engaged in a conflict with rebels in the <a href="/wiki/Ogaden" title="Ogaden">Ogaden</a> region since 2007. The biggest opposition party in 2005 was the <a href="/wiki/Coalition_for_Unity_and_Democracy" title="Coalition for Unity and Democracy">Coalition for Unity and Democracy</a> (CUD). After various internal divisions, most of the CUD party leaders have established the new <a href="/wiki/Unity_for_Democracy_and_Justice" title="Unity for Democracy and Justice">Unity for Democracy and Justice</a> party led by Judge <a href="/wiki/Birtukan_Mideksa" title="Birtukan Mideksa">Birtukan Mideksa</a>. A member of the country's <a href="/wiki/Oromo_people" title="Oromo people">Oromo</a> ethnic group, Birtukan Mideksa is the first woman to lead a political party in Ethiopia.
</p><p>In 2008, the top five opposition parties were the Unity for Democracy and Justice led by Judge Birtukan Mideksa, <a href="/wiki/United_Ethiopian_Democratic_Forces" title="United Ethiopian Democratic Forces">United Ethiopian Democratic Forces</a> led by <a href="/wiki/Beyene_Petros" title="Beyene Petros">Beyene Petros</a>, <a href="/wiki/Oromo_Federalist_Democratic_Movement" title="Oromo Federalist Democratic Movement">Oromo Federalist Democratic Movement</a> led by <a href="/wiki/Bulcha_Demeksa" title="Bulcha Demeksa">Bulcha Demeksa</a>, <a href="/wiki/Oromo_People%27s_Congress" title="Oromo People&#39;s Congress">Oromo People's Congress</a> led by <a href="/wiki/Merera_Gudina" title="Merera Gudina">Merera Gudina</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Democratic_Party" title="Ethiopian Democratic Party">United Ethiopian Democratic Party – Medhin Party</a> led by <a href="/wiki/Lidetu_Ayalew" title="Lidetu Ayalew">Lidetu Ayalew</a>.  After the 2015 elections, Ethiopia lost its single remaining opposition MP;<sup id="cite_ref-AJE_opposition_194-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AJE_opposition-194">&#91;192&#93;</a></sup> by 2015 there were no opposition MPs in the Ethiopian parliament.<sup id="cite_ref-BBC_Obama_trip_195-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC_Obama_trip-195">&#91;193&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Foreign_relations">Foreign relations</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=18" title="Edit section: Foreign relations">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Foreign_relations_of_Ethiopia" title="Foreign relations of Ethiopia">Foreign relations of Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:A_Group_photo_of_Leaders_of_G-8,_Outreach_five_countries_and_Africa_Outreach_countries_at_G_8_Summit_in_Heiligendamm,_Germany_on_June_08,_2007.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/A_Group_photo_of_Leaders_of_G-8%2C_Outreach_five_countries_and_Africa_Outreach_countries_at_G_8_Summit_in_Heiligendamm%2C_Germany_on_June_08%2C_2007.jpg/220px-A_Group_photo_of_Leaders_of_G-8%2C_Outreach_five_countries_and_Africa_Outreach_countries_at_G_8_Summit_in_Heiligendamm%2C_Germany_on_June_08%2C_2007.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="136" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/A_Group_photo_of_Leaders_of_G-8%2C_Outreach_five_countries_and_Africa_Outreach_countries_at_G_8_Summit_in_Heiligendamm%2C_Germany_on_June_08%2C_2007.jpg/330px-A_Group_photo_of_Leaders_of_G-8%2C_Outreach_five_countries_and_Africa_Outreach_countries_at_G_8_Summit_in_Heiligendamm%2C_Germany_on_June_08%2C_2007.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/A_Group_photo_of_Leaders_of_G-8%2C_Outreach_five_countries_and_Africa_Outreach_countries_at_G_8_Summit_in_Heiligendamm%2C_Germany_on_June_08%2C_2007.jpg/440px-A_Group_photo_of_Leaders_of_G-8%2C_Outreach_five_countries_and_Africa_Outreach_countries_at_G_8_Summit_in_Heiligendamm%2C_Germany_on_June_08%2C_2007.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2200" data-file-height="1359" /></a><figcaption>Ethiopian <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Ethiopia" title="Prime Minister of Ethiopia">Prime Minister</a> <a href="/wiki/Meles_Zenawi" title="Meles Zenawi">Meles Zenawi</a> in G8 Group meeting in 2007</figcaption></figure>
<p>Ethiopia was historically a <a href="/wiki/Trading_nation" title="Trading nation">trading nation</a> that exported goods such as <a href="/wiki/Gold" title="Gold">gold</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ivory" title="Ivory">ivory</a>, exotic animals, and <a href="/wiki/Incense" title="Incense">incense</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-196" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-196">&#91;194&#93;</a></sup> Many historians<sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions" title="Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch"><span title="The material near this tag possibly uses too-vague attribution or weasel words. (August 2023)">who?</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> have concluded that modern Ethiopian foreign relations began under <a href="/wiki/Tewodros_II" title="Tewodros II">Emperor Tewodros II</a>, who during his reign sought to re-establish a cohesive Ethiopian state, but was thwarted by the <a href="/wiki/1868_Expedition_to_Abyssinia" class="mw-redirect" title="1868 Expedition to Abyssinia">British expedition of 1868</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-197" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-197">&#91;195&#93;</a></sup> Since then, the country was seen redundant by world powers until the opening of <a href="/wiki/Suez_Canal" title="Suez Canal">Suez Canal</a> due to an influence of <a href="/wiki/Mahdist_War" title="Mahdist War">Mahdist War</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-198" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-198">&#91;196&#93;</a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="margin-left:0.1em; white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify" title="Wikipedia:Please clarify"><span title="The text near this tag may need clarification or removal of jargon. (August 2023)">clarification needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Abiy_with_Modi_for_BRICS_Summit.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Abiy_with_Modi_for_BRICS_Summit.jpg/180px-Abiy_with_Modi_for_BRICS_Summit.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="169" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Abiy_with_Modi_for_BRICS_Summit.jpg/270px-Abiy_with_Modi_for_BRICS_Summit.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Abiy_with_Modi_for_BRICS_Summit.jpg/360px-Abiy_with_Modi_for_BRICS_Summit.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2200" data-file-height="2062" /></a><figcaption>Ethiopian Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Abiy_Ahmed" title="Abiy Ahmed">Abiy Ahmed</a> with Indian Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Narendra_Modi" title="Narendra Modi">Narendra Modi</a> in South Africa for <a href="/wiki/BRICS" title="BRICS">BRICS</a> summit, which accepted 5 new member states including Ethiopia into the BRICS alliance</figcaption></figure>
<p>Today, Ethiopia maintains strong relations with <a href="/wiki/China%E2%80%93Ethiopia_relations" title="China–Ethiopia relations">China</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia%E2%80%93Israel_relations" title="Ethiopia–Israel relations">Israel</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia%E2%80%93Mexico_relations" title="Ethiopia–Mexico relations">Mexico</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia%E2%80%93Turkey_relations" title="Ethiopia–Turkey relations">Turkey</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia%E2%80%93India_relations" title="Ethiopia–India relations">India</a> as well as neighboring countries. Ethiopia is a strategic partner of Global <a href="/wiki/War_on_Terrorism" class="mw-redirect" title="War on Terrorism">War on Terrorism</a> and <a href="/wiki/African_Growth_and_Opportunity_Act" title="African Growth and Opportunity Act">African Growth and Opportunity Act</a> (AGOA).<sup id="cite_ref-199" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-199">&#91;197&#93;</a></sup> US. Former <a href="/wiki/President_of_the_United_States" title="President of the United States">President</a> <a href="/wiki/Barack_Obama" title="Barack Obama">Barack Obama</a> was the first incumbent US president to visit Ethiopia in July 2015; the speech he gave in <a href="/wiki/African_Union" title="African Union">African Union</a> during this trip focused on combatting Islamic terrorism.<sup id="cite_ref-200" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-200">&#91;198&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-201" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-201">&#91;199&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Emigration_from_Ethiopia" class="mw-redirect" title="Emigration from Ethiopia">Emigration from Ethiopia</a> is primarily directed towards Europe, including <a href="/wiki/Ethiopians_in_Italy" title="Ethiopians in Italy">Italy</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ethiopians_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="Ethiopians in the United Kingdom">United Kingdom</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Canadians" title="Ethiopian Canadians">Canada</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ethiopians_in_Sweden" title="Ethiopians in Sweden">Sweden</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Australians" title="Ethiopian Australians">Australia</a>, while emigration to the <a href="/wiki/Middle_East" title="Middle East">Middle East</a> is primarily to <a href="/wiki/Saudi_Arabia" title="Saudi Arabia">Saudi Arabia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Israel" title="Israel">Israel</a>. Ethiopia is founding member of the <a href="/wiki/Group_of_24" title="Group of 24">Group of 24</a> (G-24), the <a href="/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement" title="Non-Aligned Movement">Non-Aligned Movement</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Group_of_77" title="Group of 77">G77</a>. In 1963, the <a href="/wiki/Organization_of_African_Unity" class="mw-redirect" title="Organization of African Unity">Organization of African Unity</a>, which later renamed itself the African Union, was founded in Addis Ababa, which today hosts the secretariat of the African Union, the <a href="/wiki/African_Union_Commission" title="African Union Commission">African Union Commission</a>. In addition, Ethiopia is also a member of the <a href="/wiki/Pan_African_Chamber_of_Commerce_and_Industry" title="Pan African Chamber of Commerce and Industry">Pan African Chamber of Commerce and Industry</a>, the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_Economic_Commission_for_Africa" title="United Nations Economic Commission for Africa">United Nations Economic Commission for Africa</a>, the <a href="/wiki/African_Standby_Force" title="African Standby Force">African Standby Force</a> and many of  global <a href="/wiki/NGO" class="mw-redirect" title="NGO">NGOs</a> focused on Africa.
</p><p>Ethiopia's foreign relations with both <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia%E2%80%93Sudan_relations" title="Ethiopia–Sudan relations">Sudan</a> and <a href="/wiki/Egypt%E2%80%93Ethiopia_relations" title="Egypt–Ethiopia relations">Egypt</a> are somewhat fraught owing to the effects the <a href="/wiki/Grand_Ethiopian_Renaissance_Dam" title="Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam">Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam</a> project, which was escalated in 2020, would have on <a href="/wiki/Water_resources_law" title="Water resources law">water rights</a> in the region.<sup id="cite_ref-202" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-202">&#91;200&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-203" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-203">&#91;201&#93;</a></sup> Despite six upstream countries (Ethiopia, <a href="/wiki/Kenya" title="Kenya">Kenya</a>, <a href="/wiki/Uganda" title="Uganda">Uganda</a>, <a href="/wiki/Rwanda" title="Rwanda">Rwanda</a>, <a href="/wiki/Burundi" title="Burundi">Burundi</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Tanzania" title="Tanzania">Tanzania</a>) signing the Nile Basin Initiative in 2010, Egypt and Sudan rejected a water sharing treaty, citing the reduction of amount of water to the <a href="/wiki/Nile_Basin" title="Nile Basin">Nile Basin</a> and the challenge it would pose to their historic connection of <a href="/wiki/Water_rights" class="mw-redirect" title="Water rights">water rights</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-204" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-204">&#91;202&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-205" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-205">&#91;203&#93;</a></sup> In 2020, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed warned that "No force can stop Ethiopia from building a dam. If there is need to go to war, we could get millions readied."<sup id="cite_ref-206" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-206">&#91;204&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>Ethiopia is one of the African countries that as founding member of <a href="/wiki/League_of_Nations" title="League of Nations">League of Nations</a>, which served as the predecessor for the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations" title="United Nations">United Nations</a>, since 1923. UN taskforces in Ethiopia deal primarily with humanitarian issues and development. Some of its agencies<sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Avoid_weasel_words" class="mw-redirect" title="Wikipedia:Avoid weasel words"><span title="The material near this tag possibly uses too vague attribution or weasel words. (August 2023)">which?</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> maintain regional ties with <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_Economic_Commission_for_Africa" title="United Nations Economic Commission for Africa">United Nations Economic Commission for Africa</a> and the African Union. The UN prioritizes <a href="/wiki/Sustainable_development" title="Sustainable development">sustainable development</a> in Ethiopia, including fighting poverty, sustainable economic growth, climate change policy, educational and healthcare provisions, increasing employment, and environmental protection.<sup id="cite_ref-207" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-207">&#91;205&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Military">Military</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=19" title="Edit section: Military">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Military_history_of_Ethiopia" title="Military history of Ethiopia">Military history of Ethiopia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_National_Defense_Force" title="Ethiopian National Defense Force">Ethiopian National Defense Force</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:ENDF_military.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/68/ENDF_military.png/290px-ENDF_military.png" decoding="async" width="290" height="163" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/6/68/ENDF_military.png 1.5x" data-file-width="421" data-file-height="237" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_National_Defense_Force" title="Ethiopian National Defense Force">Ethiopian Defense force</a> from the Airforce, Navy, and Army seen corner to corner.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The Ethiopian army's origins and military traditions date back to the earliest <a href="/wiki/History_of_Ethiopia" title="History of Ethiopia">history of Ethiopia</a>. Due to Ethiopia's location between the Middle East and Africa, it has long been in the middle of Eastern and Western politics and has been subject to foreign invasions. In 1579, the <a href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman Empire</a>'s attempt to expand from a coastal base at <a href="/wiki/Massawa" title="Massawa">Massawa</a> during the <a href="/wiki/Ottoman_conquest_of_Habesh" title="Ottoman conquest of Habesh">Ottoman conquest of Habesh</a> was defeated.<sup id="cite_ref-208" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-208">&#91;206&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Army_of_the_Ethiopian_Empire" title="Army of the Ethiopian Empire">Army of the Ethiopian Empire</a> was also able to defeat the Egyptians in 1876 at <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Gura" title="Battle of Gura">Gura</a>, led by Ethiopian Emperor <a href="/wiki/Yohannes_IV" title="Yohannes IV">Yohannes IV</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-209" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-209">&#91;207&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Adwa" title="Battle of Adwa">Battle of Adwa</a> is the best-known victory of Ethiopian forces over foreign invaders. It maintained Ethiopia's existence as an independent state. Fought on 1 March 1896 against the <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy" title="Kingdom of Italy">Kingdom of Italy</a> near the town of <a href="/wiki/Adwa" title="Adwa">Adwa</a>, it was the decisive battle of the First Italo–Ethiopian War.
</p><p>Modernization of the Ethiopian army took place under the regency of Tafari Mekonnen, who later reigned as Emperor <a href="/wiki/Haile_Selassie_I" class="mw-redirect" title="Haile Selassie I">Haile Selassie I</a>. He created an <a href="/wiki/Imperial_Bodyguard" class="mw-redirect" title="Imperial Bodyguard">Imperial Bodyguard</a>, the <i><a href="/wiki/Kebur_Zabagna" title="Kebur Zabagna">Kebur Zabagna</a></i>, in 1917 from the earlier <i><a href="/wiki/Mahal_Safari" class="mw-redirect" title="Mahal Safari">Mahal Safari</a></i> who had traditionally attended the Ethiopian Emperor. Its elite was trained at the French <a href="/wiki/Military_academy" title="Military academy">military academy</a> at <a href="/wiki/%C3%89cole_Sp%C3%A9ciale_Militaire_de_Saint-Cyr" class="mw-redirect" title="École Spéciale Militaire de Saint-Cyr">Saint-Cyr</a>.
</p><p>The Ethiopian Army under <a href="/wiki/Kagnew_Battalion" title="Kagnew Battalion">Kagnew Battalion</a> unit involved in the <a href="/wiki/Korean_War" title="Korean War">Korean War</a> from 1950, fought as part of <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_Command" title="United Nations Command">United Nations Command</a>. Some publications stated that Ethiopian troops remained for 15 years, though other stated they left until 1975, as part of the UN Command.<sup id="cite_ref-210" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-210">&#91;208&#93;</a></sup> The battalion sized 6,037 troops at the time of the war.<sup id="cite_ref-autob_211-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-autob-211">&#91;209&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_National_Defense_Force" title="Ethiopian National Defense Force">Ethiopian National Defense Force</a> is the military force of Ethiopia. The ENDF consists of two separate branches: the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Ground_Forces" title="Ethiopian Ground Forces">Ethiopian Ground Forces</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Air_Force" title="Ethiopian Air Force">Ethiopian Air Force</a>. Since 1996, Ethiopia has lacked a navy as the country is landlocked; however, in 2018 Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed suggested on state TV that Ethiopia should expand their naval capabilities in the coming future and because of that in 2018 the Prime Minister re-established the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Navy" title="Ethiopian Navy">Navy</a> which currently is under training with a current unknown number of soldiers, it is unknown when or where the Navy will come back at full force, but efforts are being made by the government including European nations.<sup id="cite_ref-212" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-212">&#91;210&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-213" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-213">&#91;211&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Ethiopian Military is nonetheless stated to be the strongest in East Africa, and along the top five strongest militaries in the continent of Africa, and according to estimates, it is stated to be the 49th strongest in the World.<sup id="cite_ref-214" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-214">&#91;212&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-215" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-215">&#91;213&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Law_enforcement">Law enforcement</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=20" title="Edit section: Law enforcement">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Law_enforcement_in_Ethiopia" title="Law enforcement in Ethiopia">Law enforcement in Ethiopia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Crime_in_Ethiopia" title="Crime in Ethiopia">Crime in Ethiopia</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Police_brutality_in_Ethiopia" title="Police brutality in Ethiopia">Police brutality in Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Black_colored_Federal_Police_car.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/e/e9/Black_colored_Federal_Police_car.png/220px-Black_colored_Federal_Police_car.png" decoding="async" width="220" height="161" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/e/e9/Black_colored_Federal_Police_car.png/330px-Black_colored_Federal_Police_car.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/e/e9/Black_colored_Federal_Police_car.png/440px-Black_colored_Federal_Police_car.png 2x" data-file-width="1032" data-file-height="756" /></a><figcaption>An Ethiopian Federal Police car in <a href="/wiki/Addis_Ababa" title="Addis Ababa">Addis Ababa</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>The constitution guarantees law enforcement duty to the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Federal_Police" title="Ethiopian Federal Police">Ethiopian Federal Police</a> (EFP). The EFP is responsible for safeguarding and public welfare in federal level. Founded in 1995, the federal police surveyed by Federal Police Commissioner since October 2000; the Federal Police Commissioner then reports task to the <a href="/wiki/Ministry_of_Peace_(Ethiopia)" title="Ministry of Peace (Ethiopia)">Ministry of Peace</a>, however it was overrode after political reforms in 2018, and directed to the parliament. In previous years, the federal police reports the Ministry's tasks directly. In addition, the federal police have ability to disclose regional police commissions, in order for assistance. Independently, the local militias uphold security.
<sup id="cite_ref-216" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-216">&#91;214&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Nowadays, <a href="/wiki/Bribery" title="Bribery">bribery</a> is a basic concern, especially observed by traffic police. <a href="/wiki/Police_brutality_in_Ethiopia" title="Police brutality in Ethiopia">Police brutality</a> appeared as severe in recent years. On 26 August 2019, a video of handcuffed man beaten by two police officers as an elderly woman intervened the scene in Addis Ababa went viral. Recent police misconduct is said to be a failure of Federal Police Commissioner to abide Article 52 of the constitution, which states investigation of unlawful <a href="/wiki/Use_of_force" title="Use of force">use of force</a>, and dismissal of those misconducted officer. The African Union's Luanda and Robben Island Guidelines or the United Nations' Declaration on Justice for Victims of Abuse of Power and their Basic Principles on the Use of Force &amp; Firearms are once obligated to the Ethiopian government disciplinary committee to combat police brutality in both individual and systemic level.<sup id="cite_ref-217" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-217">&#91;215&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Human_rights">Human rights</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=21" title="Edit section: Human rights">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Human_rights_in_Ethiopia" title="Human rights in Ethiopia">Human rights in Ethiopia</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/War_crimes_in_the_Tigray_War" title="War crimes in the Tigray War">War crimes in the Tigray War</a></div>
<p>Human rights violations often accompany <a href="/wiki/Ethnic_discrimination_in_Ethiopia" title="Ethnic discrimination in Ethiopia">endured ethnic and communal violence in the country</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-218" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-218">&#91;216&#93;</a></sup> In a <a href="/wiki/2014%E2%80%932016_Oromo_protests" title="2014–2016 Oromo protests">2016 demonstration</a>, 100 peaceful protestors were killed by direct government gunfire in the <a href="/wiki/Oromia" title="Oromia">Oromia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Amhara_Region" title="Amhara Region">Amhara</a> regions.<sup id="cite_ref-219" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-219">&#91;217&#93;</a></sup> The UN has called for UN observers on the ground in Ethiopia to investigate this incident,<sup id="cite_ref-220" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-220">&#91;218&#93;</a></sup> however the EPRDF-dominated Ethiopian government has refused this call.<sup id="cite_ref-221" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-221">&#91;219&#93;</a></sup> The protestors are protesting land grabs and lack of basic human rights such as the freedom to elect their representatives. The TPLF-dominated EPRDF won 100% in an election marked by fraud which has resulted in Ethiopian civilians protesting on scale unseen in prior post-election protests.<sup id="cite_ref-reuters.com_222-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-reuters.com-222">&#91;220&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Merera_Gudina" title="Merera Gudina">Merera Gudina</a>, leader of the <a href="/wiki/Oromo_People%27s_Congress" title="Oromo People&#39;s Congress">Oromo People's Congress</a>, said the East African country was at a "crossroads". He added in the interview with Reuters: "People are demanding their rights", he said. "People are fed up with what the regime has been doing for a quarter of a century. They're protesting against land grabs, reparations, stolen elections, the rising cost of living, many things. "If the government continue to repress while the people are demanding their rights in the millions that (civil war) is one of the likely scenarios."<sup id="cite_ref-reuters.com_222-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-reuters.com-222">&#91;220&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Stop_-TigrayGenocide-_Columbus,_OH_(12.09.21)_IMG_9395_(51736661603).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Stop_-TigrayGenocide-_Columbus%2C_OH_%2812.09.21%29_IMG_9395_%2851736661603%29.jpg/220px-Stop_-TigrayGenocide-_Columbus%2C_OH_%2812.09.21%29_IMG_9395_%2851736661603%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Stop_-TigrayGenocide-_Columbus%2C_OH_%2812.09.21%29_IMG_9395_%2851736661603%29.jpg/330px-Stop_-TigrayGenocide-_Columbus%2C_OH_%2812.09.21%29_IMG_9395_%2851736661603%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Stop_-TigrayGenocide-_Columbus%2C_OH_%2812.09.21%29_IMG_9395_%2851736661603%29.jpg/440px-Stop_-TigrayGenocide-_Columbus%2C_OH_%2812.09.21%29_IMG_9395_%2851736661603%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2300" data-file-height="1526" /></a><figcaption>Protest against <a href="/wiki/Tigray_War" title="Tigray War">war in Tigray</a> in 2021</figcaption></figure>
<p>According to surveys in 2003 by the National Committee on Traditional Practices in Ethiopia, <a href="/wiki/Bride_kidnapping" title="Bride kidnapping">marriage by abduction</a> accounts for 69% of the nation's marriages, with around 80% in the largest region, Oromia, and as high as 92% in the <a href="/wiki/Southern_Nations,_Nationalities,_and_Peoples%27_Region" title="Southern Nations, Nationalities, and Peoples&#39; Region">Southern Nations, Nationalities, and Peoples' Region</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-223" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-223">&#91;221&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-224" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-224">&#91;222&#93;</a></sup> Journalists and activists have been threatened or <a href="/wiki/Misinformation_related_to_the_COVID-19_pandemic#Efforts_to_combat_misinformation" class="mw-redirect" title="Misinformation related to the COVID-19 pandemic">arrested</a> for their coverage of the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Ethiopia" title="COVID-19 pandemic in Ethiopia">COVID-19 pandemic in Ethiopia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-225" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-225">&#91;223&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Among the Omotic <a href="/wiki/Karo_language_(Ethiopia)" title="Karo language (Ethiopia)">Karo-speaking</a> and <a href="/wiki/Hamer_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Hamer people">Hamer peoples</a> in southern Ethiopia, adults and children with physical abnormalities are considered to be <a href="/wiki/Mingi" title="Mingi">mingi</a>, "ritually impure". The latter are believed to exert an evil influence upon others; disabled infants have traditionally been murdered without a proper burial.<sup id="cite_ref-Petros_226-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Petros-226">&#91;224&#93;</a></sup> The Karo officially banned the practice in July 2012.<sup id="cite_ref-227" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-227">&#91;225&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2013, the <a href="/wiki/Oakland_Institute" title="Oakland Institute">Oakland Institute</a> released a report accusing the Ethiopian government of forcing the relocation of "hundreds of thousands of indigenous people from their lands" in the <a href="/wiki/Gambela_Region" title="Gambela Region">Gambela Region</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:1_228-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-228">&#91;226&#93;</a></sup> According to several reports by the organization, those who refused were the subject of a variety of intimidation techniques including physical and sexual abuse, which sometimes led to deaths.<sup id="cite_ref-229" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-229">&#91;227&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-230" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-230">&#91;228&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-:2_231-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:2-231">&#91;229&#93;</a></sup> A similar 2012 report by <a href="/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch" title="Human Rights Watch">Human Rights Watch</a> also describes the Ethiopian government's 2010–2011 <a href="/wiki/Villagization" title="Villagization">villagization</a> program in Gambela, with plans to carry out similar resettlements in other regions.<sup id="cite_ref-232" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-232">&#91;230&#93;</a></sup> The Ethiopian government has denied the accusations of <a href="/wiki/Land_grabbing" title="Land grabbing">land grabbing</a> and instead pointed to the positive trajectory of the country's economy as evidence of the development program's benefits.<sup id="cite_ref-:2_231-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:2-231">&#91;229&#93;</a></sup>
A nationwide <a href="/wiki/October_2019_Ethiopian_clashes" title="October 2019 Ethiopian clashes">series of violent protests</a>, concentrated in the Oromia Region, broke out starting on 23 October 2019, sparked by activist and media owner <a href="/wiki/Jawar_Mohammed" title="Jawar Mohammed">Jawar Mohammed</a>'s allegation that security forces had attempted to detain him. According to official reports, 86 people were killed.<sup id="cite_ref-233" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-233">&#91;231&#93;</a></sup>
On 29 May 2020, <a href="/wiki/Amnesty_International" title="Amnesty International">Amnesty International</a> released a report accusing the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_National_Defense_Force" title="Ethiopian National Defense Force">security forces of Ethiopia</a> of <a href="/wiki/Detention_(imprisonment)" title="Detention (imprisonment)">mass detentions</a> and <a href="/wiki/Extrajudicial_killings" class="mw-redirect" title="Extrajudicial killings">extrajudicial killings</a>. The report stated that in 2019, at least 25 people, suspected of supporting the <a href="/wiki/Oromo_Liberation_Front" title="Oromo Liberation Front">Oromo Liberation Army</a>, were killed by the forces in parts the <a href="/wiki/Oromia_Region" class="mw-redirect" title="Oromia Region">Oromia Region</a>. Besides, between January and September 2019, at least 10,000 people were detained under suspicion, where most were "subjected to brutal beatings".<sup id="cite_ref-234" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-234">&#91;232&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="LGBT_rights">LGBT rights</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=22" title="Edit section: LGBT rights">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/LGBT_rights_in_Ethiopia" title="LGBT rights in Ethiopia">LGBT rights in Ethiopia</a></div>
<p><a href="/wiki/Homosexuality" title="Homosexuality">Homosexual acts</a> are illegal in Ethiopia. According to <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Criminal_Code" title="Ethiopian Criminal Code">Criminal Code</a> Article 629, same-sex activity is punished up to 15 years to <a href="/wiki/Life_in_prison" class="mw-redirect" title="Life in prison">life in prison</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-235" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-235">&#91;233&#93;</a></sup> Ethiopia has been a socially conservative country. The majority of people are hostile towards LGBT people and persecution is commonplace on the grounds of religious and societal norms. Homosexuality came to light in the country since the failed 2008 appeal to the Council of Ministers, and the LGBT scene began to thrive slightly in major metropolitan locations, such as Addis Ababa. Some notable hotels like <a href="/wiki/Sheraton_Addis" title="Sheraton Addis">Sheraton Addis</a> and <a href="/wiki/Hilton_Addis" title="Hilton Addis">Hilton Hotel</a> became hotbeds of accusations for alleged lobbying.<sup id="cite_ref-236" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-236">&#91;234&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Ethiopian Orthodox church plays a frontal role in opposition; some of its members formed anti-gay organizations. For example, Dereje Negash, one prominent activist, founded "Zim Anlem" in 2014, which is a traditionalism and <a href="/wiki/Anti-gender_movement" title="Anti-gender movement">anti-gender movement</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-237" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-237">&#91;235&#93;</a></sup> According to the 2007 <a href="/wiki/Pew_Global_Attitudes_Project" class="mw-redirect" title="Pew Global Attitudes Project">Pew Global Attitudes Project</a>, 97 percent<sup id="cite_ref-238" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-238">&#91;236&#93;</a></sup> of Ethiopians believe homosexuality is a way of life that society should not accept. This was the second-highest rate of non-acceptance in the 45  countries surveyed.<sup id="cite_ref-239" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-239">&#91;237&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Administrative_divisions">Administrative divisions</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=23" title="Edit section: Administrative divisions">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Subdivisions_of_Ethiopia" title="Subdivisions of Ethiopia">Subdivisions of Ethiopia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Regions_of_Ethiopia" title="Regions of Ethiopia">Regions of Ethiopia</a>, <a href="/wiki/List_of_zones_of_Ethiopia" title="List of zones of Ethiopia">List of zones of Ethiopia</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Districts_of_Ethiopia" title="Districts of Ethiopia">Districts of Ethiopia</a></div>
<p>Ethiopia is <a href="/wiki/Administrative_division" title="Administrative division">administratively divided</a> into four levels: <a href="/wiki/Regions_of_Ethiopia" title="Regions of Ethiopia">regions</a>, <a href="/wiki/List_of_zones_of_Ethiopia" title="List of zones of Ethiopia">zones</a>, <i><a href="/wiki/Districts_of_Ethiopia" title="Districts of Ethiopia">woredas</a></i> (districts) and <i><a href="/wiki/Wards_of_Ethiopia" title="Wards of Ethiopia">kebele</a></i> (wards).<sup id="cite_ref-mula_240-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-mula-240">&#91;238&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-mappr_241-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-mappr-241">&#91;239&#93;</a></sup> The country comprises 12 regions and two city administrations under these regions, plenty of zones, woredas and neighbourhood administration: kebeles. The two federal-level city administrations are Addis Ababa and Dire Dava.<sup id="cite_ref-Comparison_242-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Comparison-242">&#91;240&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-center" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Map_of_zones_of_Ethiopia.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Map_of_zones_of_Ethiopia.svg/570px-Map_of_zones_of_Ethiopia.svg.png" decoding="async" width="570" height="462" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Map_of_zones_of_Ethiopia.svg/855px-Map_of_zones_of_Ethiopia.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Map_of_zones_of_Ethiopia.svg/1140px-Map_of_zones_of_Ethiopia.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1843" data-file-height="1494" /></a><figcaption>Map of <a href="/wiki/Regions_of_Ethiopia" title="Regions of Ethiopia">regions</a> and <a href="/wiki/List_of_zones_of_Ethiopia" title="List of zones of Ethiopia">zones</a> of Ethiopia</figcaption></figure>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Geography">Geography</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=24" title="Edit section: Geography">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Geography_of_Ethiopia" title="Geography of Ethiopia">Geography of Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ethiopia_Topography.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Ethiopia_Topography.png/260px-Ethiopia_Topography.png" decoding="async" width="260" height="244" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Ethiopia_Topography.png/390px-Ethiopia_Topography.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Ethiopia_Topography.png/520px-Ethiopia_Topography.png 2x" data-file-width="1116" data-file-height="1046" /></a><figcaption>Ethiopia's topography</figcaption></figure>
<p>At 1,104,300 square kilometres (426,372.61&#160;sq&#160;mi),<sup id="cite_ref-CIA_World_Factbook_9-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CIA_World_Factbook-9">&#91;9&#93;</a></sup> Ethiopia is the world's 28th-largest country, comparable in size to <a href="/wiki/Bolivia" title="Bolivia">Bolivia</a>. It lies between the <a href="/wiki/3rd_parallel_north" title="3rd parallel north">3rd parallel north</a> and the <a href="/wiki/15th_parallel_north" title="15th parallel north">15th parallel north</a> and longitudes <a href="/wiki/33rd_meridian_east" title="33rd meridian east">33rd meridian east</a> and <a href="/wiki/48th_meridian_east" title="48th meridian east">48th meridian east</a>.
</p><p>The major portion of Ethiopia lies in the <a href="/wiki/Horn_of_Africa" title="Horn of Africa">Horn of Africa</a>, which is the easternmost part of the African landmass. The territories that have frontiers with Ethiopia are Eritrea to the north and then, moving in a clockwise direction, Djibouti, Somalia, Kenya, South Sudan and Sudan. Within Ethiopia is a vast highland complex of mountains and dissected plateaus divided by the <a href="/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley,_Ethiopia" title="Great Rift Valley, Ethiopia">Great Rift Valley</a>, which runs generally southwest to northeast and is surrounded by lowlands, <a href="/wiki/Steppe" title="Steppe">steppes</a>, or semi-desert. There is a great diversity of terrain with wide variations in climate, soils, natural vegetation and settlement patterns.
</p><p>Ethiopia is an ecologically diverse country, ranging from the deserts along the eastern border to the tropical forests in the south to extensive <a href="/wiki/Afromontane" title="Afromontane">Afromontane</a> in the northern and southwestern parts. <a href="/wiki/Lake_Tana" title="Lake Tana">Lake Tana</a> in the north is the source of the <a href="/wiki/Blue_Nile" title="Blue Nile">Blue Nile</a>. It also has many <a href="/wiki/Endemism" title="Endemism">endemic</a> species, notably the <a href="/wiki/Gelada" title="Gelada">gelada</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Walia_ibex" title="Walia ibex">walia ibex</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_wolf" title="Ethiopian wolf">Ethiopian wolf</a> ("Simien fox"). The wide range of altitude has given the country a variety of ecologically distinct areas, and this has helped to encourage the evolution of endemic species in ecological isolation.
</p><p>The nation is a land of geographical contrasts, ranging from the vast fertile west, with its forests and numerous rivers, to the world's hottest settlement of <a href="/wiki/Dallol,_Ethiopia" class="mw-redirect" title="Dallol, Ethiopia">Dallol</a> in its north. The <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Highlands" title="Ethiopian Highlands">Ethiopian Highlands</a> are the largest continuous mountain ranges in Africa, and the <a href="/wiki/Sof_Omar_Caves" title="Sof Omar Caves">Sof Omar Caves</a> contains the largest cave on the continent. Ethiopia also has the second-largest number of <a href="/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Africa" title="List of World Heritage Sites in Africa">UNESCO World Heritage Sites</a> in Africa.<sup id="cite_ref-243" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-243">&#91;241&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Climate">Climate</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=25" title="Edit section: Climate">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Climate_of_Ethiopia" title="Climate of Ethiopia">Climate of Ethiopia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Climate_change_in_Ethiopia" title="Climate change in Ethiopia">Climate change in Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:K%C3%B6ppen_climate_types_of_Ethiopia.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_types_of_Ethiopia.svg/260px-K%C3%B6ppen_climate_types_of_Ethiopia.svg.png" decoding="async" width="260" height="299" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_types_of_Ethiopia.svg/390px-K%C3%B6ppen_climate_types_of_Ethiopia.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_types_of_Ethiopia.svg/520px-K%C3%B6ppen_climate_types_of_Ethiopia.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="960" data-file-height="1104" /></a><figcaption>Köppen climate classification of Ethiopia</figcaption></figure>
<p>The predominant climate type is tropical monsoon, with wide topographic-induced variation. The <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Highlands" title="Ethiopian Highlands">Ethiopian Highlands</a> cover most of the country and have a climate which is generally considerably cooler than other regions at similar proximity to the Equator. Most of the country's major cities are located at elevations of around 2,000–2,500&#160;m (6,562–8,202&#160;ft) above sea level, including historic capitals such as Gondar and Axum.
The modern capital, Addis Ababa, is situated on the foothills of <a href="/wiki/Mount_Entoto" title="Mount Entoto">Mount Entoto</a> at an elevation of around 2,400 metres (7,900&#160;ft). It experiences a mild climate year round. With temperatures fairly uniform year round, the seasons in Addis Ababa are largely defined by rainfall: a dry season from October to February, a light rainy season from March to May, and a heavy rainy season from June to September. The average annual rainfall is approximately 1,200 millimetres (47&#160;in).
</p><p>There are on average seven hours of sunshine per day. The dry season is the sunniest time of the year, though even at the height of the rainy season in July and August there are still usually several hours per day of bright sunshine. The average annual temperature in Addis Ababa is 16&#160;°C (60.8&#160;°F), with daily maximum temperatures averaging 20–25&#160;°C (68.0–77.0&#160;°F) throughout the year, and overnight lows averaging 5–10&#160;°C (41.0–50.0&#160;°F).
</p><p>Most major cities and tourist sites in Ethiopia lie at a similar elevation to Addis Ababa and have a comparable climate. In less elevated regions, particularly the lower lying <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_xeric_grasslands_and_shrublands" title="Ethiopian xeric grasslands and shrublands">Ethiopian xeric grasslands and shrublands</a> in the east of Ethiopia, the climate can be significantly hotter and drier. <a href="/wiki/Dallol,_Ethiopia" class="mw-redirect" title="Dallol, Ethiopia">Dallol</a>, in the <a href="/wiki/Danakil_Depression" title="Danakil Depression">Danakil Depression</a> in this eastern zone, has the world's highest average annual temperature of 34&#160;°C (93.2&#160;°F).
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Blue_Nile_Falls,_Ethiopia_(51625800835).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Blue_Nile_Falls%2C_Ethiopia_%2851625800835%29.jpg/220px-Blue_Nile_Falls%2C_Ethiopia_%2851625800835%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Blue_Nile_Falls%2C_Ethiopia_%2851625800835%29.jpg/330px-Blue_Nile_Falls%2C_Ethiopia_%2851625800835%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Blue_Nile_Falls%2C_Ethiopia_%2851625800835%29.jpg/440px-Blue_Nile_Falls%2C_Ethiopia_%2851625800835%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3872" data-file-height="2581" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Blue_Nile_Falls" title="Blue Nile Falls">Blue Nile falls</a> during winter provides over 86 percent of the Nile river's water coming from melted snow in the <a href="/wiki/Simien_Mountains_National_Park" title="Simien Mountains National Park">Simien mountains</a> below 0.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (September 2023)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>Ethiopia is vulnerable to many of the effects of climate change. These include increases in temperature and changes in precipitation. Climate change in these forms threatens food security and the economy, which is agriculture based.<sup id="cite_ref-244" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-244">&#91;242&#93;</a></sup> Many Ethiopians have been forced to leave their homes and travel as far as the Gulf, Southern Africa and Europe.<sup id="cite_ref-245" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-245">&#91;243&#93;</a></sup>
