</p><p>Since April 2019, the Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has promoted <a href="/wiki/Beautifying_Sheger" title="Beautifying Sheger">Beautifying Sheger</a>, a development project that aims to reduce the negative effects of climate change – among other things – in the capital city Addis Ababa.<sup id="cite_ref-246" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-246">&#91;244&#93;</a></sup> In the following May, the government held "Dine for Sheger", a fundraising event in order to cover some of the $1&#160;billion needed through the public.<sup id="cite_ref-247" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-247">&#91;245&#93;</a></sup> $25&#160;million was raised through the expensive event, both through the cost of attending and donations.<sup id="cite_ref-248" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-248">&#91;246&#93;</a></sup> Two Chinese railway companies under the <a href="/wiki/Belt_and_Road_Initiative" title="Belt and Road Initiative">Belt and Road Initiative</a> between China and Ethiopia had supplied funds to develop 12 of the total 56 kilometres.<sup id="cite_ref-249" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-249">&#91;247&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Biodiversity">Biodiversity</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=26" title="Edit section: Biodiversity">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Wildlife_of_Ethiopia" title="Wildlife of Ethiopia">Wildlife of Ethiopia</a></div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Environmental_issues_in_Ethiopia" title="Environmental issues in Ethiopia">Environmental issues in Ethiopia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Deforestation_in_Ethiopia" title="Deforestation in Ethiopia">Deforestation in Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Capra_walie_87176348.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Capra_walie_87176348.jpg/220px-Capra_walie_87176348.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Capra_walie_87176348.jpg/330px-Capra_walie_87176348.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Capra_walie_87176348.jpg/440px-Capra_walie_87176348.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="1536" /></a><figcaption>A <a href="/wiki/Walia_ibex" title="Walia ibex">Walia Ibex</a> in <a href="/wiki/Simien_Mountains_National_Park" title="Simien Mountains National Park">Simien Mountains National Park</a>, one of the national symbols of Ethiopia only found in the Northern parts of the country</figcaption></figure>
<p>Ethiopia has 31 <a href="/wiki/Endemic" class="mw-redirect" title="Endemic">endemic</a> species of mammals.<sup id="cite_ref-Massicot_250-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Massicot-250">&#91;248&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/African_wild_dog" title="African wild dog">African wild dog</a> prehistorically had widespread distribution in the territory. However, with last sightings at <a href="/wiki/Finicha%27a" class="mw-redirect" title="Finicha&#39;a">Finicha'a</a>, this canid is thought to be potentially <a href="/wiki/Local_extinction" title="Local extinction">locally extinct</a>. The <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_wolf" title="Ethiopian wolf">Ethiopian wolf</a> is perhaps the most researched of all the endangered species within Ethiopia.
</p><p>Ethiopia is a global centre of avian diversity. To date more than 856 bird species have been recorded in Ethiopia, twenty of which are endemic to the country.<sup id="cite_ref-251" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-251">&#91;249&#93;</a></sup> Sixteen species are endangered or critically endangered. Many of these birds feed on butterflies, like the <i><a href="/wiki/Bicyclus_anynana" title="Bicyclus anynana">Bicyclus anynana</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-252" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-252">&#91;250&#93;</a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources#What_information_to_include" title="Wikipedia:Citing sources"><span title="A complete citation is needed. (March 2021)">full citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p>Historically, throughout the African continent, wildlife populations have been rapidly declining due to logging, civil wars, pollution, poaching, and other human factors.<sup id="cite_ref-253" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-253">&#91;251&#93;</a></sup> A 17-year-long civil war, along with severe drought, negatively affected Ethiopia's environmental conditions, leading to even greater habitat degradation.<sup id="cite_ref-254" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-254">&#91;252&#93;</a></sup> Habitat destruction is a factor that leads to endangerment. When changes to a habitat occur rapidly, animals do not have time to adjust. Human impact threatens many species, with greater threats expected as a result of climate change induced by <a href="/wiki/Greenhouse_gas" title="Greenhouse gas">greenhouse gases</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-255" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-255">&#91;253&#93;</a></sup> With carbon dioxide emissions in 2010 of 6,494,000 tonnes, Ethiopia contributes just 0.02% to the annual human-caused release of greenhouse gases.<sup id="cite_ref-256" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-256">&#91;254&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Ethiopia has many species listed as critically endangered and vulnerable to global extinction. The threatened species in Ethiopia can be broken down into three categories (based on <a href="/wiki/IUCN" class="mw-redirect" title="IUCN">IUCN</a> ratings): <a href="/wiki/Critically_endangered" class="mw-redirect" title="Critically endangered">critically endangered</a>, <a href="/wiki/Endangered_species" title="Endangered species">endangered</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Vulnerable_species" title="Vulnerable species">vulnerable</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Massicot_250-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Massicot-250">&#91;248&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Ethiopia is one of the eight fundamental and independent <a href="/wiki/Centres_of_origin" class="mw-redirect" title="Centres of origin">centres of origin</a> for cultivated plants in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-257" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-257">&#91;255&#93;</a></sup> However, <a href="/wiki/Deforestation" title="Deforestation">deforestation</a> is a major concern for Ethiopia as studies suggest loss of forest contributes to soil erosion, loss of nutrients in the soil, loss of animal habitats, and reduction in biodiversity. At the beginning of the 20th century, around 420,000&#160;km<sup>2</sup> (or 35%) of Ethiopia's land was covered by trees, but recent research indicates that forest cover is now approximately 11.9% of the area.<sup id="cite_ref-258" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-258">&#91;256&#93;</a></sup> The country had a 2018 <a href="/wiki/Forest_Landscape_Integrity_Index" title="Forest Landscape Integrity Index">Forest Landscape Integrity Index</a> mean score of 7.16/10, ranking it 50th globally out of 172 countries.<sup id="cite_ref-FLII-Supplementary_259-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FLII-Supplementary-259">&#91;257&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Ethiopia loses an estimated 1,410&#160;km<sup>2</sup> of natural forests each year due to firewood collection, conversion to farmland, overgrazing, and use of forest wood for building material. Between 1990 and 2005 the country lost approximately 21,000&#160;km<sup>2</sup> of forests.<sup id="cite_ref-260" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-260">&#91;258&#93;</a></sup> Current government programs to control deforestation consist of education, promoting reforestation programs, and providing raw materials which are alternatives to timber. In rural areas the government also provides non-timber fuel sources and access to non-forested land to promote agriculture without destroying forest habitat.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (February 2008)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup><sup id="cite_ref-261" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-261">&#91;259&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Organizations such as SOS and Farm Africa are working with the federal government and local governments to create a system of forest management.<sup id="cite_ref-262" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-262">&#91;260&#93;</a></sup> Working with a grant of approximately 2.3&#160;million Euros, the Ethiopian government recently began training people on reducing erosion and using proper irrigation techniques that do not contribute to deforestation. This project is assisting more than 80 communities.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (February 2008)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Economy">Economy</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=27" title="Edit section: Economy">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Economy_of_Ethiopia" title="Economy of Ethiopia">Economy of Ethiopia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Industrial_sector_in_Ethiopia" title="Industrial sector in Ethiopia">Industrial sector in Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:GDP_per_capita_development_of_Ethiopia.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/GDP_per_capita_development_of_Ethiopia.svg/220px-GDP_per_capita_development_of_Ethiopia.svg.png" decoding="async" width="220" height="155" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/GDP_per_capita_development_of_Ethiopia.svg/330px-GDP_per_capita_development_of_Ethiopia.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/GDP_per_capita_development_of_Ethiopia.svg/440px-GDP_per_capita_development_of_Ethiopia.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="850" data-file-height="600" /></a><figcaption>Development of GDP per capita</figcaption></figure>
<p>Ethiopia registered the fastest economic growth under <a href="/wiki/Premiership_of_Meles_Zenawi" title="Premiership of Meles Zenawi">Meles Zenawi's administration</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-263" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-263">&#91;261&#93;</a></sup>
According to the <a href="/wiki/IMF" class="mw-redirect" title="IMF">IMF</a>, Ethiopia was one of the fastest growing economies in the world, registering over 10% economic growth from 2004 through 2009.<sup id="cite_ref-Outlook_2012_264-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Outlook_2012-264">&#91;262&#93;</a></sup> It was the fastest-growing non-oil-dependent African economy in the years 2007 and 2008.<sup id="cite_ref-265" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-265">&#91;263&#93;</a></sup> In 2015, the World Bank highlighted that Ethiopia had witnessed rapid economic growth with real domestic product (GDP) growth averaging 10.9% between 2004 and 2014.<sup id="cite_ref-266" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-266">&#91;264&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2008 and 2011, Ethiopia's growth performance and considerable development gains were challenged by high <a href="/wiki/Inflation" title="Inflation">inflation</a> and a difficult <a href="/wiki/Balance_of_payments" title="Balance of payments">balance of payments</a> situation. Inflation surged to 40% in August 2011 because of loose <a href="/wiki/Monetary_policy" title="Monetary policy">monetary policy</a>, large <a href="/wiki/Civil_service" title="Civil service">civil service</a> wage increase in early 2011, and high food prices.<sup id="cite_ref-Ethiopia_Overview_267-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ethiopia_Overview-267">&#91;265&#93;</a></sup> For 2011–12, end-year inflation was projected to be about 22%, and single digit inflation is projected in 2012–13 with the implementation of tight monetary and fiscal policies.<sup id="cite_ref-statement_268-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-statement-268">&#91;266&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In spite of fast growth in recent years, GDP per capita is one of the lowest in the world, and the economy faces a number of serious structural problems. However, with a focused investment in public infrastructure and industrial parks, Ethiopia's economy is addressing its structural problems to become a hub for light manufacturing in Africa.<sup id="cite_ref-269" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-269">&#91;267&#93;</a></sup> In 2019 a law was passed allowing expatriate Ethiopians to invest in Ethiopia's financial service industry.<sup id="cite_ref-270" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-270">&#91;268&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ethiopian_cargo_ship_at_Port_of_Djibouti.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Ethiopian_cargo_ship_at_Port_of_Djibouti.jpg/220px-Ethiopian_cargo_ship_at_Port_of_Djibouti.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Ethiopian_cargo_ship_at_Port_of_Djibouti.jpg/330px-Ethiopian_cargo_ship_at_Port_of_Djibouti.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Ethiopian_cargo_ship_at_Port_of_Djibouti.jpg/440px-Ethiopian_cargo_ship_at_Port_of_Djibouti.jpg 2x" data-file-width="824" data-file-height="546" /></a><figcaption>An Ethiopian logistics shipping cargo docked at the red sea</figcaption></figure>
<p>The Ethiopian constitution specifies that rights to own land belong only to "the state and the people", but citizens may lease land for up to 99 years, but are unable to mortgage or sell. Renting out land for a maximum of twenty years is allowed and this is expected to ensure that land goes to the most productive user. Land distribution and administration is considered an area where corruption is institutionalized, and facilitation payments as well as bribes are often demanded when dealing with land-related issues.<sup id="cite_ref-271" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-271">&#91;269&#93;</a></sup> As there is no land ownership, infrastructural projects are most often simply done without asking the land users, which then end up being displaced and without a home or land. A lot of anger and distrust sometimes results in public protests. In addition, agricultural productivity remains low, and frequent droughts still beset the country, also leading to internal displacement.<sup id="cite_ref-272" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-272">&#91;270&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Energy_and_hydropower">Energy and hydropower</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=28" title="Edit section: Energy and hydropower">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Energy_in_Ethiopia" title="Energy in Ethiopia">Energy in Ethiopia</a> and <a href="/wiki/List_of_power_stations_in_Ethiopia" title="List of power stations in Ethiopia">List of power stations in Ethiopia</a></div>
<p>Ethiopia has 14 major rivers flowing from its highlands, including the Nile. It has the largest water reserves in Africa. As of 2012<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>, hydroelectric plants represented around 88.2% of the total installed electricity generating capacity.
</p><p>The remaining electrical power was generated from fossil fuels (8.3%) and renewable sources (3.6%).
</p><p>The electrification rate for the total population in 2016 was 42%, with 85% coverage in urban areas and 26% coverage in rural areas. As of 2016<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>, total electricity production was 11.15&#160;TW⋅h and consumption was 9.062&#160;TW⋅h. There were 0.166&#160;TW⋅h of electricity exported, 0&#160;kW⋅h imported, and 2.784&#160;GW of installed generating capacity.<sup id="cite_ref-CIA2_21-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CIA2-21">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Cement_never_sleeps_(8756743123).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Cement_never_sleeps_%288756743123%29.jpg/220px-Cement_never_sleeps_%288756743123%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Cement_never_sleeps_%288756743123%29.jpg/330px-Cement_never_sleeps_%288756743123%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Cement_never_sleeps_%288756743123%29.jpg/440px-Cement_never_sleeps_%288756743123%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5105" data-file-height="3403" /></a><figcaption>A factory in <a href="/wiki/Dire_Dawa" title="Dire Dawa">Dire Dawa</a>: one of Ethiopia's biggest economic cities</figcaption></figure>
<p>Ethiopia delivers roughly 81% of water volume to the Nile through the river basins of the <a href="/wiki/Blue_Nile" title="Blue Nile">Blue Nile</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sobat_River" title="Sobat River">Sobat River</a> and <a href="/wiki/Atbara" title="Atbara">Atbara</a>. In 1959, Egypt and Sudan signed a bilateral treaty, the <a href="/wiki/Water_politics_in_the_Nile_Basin" title="Water politics in the Nile Basin">1959 Nile Waters Agreement</a>, which gave both countries exclusive maritime rights over the Nile waters. Ever since, Egypt has discouraged almost all projects in Ethiopia that sought to use the local Nile tributaries. This had the effect of discouraging external financing of hydropower and irrigation projects in western Ethiopia, thereby impeding water resource-based economic development projects. However, Ethiopia is in the process of constructing a large 6,450 MW hydroelectric dam on the Blue Nile river. When completed, this <a href="/wiki/Grand_Ethiopian_Renaissance_Dam" title="Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam">Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam</a> is slated to be the largest hydroelectric power station in Africa.<sup id="cite_ref-273" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-273">&#91;271&#93;</a></sup>
The <a href="/wiki/Gilgel_Gibe_III_Dam" title="Gilgel Gibe III Dam">Gibe III</a> hydroelectric project is so far the largest in the country with an installed capacity of 1,870&#160;MW. For the year 2017–18 (2010 E.C) this hydroelectric dam generated 4,900&#160;GW⋅h.<sup id="cite_ref-274" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-274">&#91;272&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Agriculture">Agriculture</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=29" title="Edit section: Agriculture">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Agriculture_in_Ethiopia" title="Agriculture in Ethiopia">Agriculture in Ethiopia</a></div><p>Agriculture constitutes around 85% of the labour force. However, the service sector represents the largest portion of the <a href="/wiki/Gross_domestic_product" title="Gross domestic product">GDP</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-CIA2_21-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CIA2-21">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup> Many other economic activities depend on agriculture, including marketing, processing, and export of agricultural products. Production is overwhelmingly by small-scale farmers and enterprises, and a large part of commodity exports are provided by the small agricultural cash-crop sector. Principal crops include <a href="/wiki/Coffea" title="Coffea">coffee</a>, <a href="/wiki/Legume" title="Legume">legumes</a>, <a href="/wiki/Rapeseed" title="Rapeseed">oilseeds</a>, <a href="/wiki/Cereal" title="Cereal">cereals</a>, potatoes, <a href="/wiki/Sugarcane" title="Sugarcane">sugarcane</a>, and vegetables. Ethiopia is also a <a href="/wiki/Center_of_origin" class="mw-redirect" title="Center of origin">Vavilov</a> centre of diversity for domesticated crops, including <a href="/wiki/Ensete_ventricosum" title="Ensete ventricosum">enset</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-275" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-275">&#91;273&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Coffee_bean" title="Coffee bean">coffee</a> and <a href="/wiki/Teff" title="Teff">teff</a>.
</p><p>Exports are almost entirely agricultural commodities (with the exception of <a href="/wiki/Gold" title="Gold">Gold</a> exports), and coffee is the largest foreign exchange earner. Ethiopia is Africa's second biggest <a href="/wiki/Maize" title="Maize">maize</a> producer.<sup id="cite_ref-276" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-276">&#91;274&#93;</a></sup> According to UN estimations the per capita GDP of Ethiopia has reached $357 as of 2011<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>.<sup id="cite_ref-auto_277-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto-277">&#91;275&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Exports">Exports</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=30" title="Edit section: Exports">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Coffee_production_in_Ethiopia" title="Coffee production in Ethiopia">Coffee production in Ethiopia</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:214px;max-width:214px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:212px;max-width:212px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Addis_Ababa_LRT_by_Ben_Welle_02.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Addis_Ababa_LRT_by_Ben_Welle_02.jpg/210px-Addis_Ababa_LRT_by_Ben_Welle_02.jpg" decoding="async" width="210" height="158" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Addis_Ababa_LRT_by_Ben_Welle_02.jpg/315px-Addis_Ababa_LRT_by_Ben_Welle_02.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Addis_Ababa_LRT_by_Ben_Welle_02.jpg/420px-Addis_Ababa_LRT_by_Ben_Welle_02.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3264" data-file-height="2448" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">Light rail train in <a href="/wiki/Addis_Ababa" title="Addis Ababa">Addis Ababa</a>, Ethiopia which hosts over 100 thousand passengers a day<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (September 2023)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup></div></div></div><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:212px;max-width:212px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:ET-ASK_-_Ras_Dashen_-_Ethiopian_Airlines_-_Boeing_777-360ER_-_MSN_44550_-_VGHS.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/ET-ASK_-_Ras_Dashen_-_Ethiopian_Airlines_-_Boeing_777-360ER_-_MSN_44550_-_VGHS.jpg/210px-ET-ASK_-_Ras_Dashen_-_Ethiopian_Airlines_-_Boeing_777-360ER_-_MSN_44550_-_VGHS.jpg" decoding="async" width="210" height="118" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/ET-ASK_-_Ras_Dashen_-_Ethiopian_Airlines_-_Boeing_777-360ER_-_MSN_44550_-_VGHS.jpg/315px-ET-ASK_-_Ras_Dashen_-_Ethiopian_Airlines_-_Boeing_777-360ER_-_MSN_44550_-_VGHS.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/ET-ASK_-_Ras_Dashen_-_Ethiopian_Airlines_-_Boeing_777-360ER_-_MSN_44550_-_VGHS.jpg/420px-ET-ASK_-_Ras_Dashen_-_Ethiopian_Airlines_-_Boeing_777-360ER_-_MSN_44550_-_VGHS.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4354" data-file-height="2449" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">Ethiopia's biggest company <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Airlines" title="Ethiopian Airlines">Ethiopian Airlines</a> which has an annual revenue of 6.1 billion dollars making it the 14th biggest airlines in revenue: contributes to the country's export business<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (September 2023)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup></div></div></div><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:212px;max-width:212px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Ethio_Telecom_(25070216192).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Ethio_Telecom_%2825070216192%29.jpg/210px-Ethio_Telecom_%2825070216192%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="210" height="129" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Ethio_Telecom_%2825070216192%29.jpg/315px-Ethio_Telecom_%2825070216192%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Ethio_Telecom_%2825070216192%29.jpg/420px-Ethio_Telecom_%2825070216192%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4495" data-file-height="2757" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption"><a href="/wiki/Ethio_Telecom" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethio Telecom">Ethio Telecom</a> is one of the country's biggest companies which generates over a billion dollars annually<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (September 2023)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup></div></div></div></div></div>
<p>Ethiopia is often considered as the birthplace of <a href="/wiki/Coffee" title="Coffee">coffee</a> since cultivation began in the 9th century.<sup id="cite_ref-:6_278-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:6-278">&#91;276&#93;</a></sup> Exports from Ethiopia in the 2009–2010 financial year totalled US$1.4&#160;billion.<sup id="cite_ref-279" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-279">&#91;277&#93;</a></sup> Ethiopia produces more coffee than any other nation on the continent.<sup id="cite_ref-280" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-280">&#91;278&#93;</a></sup> "Coffee provides a livelihood for close to 15 million Ethiopians, 16% of the population. Farmers in the eastern part of the country, where a warming climate is already impacting production, have struggled in recent years, and many are currently reporting largely failed harvests as a result of a prolonged drought".<sup id="cite_ref-281" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-281">&#91;279&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Ethiopia also has the 5th largest inventory of <a href="/wiki/Arado_cattle" title="Arado cattle">cattle</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-282" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-282">&#91;280&#93;</a></sup> Other main export commodities are <a href="/wiki/Khat" title="Khat">khat</a>, gold, leather products, and oilseeds. Recent development of the <a href="/wiki/Floriculture" title="Floriculture">floriculture</a> sector means Ethiopia is poised to become one of the top flower and plant exporters in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-283" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-283">&#91;281&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Cross-border trade by pastoralists is often informal and beyond state control and regulation. In <a href="/wiki/East_Africa" title="East Africa">East Africa</a>, over 95% of cross-border trade is through unofficial channels. The unofficial trade of live cattle, camels, sheep, and goats from Ethiopia sold to <a href="/wiki/Somalia" title="Somalia">Somalia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Djibouti" title="Djibouti">Djibouti</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Kenya" title="Kenya">Kenya</a> generates an estimated total value of between 250 and US$300&#160;million annually (100 times more than the official figure).<sup id="cite_ref-ODI_284-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ODI-284">&#91;282&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>This trade helps lower food prices, increase food security, relieve border tensions, and promote regional integration.<sup id="cite_ref-ODI_284-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ODI-284">&#91;282&#93;</a></sup> However, the unregulated and undocumented nature of this trade runs risks, such as allowing disease to spread more easily across national borders. Furthermore, the government of Ethiopia is purportedly unhappy with lost tax revenue and foreign exchange revenues.<sup id="cite_ref-ODI_284-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ODI-284">&#91;282&#93;</a></sup> Recent initiatives have sought to document and regulate this trade.<sup id="cite_ref-ODI_284-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ODI-284">&#91;282&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>With the private sector growing slowly, designer leather products like bags are becoming a big export business, with Taytu becoming the first luxury designer label in the country.<sup id="cite_ref-285" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-285">&#91;283&#93;</a></sup> Additional small-scale export products include cereals, pulses, cotton, sugarcane, potatoes, and hides. With the construction of various new dams and growing hydroelectric power projects around the country, Ethiopia also plans to export electric power to its neighbours.<sup id="cite_ref-286" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-286">&#91;284&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-287" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-287">&#91;285&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Most regard Ethiopia's large water resources and potential as its "white oil" and its coffee resources as "black gold".<sup id="cite_ref-288" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-288">&#91;286&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-289" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-289">&#91;287&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Transport">Transport</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=31" title="Edit section: Transport">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Transport_in_Ethiopia" title="Transport in Ethiopia">Transport in Ethiopia</a></div>
<p>Ethiopia has 926&#160;km of electrified <span class="nowrap">1,435&#160;mm</span> (<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1154941027">.mw-parser-output .frac{white-space:nowrap}.mw-parser-output .frac .num,.mw-parser-output .frac .den{font-size:80%;line-height:0;vertical-align:super}.mw-parser-output .frac .den{vertical-align:sub}.mw-parser-output .sr-only{border:0;clip:rect(0,0,0,0);clip-path:polygon(0px 0px,0px 0px,0px 0px);height:1px;margin:-1px;overflow:hidden;padding:0;position:absolute;width:1px}</style><span class="nowrap">4&#160;ft&#160;<span class="frac" role="math">8<span class="sr-only">+</span><span class="num">1</span>&#8260;<span class="den">2</span></span>&#160;in</span>) <a href="/wiki/Standard_gauge" class="mw-redirect" title="Standard gauge">standard gauge</a> railways, 656&#160;km for the <a href="/wiki/Addis_Ababa%E2%80%93Djibouti_Railway" title="Addis Ababa–Djibouti Railway">Addis Ababa–Djibouti Railway</a> between Addis Ababa and the <a href="/wiki/Port_of_Djibouti" title="Port of Djibouti">Port of Djibouti</a> (via <a href="/wiki/Awash,_Ethiopia" title="Awash, Ethiopia">Awash</a>)<sup id="cite_ref-290" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-290">&#91;288&#93;</a></sup> and 270&#160;km for the <a href="/wiki/Awash%E2%80%93Hara_Gebeya_Railway" class="mw-redirect" title="Awash–Hara Gebeya Railway">Awash–Hara Gebeya Railway</a> between Addis Ababa and the <a href="/wiki/Twin_cities" title="Twin cities">twin cities</a> of <a href="/wiki/Dessie" title="Dessie">Dessie</a>/<a href="/wiki/Kombolcha" title="Kombolcha">Kombolcha</a><sup id="cite_ref-AKH_291-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AKH-291">&#91;289&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Ethiopia had 58 airports as of 2012<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>,<sup id="cite_ref-CIA2_21-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CIA2-21">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup> and 61 as of 2016<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>.<sup id="cite_ref-292" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-292">&#91;290&#93;</a></sup> Among these, the <a href="/wiki/Bole_International_Airport" class="mw-redirect" title="Bole International Airport">Bole International Airport</a> in Addis Ababa and the <a href="/wiki/Aba_Tenna_Dejazmach_Yilma_International_Airport" class="mw-redirect" title="Aba Tenna Dejazmach Yilma International Airport">Aba Tenna Dejazmach Yilma International Airport</a> in Dire Dawa accommodate international flights.
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Airlines" title="Ethiopian Airlines">Ethiopian Airlines</a>, a member of the <a href="/wiki/Star_Alliance" title="Star Alliance">Star Alliance</a>, is the country's <a href="/wiki/Flag_carrier" title="Flag carrier">flag carrier</a>, and is wholly owned by the <a href="/wiki/Government_of_Ethiopia" title="Government of Ethiopia">Government of Ethiopia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Eaeacp_293-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Eaeacp-293">&#91;291&#93;</a></sup> From its hub at the Bole International Airport, the airline serves a network of 102 international passenger, 20 domestic passenger, and 44 cargo destinations.<sup id="cite_ref-294" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-294">&#91;292&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Bpea_295-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bpea-295">&#91;293&#93;</a></sup> It is also one of the fastest-growing carriers in the industry and continent.<sup id="cite_ref-Ceabtdta_296-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ceabtdta-296">&#91;294&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Tourism">Tourism</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=32" title="Edit section: Tourism">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Tourism_in_Ethiopia" title="Tourism in Ethiopia">Tourism in Ethiopia</a></div>
<p><a href="/wiki/Tourism_in_Ethiopia" title="Tourism in Ethiopia">Tourism</a> in Ethiopia accounted for 5.5% of GDP growth in 2006. In 2015, the <a href="/wiki/European_Council" title="European Council">European Council</a> named Ethiopia "World's Best Tourism Destination".<sup id="cite_ref-:0_297-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-297">&#91;295&#93;</a></sup> In 2020 the country registered 518,000 tourists, ranked 126th in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-298" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-298">&#91;296&#93;</a></sup> There are nine <a href="/wiki/UNESCO_World_Heritage_Sites" class="mw-redirect" title="UNESCO World Heritage Sites">UNESCO World Heritage Sites</a> in Ethiopia:<sup id="cite_ref-299" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-299">&#91;297&#93;</a></sup> Tourist destinations include <a href="/wiki/List_of_National_Parks_of_Ethiopia" class="mw-redirect" title="List of National Parks of Ethiopia">Ethiopia's collection of national parks</a> (including <a href="/wiki/Semien_Mountains_National_Park" class="mw-redirect" title="Semien Mountains National Park">Semien Mountains National Park</a>), and historic sites, such as the cities of <a href="/wiki/Axum" title="Axum">Axum</a>, <a href="/wiki/Lalibela" title="Lalibela">Lalibela</a> and <a href="/wiki/Gondar" title="Gondar">Gondar</a>, <a href="/wiki/Harar_Jugol" class="mw-redirect" title="Harar Jugol">Harar Jugol</a> walled city, <a href="/wiki/Negash_Mosque" class="mw-redirect" title="Negash Mosque">Negash Mosque</a>, in <a href="/wiki/Negash" title="Negash">Negash</a> and <a href="/wiki/Sof_Omar_Caves" title="Sof Omar Caves">Sof Omar Caves</a>.
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Demographics">Demographics</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=33" title="Edit section: Demographics">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Demographics_of_Ethiopia" title="Demographics of Ethiopia">Demographics of Ethiopia</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Ethiopians" title="Ethiopians">Ethiopians</a> and <a href="/wiki/List_of_ethnic_groups_in_Ethiopia" title="List of ethnic groups in Ethiopia">List of ethnic groups in Ethiopia</a></div>

</div>
<p>Ethiopia is the most populous landlocked country in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-ciawfb_300-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ciawfb-300">&#91;298&#93;</a></sup> 
Its total population has grown from 38.1&#160;million in 1983 to 109.5&#160;million in 2018.<sup id="cite_ref-301" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-301">&#91;299&#93;</a></sup> The population was only about nine million in the 19th century.<sup id="cite_ref-302" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-302">&#91;300&#93;</a></sup> The 2007 Population and Housing Census results show that the population of Ethiopia grew at an average annual rate of 2.6% between 1994 and 2007, down from 2.8% during the period 1983–1994. Currently, the population growth rate is among the top ten countries in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-303" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-303">&#91;301&#93;</a></sup> According to UN estimations, life expectancy had improved substantially in recent years with male life expectancy reported to be 56 years and for women 60 years.<sup id="cite_ref-auto_277-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto-277">&#91;275&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Ethiopia's population is highly diverse, containing over 80 different ethnic groups, the four largest of which are the <a href="/wiki/Oromo_people" title="Oromo people">Oromo</a>, <a href="/wiki/Amhara_people" title="Amhara people">Amhara</a>, <a href="/wiki/Somalis" title="Somalis">Somali</a> and <a href="/wiki/Tigrayans" title="Tigrayans">Tigrayans</a>. According to the Ethiopian national census of 2007, the <a href="/wiki/Oromo_people" title="Oromo people">Oromo</a> are the largest ethnic group in Ethiopia, at 34.4% of the nation's population. The <a href="/wiki/Amhara_people" title="Amhara people">Amhara</a> represent 27.0% of the country's inhabitants, while <a href="/wiki/Somalis" title="Somalis">Somalis</a> and <a href="/wiki/Tigrayans" title="Tigrayans">Tigrayans</a> represent 6.2% and 6.1% of the population respectively. Other prominent ethnic groups are as follows: <a href="/wiki/Sidama_people" title="Sidama people">Sidama</a> 4.0%, <a href="/wiki/Gurage_people" title="Gurage people">Gurage</a> 2.5%, <a href="/wiki/Welayta_people" title="Welayta people">Welayta</a> 2.3%, <a href="/wiki/Afar_people" title="Afar people">Afar</a> 1.7%, <a href="/wiki/Hadiya_people" title="Hadiya people">Hadiya</a> 1.7%, <a href="/wiki/Gamo_people" title="Gamo people">Gamo</a> 1.5% and <a href="/wiki/List_of_ethnic_groups_in_Ethiopia" title="List of ethnic groups in Ethiopia">Others</a> 12.6%.<sup id="cite_ref-2007Census_6-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2007Census-6">&#91;6&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Afroasiatic_languages" title="Afroasiatic languages">Afroasiatic-speaking</a> communities make up the majority of the population. Among these, Semitic speakers often collectively refer to themselves as the <a href="/wiki/Habesha_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Habesha people">Habesha people</a>. The <a href="/wiki/Arabic" title="Arabic">Arabic</a> form of this term (<i>al-Ḥabasha</i>) is the etymological basis of "Abyssinia", the former name of Ethiopia in English and other European languages.<sup id="cite_ref-304" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-304">&#91;302&#93;</a></sup> Additionally, <a href="/wiki/Nilo-Saharan_languages" title="Nilo-Saharan languages">Nilo-Saharan-speaking</a> ethnic minorities inhabit the southern regions of the country, particularly in areas of the <a href="/wiki/Gambela_Region" title="Gambela Region">Gambela Region</a> which borders <a href="/wiki/South_Sudan" title="South Sudan">South Sudan</a>. The largest ethnic groups among these include the <a href="/wiki/Nuer_people" title="Nuer people">Nuer</a> and <a href="/wiki/Anuak_people" title="Anuak people">Anuak</a>.
</p><p>In addition, Ethiopia had over 75,000 <a href="/wiki/Italians_of_Ethiopia" title="Italians of Ethiopia">Italian settlers</a> during the Italian occupation of the country.<sup id="cite_ref-Istat_2010_305-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Istat_2010-305">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup> After independence, many Italians remained for decades after receiving full pardons from Emperor Selassie, as he saw the opportunity to continue modernization efforts. However, due to the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Civil_War" title="Ethiopian Civil War">Ethiopian Civil War</a> in 1974, nearly 22,000 Italo-Ethiopians left the country.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (January 2023)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> In the 2000s, some Italian companies returned to operate in Ethiopia, and many Italian technicians and managers arrived with their families, residing mainly in the metropolitan area of the capital.<sup id="cite_ref-306" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-306">&#91;304&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Southern_Nations,_Nationalities,_and_Peoples%27_Region" title="Southern Nations, Nationalities, and Peoples&#39; Region">Southern Nations, Nationalities, and Peoples' Region</a>, being an amalgam of the main homelands of numerous ethnicities, contains over 56 indigenous <a href="/wiki/List_of_ethnic_groups_in_Ethiopia" title="List of ethnic groups in Ethiopia">ethnic groups</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-307" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-307">&#91;305&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2009, Ethiopia hosted a population of refugees and asylum seekers numbering approximately 135,200. The majority of this population came from Somalia (approximately 64,300 persons), Eritrea (41,700) and Sudan (25,900). The Ethiopian government required nearly all refugees to live in refugee camps.<sup id="cite_ref-World_Refugee_Survey_2009_308-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-World_Refugee_Survey_2009-308">&#91;306&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Languages">Languages</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=34" title="Edit section: Languages">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Languages_of_Ethiopia" title="Languages of Ethiopia">Languages of Ethiopia</a></div>

<p><a href="/wiki/Languages_of_Ethiopia" title="Languages of Ethiopia">Languages of Ethiopia</a> as of 2007<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup> Census<sup id="cite_ref-2007Census_6-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2007Census-6">&#91;6&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r981673959">.mw-parser-output .legend{page-break-inside:avoid;break-inside:avoid-column}.mw-parser-output .legend-color{display:inline-block;min-width:1.25em;height:1.25em;line-height:1.25;margin:1px 0;text-align:center;border:1px solid black;background-color:transparent;color:black}.mw-parser-output .legend-text{}</style><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Green; color:black;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Amharic" title="Amharic">Amharic</a> (29.3%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Red; color:black;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Somali_language" title="Somali language">Somali</a> (6.2%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Blue; color:white;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Tigrinya_language" title="Tigrinya language">Tigrinya</a> (5.9%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Purple; color:white;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Sidamo_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Sidamo language">Sidamo</a> (4.0%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Black; color:white;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Wolaytta_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Wolaytta language">Wolaytta</a> (2.2%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Brown; color:white;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Gurage_languages" title="Gurage languages">Gurage</a> (2.0%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Orange; color:black;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Afar_language" title="Afar language">Afar</a> (1.7%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Teal; color:white;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Hadiyya_language" title="Hadiyya language">Hadiyya</a> (1.7%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Gray; color:black;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Gamo-Gofa-Dawro_language" title="Gamo-Gofa-Dawro language">Gamo</a> (1.5%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:white; color:black;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Languages_of_Ethiopia#Overview" title="Languages of Ethiopia">others</a> (11.6%)</div>
</div>
</div></div>
<p>According to <a href="/wiki/Glottolog" title="Glottolog">Glottolog</a>, there are 109 languages spoken in Ethiopia, while <i><a href="/wiki/Ethnologue" title="Ethnologue">Ethnologue</a></i> lists 90 individual languages spoken in the country.<sup id="cite_ref-309" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-309">&#91;307&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Ethnologue_310-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ethnologue-310">&#91;308&#93;</a></sup> Most people in the country speak <a href="/wiki/Afroasiatic_languages" title="Afroasiatic languages">Afroasiatic languages</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Cushitic_languages" title="Cushitic languages">Cushitic</a> or <a href="/wiki/Semitic_languages" title="Semitic languages">Semitic</a> branches. The former includes the <a href="/wiki/Oromo_language" title="Oromo language">Oromo language</a>, spoken by the <a href="/wiki/Oromo_people" title="Oromo people">Oromo</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Somali_language" title="Somali language">Somali</a>, spoken by the <a href="/wiki/Somalis" title="Somalis">Somalis</a>; the latter includes <a href="/wiki/Amharic" title="Amharic">Amharic</a>, spoken by the <a href="/wiki/Amhara_people" title="Amhara people">Amhara</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Tigrinya_language" title="Tigrinya language">Tigrinya</a>, spoken by the <a href="/wiki/Tigrayans" title="Tigrayans">Tigrayans</a>. Together, these four groups make up about three-quarters of Ethiopia's population. Other Afroasiatic languages with a significant number of speakers include the Cushitic <a href="/wiki/Sidamo_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Sidamo language">Sidamo</a>, <a href="/wiki/Afar_language" title="Afar language">Afar</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hadiyya_language" title="Hadiyya language">Hadiyya</a> and <a href="/wiki/Agaw_languages" title="Agaw languages">Agaw languages</a>, as well as the Semitic <a href="/wiki/Gurage_languages" title="Gurage languages">Gurage languages</a>, <a href="/wiki/Harari_language" title="Harari language">Harari</a>, <a href="/wiki/Silt%27e_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Silt&#39;e language">Silt'e</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Argobba_language" title="Argobba language">Argobba</a> languages.<sup id="cite_ref-2007Census_6-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2007Census-6">&#91;6&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Arabic" title="Arabic">Arabic</a>, which also belongs to the Afroasiatic family, is likewise spoken in some areas.<sup id="cite_ref-311" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-311">&#91;309&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Additionally, <a href="/wiki/Omotic_languages" title="Omotic languages">Omotic languages</a> are spoken by Omotic ethnic minority groups inhabiting the southern regions. Among these languages are <a href="/wiki/Aari_language" title="Aari language">Aari</a>, <a href="/wiki/Bench_language" title="Bench language">Bench</a>, <a href="/wiki/Dime_language" title="Dime language">Dime</a>, <a href="/wiki/Dizin_language" title="Dizin language">Dizin</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gamo-Gofa-Dawro_language" title="Gamo-Gofa-Dawro language">Gamo-Gofa-Dawro</a>, <a href="/wiki/Maale_language" title="Maale language">Maale</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hamer_language" title="Hamer language">Hamer</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Wolaytta_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Wolaytta language">Wolaytta</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-2007Census_6-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2007Census-6">&#91;6&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Languages from the putative <a href="/wiki/Nilo-Saharan_languages" title="Nilo-Saharan languages">Nilo-Saharan family</a> are also spoken by ethnic minorities concentrated in the southwestern parts of the country. These languages include <a href="/wiki/Nuer_language" title="Nuer language">Nuer</a>, <a href="/wiki/Anuak_language" title="Anuak language">Anuak</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Nyangatom_language" title="Nyangatom language">Nyangatom</a> (all <a href="/wiki/Nilotic_languages" title="Nilotic languages">Nilotic</a>), <a href="/wiki/Majang_language" title="Majang language">Majang</a>, <a href="/wiki/Suri_language" title="Suri language">Suri</a>, <a href="/wiki/Me%27en_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Me&#39;en language">Me'en</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Mursi_language" title="Mursi language">Mursi</a> (all <a href="/wiki/Surmic_languages" title="Surmic languages">Surmic</a>).<sup id="cite_ref-2007Census_6-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2007Census-6">&#91;6&#93;</a></sup> Other small families and <a href="/wiki/Language_isolate" title="Language isolate">isolates</a> according to Glottolog include: <a href="/wiki/Koman_languages" title="Koman languages">Koman</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gumuz_languages" class="mw-redirect" title="Gumuz languages">Gumuz</a>, <a href="/wiki/Dizoid_languages" title="Dizoid languages">Dizoic</a>, <a href="/wiki/Berta_language" title="Berta language">Berta</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mao_languages" title="Mao languages">Blue Nile Mao</a>, <a href="/wiki/Shabo_language" title="Shabo language">Shabo</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ongota_language" title="Ongota language">Ongota</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Kunama_language" title="Kunama language">Kunama</a>.
</p><p>English is the most widely spoken foreign language, the medium of instruction in secondary schools and all tertiary education; federal laws are also published in British English in the <a href="/wiki/Federal_Negarit_Gazeta" title="Federal Negarit Gazeta">Federal Negarit Gazeta</a> including the 1995 constitution.<sup id="cite_ref-FDRE_312-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FDRE-312">&#91;310&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Amharic was the language of primary school instruction, but has been replaced in many areas by regional languages such as Oromo, Somali or Tigrinya.<sup id="cite_ref-Llicuv_313-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Llicuv-313">&#91;311&#93;</a></sup> While all languages enjoy equal state recognition in the <a href="/wiki/1995_Constitution_of_Ethiopia" title="1995 Constitution of Ethiopia">1995 Constitution of Ethiopia</a><sup id="cite_ref-Constitution2_154-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Constitution2-154">&#91;152&#93;</a></sup> and Oromo is the most populous language by native speakers, Amharic is the most populous by number of total speakers.
</p><p>The various <a href="/wiki/Regions_of_Ethiopia" title="Regions of Ethiopia">regions of Ethiopia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Charter_city" title="Charter city">chartered cities</a> are free to determine their own working languages.<sup id="cite_ref-Llicuv_313-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Llicuv-313">&#91;311&#93;</a></sup> Amharic is recognised as the official working language of <a href="/wiki/Amhara_Region" title="Amhara Region">Amhara Region</a>, <a href="/wiki/Benishangul-Gumuz" class="mw-redirect" title="Benishangul-Gumuz">Benishangul-Gumuz</a>, <a href="/wiki/Southern_Nations,_Nationalities,_and_Peoples%27_Region" title="Southern Nations, Nationalities, and Peoples&#39; Region">Southern Nations, Nationalities, and Peoples' Region</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gambela_Region" title="Gambela Region">Gambela Region</a>, <a href="/wiki/Addis_Ababa" title="Addis Ababa">Addis Ababa</a> and <a href="/wiki/Dire_Dawa" title="Dire Dawa">Dire Dawa</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-314" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-314">&#91;312&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Oromo_language" title="Oromo language">Oromo language</a> serves as the official working language and the primary language of education in the Oromia,<sup id="cite_ref-CIA2_21-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CIA2-21">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Harar" title="Harar">Harar</a> and <a href="/wiki/Dire_Dawa" title="Dire Dawa">Dire Dawa</a> and of the <a href="/wiki/Oromia_Zone" title="Oromia Zone">Oromia Zone</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Amhara_Region" title="Amhara Region">Amhara Region</a>. Somali is the official working language of <a href="/wiki/Somali_Region" title="Somali Region">Somali Region</a> and <a href="/wiki/Dire_Dawa" title="Dire Dawa">Dire Dawa</a>, while Afar,<sup id="cite_ref-315" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-315">&#91;313&#93;</a></sup> Harari,<sup id="cite_ref-316" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-316">&#91;314&#93;</a></sup> and Tigrinya<sup id="cite_ref-317" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-317">&#91;315&#93;</a></sup> are recognized as official working languages in their respective regions. Recently the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Government" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethiopian Government">Ethiopian Government</a> announced that <a href="/wiki/Afar_language" title="Afar language">Afar</a>, <a href="/wiki/Amharic_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Amharic language">Amharic</a>, <a href="/wiki/Oromo_language" title="Oromo language">Oromo</a>, <a href="/wiki/Somali_language" title="Somali language">Somali</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Tigrinya_language" title="Tigrinya language">Tigrinya</a> are adopted as official federal working languages of Ethiopia.<sup id="cite_ref-Ventures_1-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ventures-1">&#91;1&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Nazret_2-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Nazret-2">&#91;2&#93;</a></sup>
<a href="/wiki/Italian_language" title="Italian language">Italian</a> is still spoken by some parts of the population, mostly among the older generation, and is taught in some schools (most notably the <a href="/wiki/Istituto_Statale_Italiano_Omnicomprensivo_di_Addis_Abeba" title="Istituto Statale Italiano Omnicomprensivo di Addis Abeba">Istituto Statale Italiano Omnicomprensivo di Addis Abeba</a>). Amharic and Tigrinya have both borrowed some words from the Italian language.<sup id="cite_ref-beyene2011prestiti_318-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-beyene2011prestiti-318">&#91;316&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-treccani_319-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-treccani-319">&#91;317&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Script">Script</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=35" title="Edit section: Script">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h4>
<p>Ethiopia's principal orthography is the <a href="/wiki/Ge%27ez_script" class="mw-redirect" title="Ge&#39;ez script">Ge'ez script</a>. Employed as an <a href="/wiki/Abugida" title="Abugida">abugida</a> for several of the country's languages, it first came into usage in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE as an <a href="/wiki/Abjad" title="Abjad">abjad</a> to transcribe the Semitic <a href="/wiki/Ge%27ez_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Ge&#39;ez language">Ge'ez language</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-320" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-320">&#91;318&#93;</a></sup> Ge'ez now serves as the liturgical language of both the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Orthodox_Tewahedo_Church" title="Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church">Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo</a> and <a href="/wiki/Eritrean_Orthodox_Tewahedo_Church" title="Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church">Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo</a> Churches. During the 1980s, the Ethiopic character set was computerized. It is today part of the <a href="/wiki/Unicode" title="Unicode">Unicode</a> standard as Ethiopic, <a href="/wiki/Ethiopic_Extended" title="Ethiopic Extended">Ethiopic Extended</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ethiopic_Supplement" title="Ethiopic Supplement">Ethiopic Supplement</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ethiopic_Extended-A" title="Ethiopic Extended-A">Ethiopic Extended-A</a>.
</p><p>Other <a href="/wiki/Writing_system" title="Writing system">writing systems</a> have also been used over the years by different Ethiopian communities. The latter include <a href="/wiki/Bakri_Sapalo" title="Bakri Sapalo">Bakri Sapalo</a>'s script for <a href="/wiki/Oromo_language" title="Oromo language">Oromo</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-HH-551_321-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-HH-551-321">&#91;319&#93;</a></sup>
</p>

<p>Religion in Ethiopia (2016 estimate)<sup id="cite_ref-322" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-322">&#91;320&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Orchid; color:black;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Orthodox_Church" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethiopian Orthodox Church">Ethiopian Orthodoxy</a> (43.8%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Blue; color:white;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/P%27ent%27ay" title="P&#39;ent&#39;ay">P'ent'ay</a> (22.8%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Purple; color:white;">&#160;</span>&#160;Other <a href="/wiki/Christian" class="mw-redirect" title="Christian">Christian</a> (0.7%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Green; color:white;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Islam_in_Ethiopia" title="Islam in Ethiopia">Islam</a> (31.3%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Yellow; color:black;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Traditional_African_religion" class="mw-redirect" title="Traditional African religion">Traditional faiths</a> (0.6%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Red; color:black;">&#160;</span>&#160;Other (0.8%)</div>
</div>
</div></div>
<p>Ethiopia has close historical ties with all three of the world's major <a href="/wiki/Abrahamic_religions" title="Abrahamic religions">Abrahamic religions</a>. In the 4th century, the Ethiopian empire was one of the first in the world to officially adopt Christianity as the state religion. As a result of the resolutions of the <a href="/wiki/Council_of_Chalcedon" title="Council of Chalcedon">Council of Chalcedon</a>, in 451 the <a href="/wiki/Miaphysitism" title="Miaphysitism">Miaphysites</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-first_seven_323-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-first_seven-323">&#91;321&#93;</a></sup> which included the vast majority of Christians in Egypt and Ethiopia, were accused of <a href="/wiki/Monophysitism" title="Monophysitism">monophysitism</a> and designated as heretics under the common name of <a href="/wiki/Coptic_Orthodox_Church_of_Alexandria" class="mw-redirect" title="Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria">Coptic Christianity</a> (see <a href="/wiki/Oriental_Orthodoxy" class="mw-redirect" title="Oriental Orthodoxy">Oriental Orthodoxy</a>). While no longer distinguished as a state religion, the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Orthodox_Tewahedo_Church" title="Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church">Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church</a> remains the majority <a href="/wiki/Christian_denomination" title="Christian denomination">Christian denomination</a>. There is also a substantial Muslim demographic, representing around a third of the population. Ethiopia was the destination of the <a href="/wiki/First_Hijrah" class="mw-redirect" title="First Hijrah">First Hijrah</a>, a major emigration in Islamic history. A town in the Tigray Region, <a href="/wiki/Negash" title="Negash">Negash</a> is the oldest Muslim settlement in Africa.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ethiopia_-_sunset_at_Church_of_Saint_George,_Lalibela_01.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Ethiopia_-_sunset_at_Church_of_Saint_George%2C_Lalibela_01.jpg/220px-Ethiopia_-_sunset_at_Church_of_Saint_George%2C_Lalibela_01.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Ethiopia_-_sunset_at_Church_of_Saint_George%2C_Lalibela_01.jpg/330px-Ethiopia_-_sunset_at_Church_of_Saint_George%2C_Lalibela_01.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Ethiopia_-_sunset_at_Church_of_Saint_George%2C_Lalibela_01.jpg/440px-Ethiopia_-_sunset_at_Church_of_Saint_George%2C_Lalibela_01.jpg 2x" data-file-width="6718" data-file-height="4478" /></a><figcaption>The subterranean rock-hewn <a href="/wiki/Church_of_Saint_George,_Lalibela" title="Church of Saint George, Lalibela">Church of Saint George</a> in <a href="/wiki/Lalibela" title="Lalibela">Lalibela</a> is a <a href="/wiki/World_Heritage_Site" title="World Heritage Site">UNESCO World Heritage Site</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>According to the 2007 National Census, Christians make up 62.8% of the country's population (43.5% Ethiopian Orthodox, 19.3% other denominations), Muslims 33.9%, practitioners of traditional faiths 2.6%, and other religions 0.6%.<sup id="cite_ref-2007Census_6-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2007Census-6">&#91;6&#93;</a></sup> The ratio of the Christian to Muslim population has largely remained stable when compared to previous censuses conducted decades ago.<sup id="cite_ref-bx_324-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bx-324">&#91;322&#93;</a></sup> Sunnis form the majority of Muslims with <a href="/wiki/Non-denominational_Muslim" title="Non-denominational Muslim">non-denominational Muslims</a> being the second largest group of Muslims, and <a href="/wiki/Shia_Islam" title="Shia Islam">the Shia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ahmadiyya" title="Ahmadiyya">Ahmadiyyas</a> are a minority. Sunnis are largely <a href="/wiki/Shafi%27i" class="mw-redirect" title="Shafi&#39;i">Shafi'is</a> or <a href="/wiki/Salafi_movement" title="Salafi movement">Salafis</a>, and there are also many <a href="/wiki/Sufism" title="Sufism">Sufi</a> Muslims there.<sup id="cite_ref-325" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-325">&#91;323&#93;</a></sup> The large Muslim population in the northern Afar region has resulted in a Muslim separatist movement called the "Islamic State of Afaria" seeking a <a href="/wiki/Sharia" title="Sharia">sharia</a>-compliant constitution.<sup id="cite_ref-326" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-326">&#91;324&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Some critics asserted that the Haile Selassie regime had been fabricating the census to present Ethiopia as a Christian country to the outside world, stating that Islam made up 50% of the total population in 1991, based on the 1984 census commissioned by the <a href="/wiki/Derg" title="Derg">Derg</a> regime.<sup id="cite_ref-327" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-327">&#91;325&#93;</a></sup> Several Muslim observers and bloggers claim that Muslims are in the majority and disagree with the above census numbers, without providing factual data supporting their claims.<sup id="cite_ref-328" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-328">&#91;326&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Axum" class="mw-redirect" title="Kingdom of Axum">Kingdom of Axum</a> was one of the first polities to officially embrace Christianity, when <a href="/wiki/Frumentius" title="Frumentius">Frumentius</a> of <a href="/wiki/Tyre,_Lebanon" title="Tyre, Lebanon">Tyre</a>, called Fremnatos or Abba Selama ("Father of Peace") in Ethiopia, converted Emperor <a href="/wiki/Ezana_of_Axum" title="Ezana of Axum">Ezana</a> during the 4th century.<sup id="cite_ref-isbn0-313-32273-2_78-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-isbn0-313-32273-2-78">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Ofcansky_329-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ofcansky-329">&#91;327&#93;</a></sup> According to the <a href="/wiki/New_Testament" title="New Testament">New Testament</a>, Christianity had entered Ethiopia even earlier, when an official in the Ethiopian royal treasury was baptized by <a href="/wiki/Philip_the_Evangelist" title="Philip the Evangelist">Philip the Evangelist</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-330" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-330">&#91;328&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:NegashMosque.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/NegashMosque.jpg/220px-NegashMosque.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/NegashMosque.jpg/330px-NegashMosque.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/NegashMosque.jpg/440px-NegashMosque.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4032" data-file-height="3024" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Al_Nejashi_Mosque" title="Al Nejashi Mosque">Al Negashi Mosque</a> is the second oldest Mosque in the World dating back to the 6th century, the oldest in the country<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (September 2023)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Orthodox_Tewahedo_Church" title="Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church">Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church</a> is part of <a href="/wiki/Oriental_Orthodoxy" class="mw-redirect" title="Oriental Orthodoxy">Oriental Orthodoxy</a>. It is by far the largest Christian denomination, although a number of <a href="/wiki/P%27ent%27ay" title="P&#39;ent&#39;ay">P'ent'ay</a> (<a href="/wiki/Protestantism" title="Protestantism">Protestant</a>) churches have recently gained ground. Since 1930, a relatively  small <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Catholic_Church" title="Ethiopian Catholic Church">Ethiopian Catholic Church</a> has existed in <a href="/wiki/Full_communion" title="Full communion">full communion</a> with Rome, with adherents making up less than 1% of the total population.<sup id="cite_ref-bx_324-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bx-324">&#91;322&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-331" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-331">&#91;329&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Islam_in_Ethiopia" title="Islam in Ethiopia">Islam in Ethiopia</a> dates back to the founding of the religion in 622 when a group of Muslims were counselled by <a href="/wiki/Muhammad" title="Muhammad">Muhammad</a> to escape persecution in <a href="/wiki/Mecca" title="Mecca">Mecca</a>. The disciples subsequently <a href="/wiki/Migrated_to_Abyssinia" class="mw-redirect" title="Migrated to Abyssinia">migrated to Abyssinia</a> via modern-day Eritrea, which was at the time ruled by <a href="/wiki/Ashama_ibn-Abjar" class="mw-redirect" title="Ashama ibn-Abjar">Ashama ibn-Abjar</a>, a pious Christian emperor.<sup id="cite_ref-Ofcansky_329-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ofcansky-329">&#91;327&#93;</a></sup> Also, the largest single ethnic group of <a href="/wiki/List_of_non-Arab_Sahabah" title="List of non-Arab Sahabah">non-Arab Sahabah</a> was that of the Ethiopians.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (February 2013)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Human_rights_group" title="Human rights group">Human rights groups</a> have regularly accused the government of arresting activists, journalists and bloggers to stamp out dissent among some religious communities. Lengthy prison terms were handed to 17 Muslim activists on 3<span class="nowrap">&#160;</span>August 2015 ranging from seven to 22 years. They were charged with trying to create an Islamic state in the majority Christian country. All the defendants denied the charges and claimed that they were merely protesting in defence of their rights.<sup id="cite_ref-332" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-332">&#91;330&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-333" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-333">&#91;331&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-334" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-334">&#91;332&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Urbanization">Urbanization</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=37" title="Edit section: Urbanization">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Ethiopia" title="List of cities and towns in Ethiopia">List of cities and towns in Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:AddisView.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/AddisView.jpg/220px-AddisView.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/AddisView.jpg/330px-AddisView.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/AddisView.jpg/440px-AddisView.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="1366" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Sheger_Park" title="Sheger Park">Sheger Park</a> is the largest park in the country, hosting hundreds of thousands of visitors a year since its opening</figcaption></figure>
<p>Population growth, migration, and urbanization are all straining both governments' and ecosystems' capacity to provide people with basic services.<sup id="cite_ref-335" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-335">&#91;333&#93;</a></sup> Urbanization has steadily been increasing in Ethiopia, with two periods of significantly rapid growth. First, in 1936–1941 during the Italian occupation under Mussolini's fascist government, and then from 1967 to 1975 when the populations of urban areas tripled.<sup id="cite_ref-countrystudies1991_336-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-countrystudies1991-336">&#91;334&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1936, Italy annexed Ethiopia, building infrastructure to connect major cities, and a dam providing power and water.<sup id="cite_ref-Accessed_15_May_2008_337-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Accessed_15_May_2008-337">&#91;335&#93;</a></sup> This, along with the influx of Italians and labourers, was the major cause of rapid growth during this period. The second period of growth was from 1967 to 1975, when rural populations migrated to towns seeking work and better living conditions.<sup id="cite_ref-countrystudies1991_336-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-countrystudies1991-336">&#91;334&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>This pattern slowed due to the 1975 Land Reform program instituted by the government, which provided incentives for people to stay in rural areas. As people moved from rural areas to the cities, there were fewer people to grow food for the population. The Land Reform Act was meant to increase agriculture since food production was not keeping up with population growth over the period of 1970–1983. This program encouraged the formation of peasant associations, large villages based on agriculture. The legislation did lead to an increase in food production, although there is debate over the cause; it may be related to weather conditions more than the reform.<sup id="cite_ref-Anderson,_Frank_1991._Pages_159-175_338-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Anderson,_Frank_1991._Pages_159-175-338">&#91;336&#93;</a></sup> Urban populations have continued to grow with an 8.1% increase from 1975 to 2000.<sup id="cite_ref-Accessed_5-10-08_339-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Accessed_5-10-08-339">&#91;337&#93;</a></sup>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1148739982">.mw-parser-output .largestCities-table-background{background:#f9f9f9}.mw-parser-output .largestCities-cell-background{background:#f0f0f0}</style>
</p>
