<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Rural_and_urban_life">Rural and urban life</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=38" title="Edit section: Rural and urban life">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Rural_flight_in_Ethiopia" title="Rural flight in Ethiopia">Rural flight in Ethiopia</a></div>
<p>Migration to urban areas is usually motivated by the hope of better lives. In peasant associations daily life is a struggle to survive. About 16% of the population in Ethiopia lives on less than one dollar per day (2008). Only 65% of rural households in Ethiopia consume the <a href="/wiki/World_Health_Organization" title="World Health Organization">World Health Organization</a>'s (WHO's) minimum standard of food per day (2,200 kilocalories), with 42% of children under 5 years old being underweight.<sup id="cite_ref-Crawley_341-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Crawley-341">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Most poor families (75%) share their sleeping quarters with livestock, and 40% of children sleep on the floor, where nighttime temperatures average 5 degrees Celsius in the cold season.<sup id="cite_ref-Crawley_341-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Crawley-341">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup> The average family size is six or seven, living in a 30 square metre mud and thatch hut, with less than two hectares of land to cultivate.<sup id="cite_ref-Crawley_341-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Crawley-341">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The peasant associations face a cycle of poverty. Since the landholdings are so small, farmers cannot allow the land to lie fallow, which reduces soil fertility.<sup id="cite_ref-Crawley_341-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Crawley-341">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup> This <a href="/wiki/Land_degradation" title="Land degradation">land degradation</a> reduces the production of fodder for livestock, which causes low milk yields.<sup id="cite_ref-Crawley_341-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Crawley-341">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup> Since the community burns livestock manure as fuel, rather than plowing the nutrients back into the land, the crop production is reduced.<sup id="cite_ref-Crawley_341-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Crawley-341">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup> The low productivity of agriculture leads to inadequate incomes for farmers, hunger, malnutrition and disease. These unhealthy farmers have difficulty working the land and the productivity drops further.<sup id="cite_ref-Crawley_341-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Crawley-341">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Although conditions are drastically better in cities, all of Ethiopia suffers from poverty and poor sanitation. However, poverty in Ethiopia fell from 44% to 29.6% during 2000–2011, according to the World Bank.<sup id="cite_ref-342" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-342">&#91;340&#93;</a></sup> In the capital city of Addis Ababa, 55% of the population used to live in slums.<sup id="cite_ref-Accessed_15_May_2008_337-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Accessed_15_May_2008-337">&#91;335&#93;</a></sup> Now, however, a construction boom in both the private and the public sector has led to a dramatic improvement in living standards in major cities, particularly in Addis Ababa. Notably, government-built condominium housing complexes have sprung up throughout the city, benefiting close to 600,000 individuals.<sup id="cite_ref-343" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-343">&#91;341&#93;</a></sup> Sanitation is the most pressing need in the city, with most of the population lacking access to waste treatment facilities. This contributes to the spread of illness through unhealthy water.<sup id="cite_ref-Accessed_15_May_2008_337-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Accessed_15_May_2008-337">&#91;335&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Despite the living conditions in the cities, the people of Addis Ababa are much better off than people living in the peasant associations owing to their educational opportunities. Unlike rural children, 69% of urban children are enrolled in primary school, and 35% of those are eligible to attend secondary school.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="margin-left:0.1em; white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify" title="Wikipedia:Please clarify"><span title="The text near this tag may need clarification or removal of jargon. (December 2016)">clarification needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup><sup id="cite_ref-Accessed_15_May_2008_337-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Accessed_15_May_2008-337">&#91;335&#93;</a></sup> Addis Ababa has its own <a href="/wiki/Addis_Ababa_University" title="Addis Ababa University">university</a> as well as many other secondary schools. The literacy rate is 82%.<sup id="cite_ref-Accessed_15_May_2008_337-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Accessed_15_May_2008-337">&#91;335&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Many NGOs (Non-Governmental Organizations) are working to solve this problem; however, most are far apart, uncoordinated, and working in isolation.<sup id="cite_ref-Accessed_5-10-08_339-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Accessed_5-10-08-339">&#91;337&#93;</a></sup> The Sub-Saharan Africa NGO Consortium is attempting to coordinate efforts.<sup id="cite_ref-Accessed_5-10-08_339-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Accessed_5-10-08-339">&#91;337&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Health">Health</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=39" title="Edit section: Health">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Health_in_Ethiopia" title="Health in Ethiopia">Health in Ethiopia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Healthcare_in_Ethiopia" title="Healthcare in Ethiopia">Healthcare in Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Child_mortality_in_Sub-Saharan_Africa_and_Ethiopia.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Child_mortality_in_Sub-Saharan_Africa_and_Ethiopia.svg/220px-Child_mortality_in_Sub-Saharan_Africa_and_Ethiopia.svg.png" decoding="async" width="220" height="155" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Child_mortality_in_Sub-Saharan_Africa_and_Ethiopia.svg/330px-Child_mortality_in_Sub-Saharan_Africa_and_Ethiopia.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Child_mortality_in_Sub-Saharan_Africa_and_Ethiopia.svg/440px-Child_mortality_in_Sub-Saharan_Africa_and_Ethiopia.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="850" data-file-height="600" /></a><figcaption>Declining child mortality in Sub-Saharan Africa and Ethiopia since 1950</figcaption></figure>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/World_Health_Organization" title="World Health Organization">World Health Organization</a>'s 2006 World Health Report gives a figure of 1,936 physicians (for 2003),<sup id="cite_ref-344" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-344">&#91;342&#93;</a></sup> which comes to about 2.6 per 100,000. A <a href="/wiki/Brain_drain" class="mw-redirect" title="Brain drain">brain drain</a> associated with <a href="/wiki/Globalization" title="Globalization">globalization</a> is said to affect the country, with many educated professionals leaving Ethiopia for better economic opportunities in the West.
</p><p>Ethiopia's main health problems are said to be communicable (contagious) diseases worsened by poor sanitation and <a href="/wiki/Malnutrition" title="Malnutrition">malnutrition</a>. Over 58&#160;million people (nearly half the population) do not have access to clean water as of 2023.<sup id="cite_ref-345" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-345">&#91;343&#93;</a></sup> These problems are exacerbated by the shortage of trained doctors and nurses and health facilities.<sup id="cite_ref-346" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-346">&#91;344&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Only a minority of Ethiopians are born in hospitals, while most are born in rural households. Those who are expected to give birth at home have elderly women serve as midwives who assist with the delivery.<sup id="cite_ref-347" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-347">&#91;345&#93;</a></sup> The "WHO estimates that a majority of maternal fatalities and disabilities could be prevented if deliveries were to take place at well-equipped health centres, with adequately trained staff".<sup id="cite_ref-348" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-348">&#91;346&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Birth_rate" title="Birth rate">Birth rates</a>, <a href="/wiki/Infant_mortality_rate" class="mw-redirect" title="Infant mortality rate">infant mortality rates</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Death_rate" class="mw-redirect" title="Death rate">death rates</a> are lower in cities than in rural areas due to better access to education, medicines, and hospitals.<sup id="cite_ref-Accessed_15_May_2008_337-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Accessed_15_May_2008-337">&#91;335&#93;</a></sup> Life expectancy is better in cities compared to rural areas, but there have been significant improvements witnessed throughout the country as of 2016, the average Ethiopian living to be 62.2 years old, according to a <a href="/wiki/UNDP" class="mw-redirect" title="UNDP">UNDP</a> report.<sup id="cite_ref-349" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-349">&#91;347&#93;</a></sup> Despite sanitation being a problem, use of improved water sources is also on the rise; 81% in cities compared to 11% in rural areas.<sup id="cite_ref-Accessed_5-10-08_339-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Accessed_5-10-08-339">&#91;337&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In early 2005,<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup> the WHO reported that Ethiopia had 119 hospitals (12 in Addis Ababa) and 412 health centres.<sup id="cite_ref-who_2005_350-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-who_2005-350">&#91;348&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Infant_mortality" title="Infant mortality">Infant mortality</a> rates are relatively high, as 41 infants die per 1,000 live births.<sup id="cite_ref-351" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-351">&#91;349&#93;</a></sup> Ethiopia succeeded in reducing its under-five mortality rate by two-thirds (one of the <a href="/wiki/Millennium_Development_Goals" title="Millennium Development Goals">Millennium Development Goals</a>) between 1990 and 2012.<sup id="cite_ref-352" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-352">&#91;350&#93;</a></sup> Although this is a dramatic decrease, birth-related complications such as <a href="/wiki/Obstetric_fistula" title="Obstetric fistula">obstetric fistula</a> affect many of the nation's women.<sup id="cite_ref-353" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-353">&#91;351&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/HIV/AIDS_in_Ethiopia" title="HIV/AIDS in Ethiopia">HIV/AIDS in Ethiopia</a> stood at 1.1% in 2014, a dramatic decrease from 4.5% 15 years ago.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (June 2019)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> The most affected are poor communities and women, due to lack of health education, empowerment, awareness and lack of social well-being. The government of Ethiopia and many international organizations like <a href="/wiki/World_Health_Organization" title="World Health Organization">World Health Organization</a> (WHO), and the United Nations, are launching campaigns and are working aggressively to improve Ethiopia's health conditions and promote health awareness on AIDS and other communicable diseases.<sup id="cite_ref-354" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-354">&#91;352&#93;</a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items" title="Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers"><span title="The date of the event predicted near this tag has passed. (September 2023)">needs update</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p>Ethiopia has a high prevalence of FGM, but prevalence is lower among young girls. Ethiopia's 2005 Demographic and Health Survey (EDHS) noted that the national prevalence rate is 74% among women ages 15–49.<sup id="cite_ref-355" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-355">&#91;353&#93;</a></sup> According to a 2010 study performed by the Population Reference Bureau, Ethiopia has a prevalence rate of 81% among women ages 35 to 39 and 62% among women ages 15–19.<sup id="cite_ref-356" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-356">&#91;354&#93;</a></sup> A 2014 UNICEF report found that only 24% of girls under 14 had undergone FGM.<sup id="cite_ref-357" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-357">&#91;355&#93;</a></sup> Male <a href="/wiki/Circumcision" title="Circumcision">circumcision</a> is also practised in the country, and about 76% of Ethiopia's male population is reportedly circumcised.<sup id="cite_ref-Ahuja_358-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ahuja-358">&#91;356&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The National Mental Health Strategy, published in 2012, introduced the development of policy designed to improve mental health care in Ethiopia. This strategy mandated that mental health be integrated into the primary health care system.<sup id="cite_ref-359" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-359">&#91;357&#93;</a></sup> However, the success of the National Mental Health Strategy has been limited. For example, the burden of depression is estimated to have increased 34.2% from 2007 to 2017.<sup id="cite_ref-360" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-360">&#91;358&#93;</a></sup> Furthermore, the prevalence of stigmatizing attitudes, inadequate leadership and co-ordination of efforts, as well as a lack of mental health awareness in the general population, all remain as obstacles to successful mental health care.<sup id="cite_ref-361" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-361">&#91;359&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Education">Education</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=40" title="Edit section: Education">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Education_in_Ethiopia" title="Education in Ethiopia">Education in Ethiopia</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Higher_education_in_Ethiopia" title="Higher education in Ethiopia">Higher education in Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Parco_dell%27universit%C3%A0_di_addis_abeba,_09.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Parco_dell%27universit%C3%A0_di_addis_abeba%2C_09.jpg/220px-Parco_dell%27universit%C3%A0_di_addis_abeba%2C_09.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="171" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Parco_dell%27universit%C3%A0_di_addis_abeba%2C_09.jpg/330px-Parco_dell%27universit%C3%A0_di_addis_abeba%2C_09.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Parco_dell%27universit%C3%A0_di_addis_abeba%2C_09.jpg/440px-Parco_dell%27universit%C3%A0_di_addis_abeba%2C_09.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4520" data-file-height="3504" /></a><figcaption>Entrance of <a href="/wiki/Addis_Ababa_University" title="Addis Ababa University">Addis Ababa University</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Educational system of Ethiopia was dominated by the <a href="/wiki/Orthodox_Tewahedo" title="Orthodox Tewahedo">Orthodox Tewahedo</a> Church since the Axumite Christian era in 330 CE. An <a href="/wiki/Traditional_education_in_Ethiopia" title="Traditional education in Ethiopia">ancient form of Ethiopian Christian education</a> was conducted by clergymen, with highly emphasized its dogma. Graduation of students leads to earning priesthood and intellectual elite known as <a href="/wiki/Debtera" title="Debtera">debtera</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-362" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-362">&#91;360&#93;</a></sup> Modern education was introduced in 1908 when Emperor Menelik II opened the first school in Addis Ababa, <a href="/wiki/Menelik_II_School" title="Menelik II School">Menelik II School</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-363" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-363">&#91;361&#93;</a></sup> In addition, Emperor Haile Selassie I also contributed to open the first university, <a href="/wiki/Addis_Ababa_University" title="Addis Ababa University">Addis Ababa University</a>, founded in 1950 after it was renamed "Haile Selassie I University" until 1975. More recently, the government is improving numerous regional universities and facilities.<sup id="cite_ref-364" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-364">&#91;362&#93;</a></sup> 
The current system follows school expansion schemes which are very similar to the system in the rural areas during the 1980s, with an addition of deeper regionalization, providing rural education in students' own languages starting at the elementary level, and with more budgetary financing allocated to the education sector. Public education is free at primary levels and usually offers between age 7 and 12. The sequence of general education in Ethiopia is six years of primary school, then four years of lower secondary school followed by two years of higher secondary school.<sup id="cite_ref-365" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-365">&#91;363&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Top_floor_of_the_first_science_museum_in_Ethiopia.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Top_floor_of_the_first_science_museum_in_Ethiopia.jpg/220px-Top_floor_of_the_first_science_museum_in_Ethiopia.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Top_floor_of_the_first_science_museum_in_Ethiopia.jpg/330px-Top_floor_of_the_first_science_museum_in_Ethiopia.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Top_floor_of_the_first_science_museum_in_Ethiopia.jpg/440px-Top_floor_of_the_first_science_museum_in_Ethiopia.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4032" data-file-height="3024" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia_Museum_of_Art_and_Science" title="Ethiopia Museum of Art and Science">Addis Ababa Science Museum of Art and Science</a> serves as the country's biggest hub which showcases the country's newest innovations</figcaption></figure>
<p>The Ethiopian education is governed by <a href="/wiki/Ministry_of_Education_(Ethiopia)" title="Ministry of Education (Ethiopia)">Ministry of Education</a> and its cycle consists 4+4+2+2 system; elementary education consists of eight years, divided into two cycles of four years, and four years of secondary education, divided into two stages of two years.<sup id="cite_ref-366" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-366">&#91;364&#93;</a></sup> National exams are conducted by the <a href="/wiki/National_Educational_Assessment_and_Examination_Agency" title="National Educational Assessment and Examination Agency">National Education Assessment and Examination Agency</a> (NEAEA). Since 2018, there are two national exams: the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_General_Secondary_Education_Certificate_Examination" title="Ethiopian General Secondary Education Certificate Examination">Ethiopian General Secondary Education Certificate Examination</a> (EGSECE), also known as Grade 10 national exam and  Grade 12 national exam.<sup id="cite_ref-367" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-367">&#91;365&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Today, there are 30 public universities. Prior to 1991, Ethiopia did not have tertiary institution, but now there are 61 accredited private HEIs. The overall number of tertiary students in both public and private institutions exploded by more than 2,000 percent, from 34,000 in 1991 to 757,000 in 2014, per UIS data.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_297-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-297">&#91;295&#93;</a></sup>
Access to education in Ethiopia has improved significantly. Approximately three million people were in primary school in 1994–95 but by 2008–09, primary enrolment had risen to 15.5&#160;million – an increase of over 500%.<sup id="cite_ref-368" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-368">&#91;366&#93;</a></sup> In 2013–14, Ethiopia had witnessed a significant boost in gross enrolment across all regions.<sup id="cite_ref-369" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-369">&#91;367&#93;</a></sup> The national GER was 104.8% for boys, 97.8% for girls and 101.3% across both sexes.<sup id="cite_ref-370" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-370">&#91;368&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The literacy rate has increased in recent years: according to the 1994 census, the literacy rate in Ethiopia was 23.4%.<sup id="cite_ref-Ethnologue_310-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ethnologue-310">&#91;308&#93;</a></sup> In 2007 it was estimated to be 39% (male 49.1% and female 28.9%).<sup id="cite_ref-371" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-371">&#91;369&#93;</a></sup> A report by UNDP in 2011 showed that the literacy rate in Ethiopia was 46.7%. The same report also indicated that the female literacy rate had increased from 27 to 39 per cent from 2004 to 2011, and the male literacy rate had increased from 49 to 59 per cent over the same period for persons 10 years and older.<sup id="cite_ref-372" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-372">&#91;370&#93;</a></sup> By 2015, the literacy rate had further increased, to 49.1% (57.2% male and 41.1% female).<sup id="cite_ref-373" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-373">&#91;371&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Culture">Culture</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=41" title="Edit section: Culture">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Culture_of_Ethiopia" title="Culture of Ethiopia">Culture of Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ethiopia_IMG_5782_Addis_Abeba_(25052967317).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/83/Ethiopia_IMG_5782_Addis_Abeba_%2825052967317%29.jpg/220px-Ethiopia_IMG_5782_Addis_Abeba_%2825052967317%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="130" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/83/Ethiopia_IMG_5782_Addis_Abeba_%2825052967317%29.jpg/330px-Ethiopia_IMG_5782_Addis_Abeba_%2825052967317%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/83/Ethiopia_IMG_5782_Addis_Abeba_%2825052967317%29.jpg/440px-Ethiopia_IMG_5782_Addis_Abeba_%2825052967317%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3184" data-file-height="1884" /></a><figcaption>Cultural performance in Addis Ababa</figcaption></figure>
<p>Ethiopia's rich and diverse culture heavily influenced by the local population, an interaction of Semitic, Cushitic and less populous Nilo-Saharan speaking people, which evolved from first millennium BCE. Semitic Tigrayans and Amharas, who dominated the politics in the past, distinguished from other population by hierarchical structure and agrarian life derived partly from South Arabia as a result of back migration, while the southern Cushitic (Oromo and Somali) are strong adherents to <a href="/wiki/Egalitarianism" title="Egalitarianism">egalitarianism</a> and pastoral life. Others including Kaffa, Sidamo, and Afar tradition derived from the latter people.<sup id="cite_ref-374" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-374">&#91;372&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The most common recognized culture observed in <a href="/wiki/Coffee_ceremony_of_Ethiopia_and_Eritrea" title="Coffee ceremony of Ethiopia and Eritrea">coffee ceremony</a>. Unlike most countries, coffee is served in presence of social gathering, in family, friend or neighborhood level. There are three rounds of coffee drinking: the first one called "awol" (<a href="/wiki/Tigrinya_language" title="Tigrinya language">Tigrinya</a>: <span lang="ti">ኣዎል</span>), the second "tona" (ቶና) and the third "baraka" (ባርካ). The tradition of coffee legend goes back to Kaldi, a <a href="/wiki/Goatherd" title="Goatherd">goat herder</a> from <a href="/wiki/Keffa_Zone" title="Keffa Zone">Keffa Zone</a> who noticed his goat was caught up with <a href="/wiki/Hysteria" title="Hysteria">hysteria</a> after they eat shrub that stimulate them to dance uncontrollably with rampant. After holding berries, he was advised exhibit to priests in nearby monastery. One monk called the generosity of Kaldi "the Devil work" and tossed to the fire, generating aromatic odor. The legend told that Kaldi lived in 850 CE, commonly associated with belief of starting coffee cultivation in Ethiopia in the 9th century.<sup id="cite_ref-:6_278-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:6-278">&#91;276&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Arts">Arts</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=42" title="Edit section: Arts">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_art" title="Ethiopian art">Ethiopian art</a></div>
<figure class="mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Afewerk_Tekle_1965.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Afewerk_Tekle_1965.jpg/156px-Afewerk_Tekle_1965.jpg" decoding="async" width="156" height="230" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Afewerk_Tekle_1965.jpg/234px-Afewerk_Tekle_1965.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Afewerk_Tekle_1965.jpg/312px-Afewerk_Tekle_1965.jpg 2x" data-file-width="696" data-file-height="1024" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Afewerk_Tekle" title="Afewerk Tekle">Afewerk Tekle</a> was a renowned laureate modern Ethiopian artist known for his paintings in the 50s through 70s which depicted Ethiopian culture</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Garima_Gospels.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Garima_Gospels.jpg/220px-Garima_Gospels.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="144" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Garima_Gospels.jpg/330px-Garima_Gospels.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/30/Garima_Gospels.jpg 2x" data-file-width="440" data-file-height="288" /></a><figcaption>An Orthodox bible dated at least 1,500 Years, being the oldest illustrating bible in the world, depicts <a href="/wiki/Corinthian_order" title="Corinthian order">Corinthian pillars</a></figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_art" title="Ethiopian art">Arts of Ethiopia</a> were largely influenced by Christian iconography throughout much of its history. This consisted of <a href="/wiki/Illuminated_manuscripts" class="mw-redirect" title="Illuminated manuscripts">illuminated manuscripts</a>, <a href="/wiki/Painting" title="Painting">painting</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_cross" title="Ethiopian cross">crosses</a>, <a href="/wiki/Icon" title="Icon">icons</a> and other <a href="/wiki/Metalwork" class="mw-redirect" title="Metalwork">metalwork</a> such as crowns. Most historical arts were commissioned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, the state religion for a millennium. The earlier Aksumite period arts were stone carvings as evidenced in their stelae, though there is no surviving Christian art from this era. As Christianity was introduced, its iconography was partly influenced by <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">Byzantine art</a>. Most remaining arts beyond the early modern period were ruined as a result of invasion of the <a href="/wiki/Adal_Sultanate" title="Adal Sultanate">Adal Sultanate</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Highlands" title="Ethiopian Highlands">Ethiopian Highlands</a>, but were revived by Catholic emissaries. The <a href="/wiki/Western_art" class="mw-redirect" title="Western art">Western</a> intervention in Ethiopian art began in the 20th century, with also maintaining traditional Ethiopian character.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (July 2022)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Architecture">Architecture</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=43" title="Edit section: Architecture">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Architecture_of_Ethiopia" title="Architecture of Ethiopia">Architecture of Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Aksum_obelisk.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Aksum_obelisk.jpg/220px-Aksum_obelisk.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Aksum_obelisk.jpg/330px-Aksum_obelisk.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Aksum_obelisk.jpg/440px-Aksum_obelisk.jpg 2x" data-file-width="6000" data-file-height="4000" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Axum_stelae" class="mw-redirect" title="Axum stelae">Axumite Stella</a>'s in the Northern Part of Ethiopia dating well over a thousand year's serve as a remembrance of Ethiopia's past architecture.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The "Bete Medhane Alem" or "House of our Saviour" is one of the 12 churches in <a href="/wiki/Lalibela" title="Lalibela">Lalibela</a> built under Emperor <a href="/wiki/Lalibela_(Emperor_of_Ethiopia)" class="mw-redirect" title="Lalibela (Emperor of Ethiopia)">Lalibela I</a>Perhaps the most impressive architecture in antiquity was founded during Dʿmt period. <a href="/wiki/Ashlar_masonry" class="mw-redirect" title="Ashlar masonry">Ashlar masonry</a> was an archetype of <a href="/wiki/South_Arabia" title="South Arabia">South Arabian</a> architecture with most architectural structure similarity.<sup id="cite_ref-375" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-375">&#91;373&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Aksumite continued to flourish its architecture around the 4th century CE. Aksumite stelae commonly used single block and rocks. The Tomb of the False Door built for Aksumite emperors used monolithic style.<sup id="cite_ref-376" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-376">&#91;374&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Lalibela" title="Lalibela">Lalibela</a> civilization was largely of Aksumite influence, but the layer of stones or wood is quite different for some dwelling.<sup id="cite_ref-377" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-377">&#91;375&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>In Gondarine period, the architecture of Ethiopia was infused by Baroque, Arab, Turkish and Gujarati Indian styles independently taught by Portuguese emissaries in the 16th and 17th centuries. Example includes the imperial fortress <a href="/wiki/Fasil_Ghebbi" title="Fasil Ghebbi">Fasil Ghebbi</a>, which is influenced by either of these styles. The medieval architecture also forborne the later 19th- and 20th-century era of designations.<sup id="cite_ref-378" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-378">&#91;376&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Philosophy">Philosophy</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=44" title="Edit section: Philosophy">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_philosophy" title="Ethiopian philosophy">Ethiopian philosophy</a></div>
<p>Ethiopian philosophy has been superlatively prolific since ancient times in Africa, though offset of <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Greek_philosophy" title="Ancient Greek philosophy">Greek</a> and <a href="/wiki/Patristic" class="mw-redirect" title="Patristic">Patristic</a> philosophy. The best known philosophical revival was in the early modern period figures such as <a href="/wiki/Zera_Yacob_(philosopher)" title="Zera Yacob (philosopher)">Zera Yacob</a> (1599–1692) and his student <a href="/wiki/Walda_Heywat" title="Walda Heywat">Walda Heywat</a>, who wrote <i><a href="/wiki/Hatata" title="Hatata">Hatata</a></i> (<i>Inquiry</i>) in 1667 as an argument for the <a href="/wiki/Existence_of_God" title="Existence of God">existence of God</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Literature">Literature</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=45" title="Edit section: Literature">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_literature" title="Ethiopian literature">Ethiopian literature</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Giyorgis_MET_DP367372.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Giyorgis_MET_DP367372.jpg/220px-Giyorgis_MET_DP367372.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Giyorgis_MET_DP367372.jpg/330px-Giyorgis_MET_DP367372.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Giyorgis_MET_DP367372.jpg/440px-Giyorgis_MET_DP367372.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="3001" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Giyorgis_of_Segla" title="Giyorgis of Segla">Giyorgis of Segla</a>, prolific religious author in the <a href="/wiki/Late_Middle_Ages" title="Late Middle Ages">Late Middle Ages</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_literature" title="Ethiopian literature">Ethiopian literature</a> traced back to the Aksumite period in the 4th century, most of them are merely religious motifs. In royal inscription, they employed both <a href="/wiki/Ge%CA%BDez_script" title="Geʽez script">Ge'ez</a> and <a href="/wiki/Greek_language" title="Greek language">Greek</a> language, but the latter was dismissed in 350. Unlike most Sub-Saharan African countries, Ethiopia has ancient distinct language, the Ge'ez, which dominated political and educational aspects. In spite of the current political instability in the country instigates endangering cultural heritage of these works, some improvements are made for preservation in recent years.<sup id="cite_ref-:4_379-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-379">&#91;377&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Ethiopian literary works mostly consisted of handwritten <a href="/wiki/Codex" title="Codex">codex</a> (branna, or ብራና in Amharic). It is prepared by gathering parchment leaves and sewing to stick together. The codex size is considerably varies depending on volumes and preparation. For example, pocket size codex lengthens 45&#160;cm, which is heavier in weight. Historians speculated that archaic codex is existed in Ethiopia. Today manuscripts resembling primitive codex are still evident for existence where parchment leaves are convenient for writing.<sup id="cite_ref-:4_379-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-379">&#91;377&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Another notable writing book is protective (or magic) <a href="/wiki/Scroll" title="Scroll">scroll</a>, serving as written amulet. Some of these were intended for magical purpose, for example <i>ketab</i> is used for magical defence. Scrolls typically produced by <i><a href="/wiki/Debtera" title="Debtera">debtera</a></i>, non-ordained clergy expertise on <a href="/wiki/Exorcism" title="Exorcism">exorcism</a> and healings. About 30&#160;cm scroll is portable whereas 2&#160;cm is often unrolled and hanged to the wall of house. Scrolls emulating original medium of Ethiopia literature is highly disputed, where there is overwhelming evidence that Ge'ez language books were written in codex. In lesser, Ethiopia used accordion books (called <i>sensul</i>) which was dated to late 15th or 16th century, made up of folded parchment paper, with or without cover. Those book usually contain pictorial representation of life and death of religious figures, or significant texts have also juxtaposed.<sup id="cite_ref-:4_379-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-379">&#91;377&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Poetry">Poetry</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=46" title="Edit section: Poetry">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h4>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Tsegaye_Gabre-Medhin_2.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Tsegaye_Gabre-Medhin_2.jpg/150px-Tsegaye_Gabre-Medhin_2.jpg" decoding="async" width="150" height="164" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Tsegaye_Gabre-Medhin_2.jpg/225px-Tsegaye_Gabre-Medhin_2.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Tsegaye_Gabre-Medhin_2.jpg/300px-Tsegaye_Gabre-Medhin_2.jpg 2x" data-file-width="326" data-file-height="356" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Tsegaye_Gabre-Medhin" title="Tsegaye Gabre-Medhin">Tsegaye Gebre-Medhin</a> in 1980s one of Ethiopia's renowned writers</figcaption></figure>
<p>Ethiopia is highly popularized in <a href="/wiki/Poetry" title="Poetry">poetry</a>. Most poets recount past events, social unrests, poverty and famine. <i><a href="/wiki/Qene" title="Qene">Qene</a></i> is the most used element of Ethiopian poetry – regarded as a form of Amharic poetry, though the term generally refers to any poems. True qene requires advanced ingenious mindset. By providing two metaphorical words, i.e. one with obvious clues and the other is too convoluted conundrum, one must answer parallel meanings. Thus, this is called <i>sem ena work</i> (gold and wax).<sup id="cite_ref-:9_380-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:9-380">&#91;378&#93;</a></sup> The most notable poets are <a href="/wiki/Tsegaye_Gabre-Medhin" title="Tsegaye Gabre-Medhin">Tsegaye Gebre-Medhin</a>, <a href="/wiki/Kebede_Michael" title="Kebede Michael">Kebede Michael</a> and <a href="/wiki/Mengistu_Lemma" title="Mengistu Lemma">Mengistu Lemma</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Calendar">Calendar</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=47" title="Edit section: Calendar">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_calendar" title="Ethiopian calendar">Ethiopian calendar</a> and <a href="/wiki/Oromo_calendar" class="mw-redirect" title="Oromo calendar">Oromo calendar</a></div><p>Ethiopia has several local calendars. The most widely known is the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_calendar" title="Ethiopian calendar">Ethiopian calendar</a>, also known as the Ge'ez calendar, and written with the ancient <a href="/wiki/Ge%27ez_script" class="mw-redirect" title="Ge&#39;ez script">Ge'ez script</a>, one of the oldest alphabets still in use in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-Wilfpag_381-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Wilfpag-381">&#91;379&#93;</a></sup> It is based on the older Alexandrian or <a href="/wiki/Coptic_calendar" title="Coptic calendar">Coptic calendar</a>, which in turn derives from the <a href="/wiki/Egyptian_calendar" title="Egyptian calendar">Egyptian calendar</a>. Like the Coptic calendar, the Ethiopian calendar has twelve months of exactly 30 days each plus five or six <a href="/wiki/Epagomenal" class="mw-redirect" title="Epagomenal">epagomenal</a> days, which form a thirteenth month. The Ethiopian months begin on the same days as those of the Coptic calendar, but their names are in Ge'ez<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (January 2022)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p>Like the <a href="/wiki/Julian_calendar" title="Julian calendar">Julian calendar</a>, the sixth epagomenal day—which in essence is a <a href="/wiki/Leap_day" class="mw-redirect" title="Leap day">leap day</a>—is added every four years without exception on 29 August of the Julian calendar, six months before the Julian leap day. Thus, the first day of the Ethiopian year, 1<span class="nowrap">&#160;</span>Mäskäräm, for years between 1901 and 2099 (inclusive), is usually 11 September (<a href="/wiki/Gregorian_calendar" title="Gregorian calendar">Gregorian</a>), but falls on 12 September in years before the Gregorian leap year. It is approximately seven years and three months behind the Gregorian calendar because of an alternate calculation in determining the date of the <a href="/wiki/Annunciation" title="Annunciation">Annunciation</a> of Jesus.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (January 2022)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p>Another calendrical system was developed around 300&#160;BCE by the <a href="/wiki/Oromo_people" title="Oromo people">Oromo people</a>. A lunar-stellar calendar, this <a href="/wiki/Oromo_calendar" class="mw-redirect" title="Oromo calendar">Oromo calendar</a> relies on astronomical observations of the moon in conjunction with seven particular stars or constellations. Oromo months (stars/lunar phases) are <i>Bittottessa</i> (Iangulum), <i>Camsa</i> (Pleiades), <i>Bufa</i> (Aldebarran), <i>Waxabajjii</i> (Belletrix), <i>Obora Gudda</i> (Central Orion-Saiph), <i>Obora Dikka</i> (Sirius), <i>Birra</i> (full moon), <i>Cikawa</i> (gibbous moon), <i>Sadasaa</i> (quarter moon), <i>Abrasa</i> (large crescent), <i>Ammaji</i> (medium crescent), and <i>Gurrandala</i> (small crescent).<sup id="cite_ref-382" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-382">&#91;380&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Cuisine">Cuisine</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=48" title="Edit section: Cuisine">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_cuisine" title="Ethiopian cuisine">Ethiopian cuisine</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/List_of_Ethiopian_dishes_and_foods" class="mw-redirect" title="List of Ethiopian dishes and foods">List of Ethiopian dishes and foods</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Injera_with_eight_kinds_of_stew.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Injera_with_eight_kinds_of_stew.jpg/220px-Injera_with_eight_kinds_of_stew.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="216" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Injera_with_eight_kinds_of_stew.jpg/330px-Injera_with_eight_kinds_of_stew.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Injera_with_eight_kinds_of_stew.jpg/440px-Injera_with_eight_kinds_of_stew.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2969" data-file-height="2909" /></a><figcaption>This meal consisting of <i><a href="/wiki/Injera" title="Injera">injera</a></i> and several kinds of <i><a href="/wiki/Wat_(food)" title="Wat (food)">wat</a></i> (stew) is typical of Ethiopian cuisine.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The best-known <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_cuisine" title="Ethiopian cuisine">Ethiopian cuisine</a> consists of various types of thick meat <a href="/wiki/Stew" title="Stew">stews</a>, known as <i><a href="/wiki/Wat_(food)" title="Wat (food)">wat</a></i> in Ethiopian culture, and vegetable side dishes served on top of <a href="/wiki/Injera" title="Injera">injera</a>, a large <a href="/wiki/Sourdough" title="Sourdough">sourdough</a> <a href="/wiki/Flatbread" title="Flatbread">flatbread</a> made of <a href="/wiki/Teff" title="Teff">teff</a> flour. This is not eaten with utensils, but instead the injera is used to scoop up the entrées and side dishes. Almost universally in Ethiopia, it is common to eat from the same dish in the middle of the table with a group of people. It is also a common custom to feed others within a group or own hands—a tradition referred to as "<a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_cuisine#Gursha" title="Ethiopian cuisine">gursha</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-383" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-383">&#91;381&#93;</a></sup> Traditional Ethiopian cuisine employs no <a href="/wiki/Pork" title="Pork">pork</a> or <a href="/wiki/Shellfish" title="Shellfish">shellfish</a> of any kind, as both are forbidden in the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Orthodox" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethiopian Orthodox">Ethiopian Orthodox</a> Christian, Islamic and Jewish faiths.
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Fit-fit#Kitcha_fit-fit" title="Fit-fit">Chechebsa</a>, Marqa, Chukko, Michirra and Dhanga are the most popular dishes from the <a href="/wiki/Oromo_people" title="Oromo people">Oromo</a>. <a href="/wiki/Kitfo" title="Kitfo">Kitfo</a>, which originated among the <a href="/wiki/Gurage_people" title="Gurage people">Gurage</a>, is one of the country's most popular delicacies. In addition, <i>Doro Wot</i> (ዶሮ ወጥ in <a href="/wiki/Amharic" title="Amharic">Amharic</a>) and Tsebehi Derho (ጽብሒ ድርሆ in <a href="/wiki/Tigrinya_language" title="Tigrinya language">Tigrinya</a>), are other popular dishes, originating from northwestern Ethiopia.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (January 2017)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> <a href="/wiki/Tihlo" title="Tihlo">Tihlo</a> (ጥሕሎ)—which is a type of <a href="/wiki/Dumpling" title="Dumpling">dumpling</a>—is prepared from roasted barley flour and originated in the <a href="/wiki/Tigray_Region" title="Tigray Region">Tigray Region</a>. Tihlo is now very popular in <a href="/wiki/Amhara_Region" title="Amhara Region">Amhara</a> and spreading further south.<sup id="cite_ref-384" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-384">&#91;382&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Media">Media</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=49" title="Edit section: Media">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Communications_in_Ethiopia" class="mw-redirect" title="Communications in Ethiopia">Communications in Ethiopia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Media_in_Ethiopia" class="mw-redirect" title="Media in Ethiopia">Media in Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ethiopian_Television.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Ethiopian_Television.JPG/220px-Ethiopian_Television.JPG" decoding="async" width="220" height="221" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Ethiopian_Television.JPG/330px-Ethiopian_Television.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Ethiopian_Television.JPG/440px-Ethiopian_Television.JPG 2x" data-file-width="2750" data-file-height="2767" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/ETV_(Ethiopia)" class="mw-redirect" title="ETV (Ethiopia)">Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation</a> former headquarters in Addis Ababa</figcaption></figure>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Broadcasting_Corporation" title="Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation">Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation</a> (EBC), formerly known as ETV, is the <a href="/wiki/State_media" title="State media">state media</a>. Radio broadcasting was commenced earlier in 1935 before the television service began in 1962 with assistance of British firm Thomson and Emperor Haile Selassie.<sup id="cite_ref-africanews.com_3-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-africanews.com-3">&#91;3&#93;</a></sup> Since 2015, EBC has upgraded its studios with modernized transmission.
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Kana_TV" title="Kana TV">Kana TV</a> is the most popular TV channel in Ethiopia.<sup id="cite_ref-385" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-385">&#91;383&#93;</a></sup> It is mainly known for <a href="/wiki/Dubbing_(filmmaking)" class="mw-redirect" title="Dubbing (filmmaking)">dubbing</a> foreign content into <a href="/wiki/Amharic" title="Amharic">Amharic</a>. Over several decades, the state television has served as the major mass media until in the late 2000s, when <a href="/wiki/EBS_TV_(Ethiopia)" title="EBS TV (Ethiopia)">EBS TV</a> launched as the first private television channel. Moreover, numerous private channels were commenced in 2016, culminating in the growth of privately owned media companies in the country. As an example, <a href="/wiki/Fana_TV" title="Fana TV">Fana TV</a> has been the largest TV network since its launch in 2017.
</p><p>The most widely circulated newspapers in Ethiopia are <a href="/wiki/Addis_Fortune" title="Addis Fortune">Addis Fortune</a>, <a href="/wiki/Capital_Ethiopia" class="mw-redirect" title="Capital Ethiopia">Capital Ethiopia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Reporter" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethiopian Reporter">Ethiopian Reporter</a>, Addis Zemen<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (September 2017)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> (<i>Amharic</i>) and <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Herald" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethiopian Herald">Ethiopian Herald</a>.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (September 2017)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p>The sole internet service provider is the national telecommunications firm <a href="/wiki/Ethio_telecom" title="Ethio telecom">Ethio telecom</a>. A large portion of users in the country access the internet through mobile devices.<sup id="cite_ref-:3_386-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:3-386">&#91;384&#93;</a></sup> As of July&#160;2016<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>, there are around 4.29&#160;million people who have internet access at their home as compared to a quarter of a million users a decade before that.<sup id="cite_ref-387" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-387">&#91;385&#93;</a></sup> The Ethiopian government has at times intentionally shut down internet service in the country or restricted access to certain social media sites during periods of political unrest. In August 2016, following protest and demonstration in the Oromia Region, all access to the internet was shut down for a period of two days.<sup id="cite_ref-388" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-388">&#91;386&#93;</a></sup> In June 2017, the government shut down access to the internet for mobile users during a period that coincided with the administration of university entrance examination. Although the reason for the restriction was not confirmed by the government,<sup id="cite_ref-:3_386-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:3-386">&#91;384&#93;</a></sup> the move was similar to a measure taken during the same period in 2016, after a leak of test questions.<sup id="cite_ref-389" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-389">&#91;387&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-390" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-390">&#91;388&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Science_and_technology">Science and technology</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=50" title="Edit section: Science and technology">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Science_and_technology_in_Ethiopia" title="Science and technology in Ethiopia">Science and technology in Ethiopia</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/List_of_Ethiopian_scientists" title="List of Ethiopian scientists">List of Ethiopian scientists</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:258px;max-width:258px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:127px;max-width:127px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Portrait-aklilu-lemma-11.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Portrait-aklilu-lemma-11.jpg/125px-Portrait-aklilu-lemma-11.jpg" decoding="async" width="125" height="177" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Portrait-aklilu-lemma-11.jpg/188px-Portrait-aklilu-lemma-11.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Portrait-aklilu-lemma-11.jpg/250px-Portrait-aklilu-lemma-11.jpg 2x" data-file-width="902" data-file-height="1276" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">Pathobiologist <a href="/wiki/Aklilu_Lemma" title="Aklilu Lemma">Aklilu Lemma</a>. In 1964, he discovered an <a href="/wiki/Alternative_medicine" title="Alternative medicine">alternative</a> treatment for <a href="/wiki/Schistosomiasis" title="Schistosomiasis">schistosomiasis</a>, known as snail fever.<sup id="cite_ref-391" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-391">&#91;389&#93;</a></sup></div></div><div class="tsingle" style="width:127px;max-width:127px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Zeresenay_Alemseged_(2013-01).JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Zeresenay_Alemseged_%282013-01%29.JPG/125px-Zeresenay_Alemseged_%282013-01%29.JPG" decoding="async" width="125" height="174" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Zeresenay_Alemseged_%282013-01%29.JPG/188px-Zeresenay_Alemseged_%282013-01%29.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Zeresenay_Alemseged_%282013-01%29.JPG/250px-Zeresenay_Alemseged_%282013-01%29.JPG 2x" data-file-width="1043" data-file-height="1449" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">Paleoanthropologist <a href="/wiki/Zeresenay_Alemseged" title="Zeresenay Alemseged">Zeresenay Alemseged</a> in 2013. He was best known for discovering fossilized <a href="/wiki/Hominin" class="mw-redirect" title="Hominin">hominin</a> called <i><a href="/wiki/Selam_(Australopithecus)" title="Selam (Australopithecus)">Selam</a></i> or "Lucy's baby" in December 2000.<sup id="cite_ref-392" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-392">&#91;390&#93;</a></sup></div></div></div></div></div>
<p>Science and technology in Ethiopia emerging as progressive due to lack of organized institutions. Manufacturing and service providers often place themselves in <a href="/wiki/Competitive_programming" title="Competitive programming">competitive programming</a> in order to advance innovative and technological solutions through in-house arenas. The <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Space_Science_and_Technology_Institute" title="Ethiopian Space Science and Technology Institute">Ethiopian Space Science and Technology</a> is responsible for conducting multifaceted tasks regarding space and technology. In addition, Ethiopia also launched 70&#160;kg ET-RSS1 multi-spectral remote sensing satellite in December 2019. The President Sahle-Work Zewde told prior in October 2019 that "the satellite will provide all the necessary data on changes in climate and weather-related phenomena that would be used for the country's key targets in agriculture, forestry as well as natural resources protection initiatives." By January 2020, satellite manufacturing, assembling, integrating and testing began. This would also incremented facility built by French company funded by European Investment Bank (EIB). The main observatory Entoto Observatory and Space Science Research Center (EORC) allocated space programmes. The Ethiopian Biotechnology Institute is a part of Scientific Research &amp; Development Services Industry, responsible for environmental and climate conservation.<sup id="cite_ref-393" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-393">&#91;391&#93;</a></sup> Numerous profound scientists have contributed degree of honours and reputations. Some are <a href="/wiki/Kitaw_Ejigu" title="Kitaw Ejigu">Kitaw Ejigu</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mulugeta_Bekele" title="Mulugeta Bekele">Mulugeta Bekele</a>, <a href="/wiki/Aklilu_Lemma" title="Aklilu Lemma">Aklilu Lemma</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gebisa_Ejeta" title="Gebisa Ejeta">Gebisa Ejeta</a> and <a href="/wiki/Melaku_Worede" title="Melaku Worede">Melaku Worede</a>.
</p><p>Ethiopia is known for use of <a href="/wiki/Traditional_medicine" title="Traditional medicine">traditional medicine</a> since millennia. The first epidemic occurred in Ethiopia was in 849, causing the Aksumite Emperor Abba Yohannes evicted from place due to "God's punishment for misdeeds". The first traditional medicine was claimed to be derived from this catastrophe, but the exact source is debated. Though differ from ethnic groups, traditional medicine often implements herbs, spiritual healing, bone-setting and minor surgical procedures in treating disease.<sup id="cite_ref-394" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-394">&#91;392&#93;</a></sup> Others fields include  conventional <a href="/wiki/Mathematics_in_Ethiopia" title="Mathematics in Ethiopia">mathematics</a> used to measure astrology, calendar and unit of measurement.
</p><p>Ethiopia was ranked 126th in the <a href="/wiki/Global_Innovation_Index" title="Global Innovation Index">Global Innovation Index</a> in 2021.<sup id="cite_ref-395" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-395">&#91;393&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Music">Music</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=51" title="Edit section: Music">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Music_of_Ethiopia" title="Music of Ethiopia">Music of Ethiopia</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Golden_Age_of_music" title="Ethiopian Golden Age of music">Ethiopian Golden Age of music</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Yared.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Yared.jpg/220px-Yared.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="144" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Yared.jpg/330px-Yared.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/07/Yared.jpg 2x" data-file-width="360" data-file-height="235" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Yared" title="Yared">Yared</a> in a piece of 15th century Ethiopian sacred art holding a mequamia (prayer stick)</figcaption></figure>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Music_of_Ethiopia" title="Music of Ethiopia">music of Ethiopia</a> is extremely diverse, with each of the country's 80 ethnic groups being associated with unique sounds. Ethiopian music uses a distinct <a href="/wiki/Musical_mode" class="mw-redirect" title="Musical mode">modal system</a> that is <a href="/wiki/Pentatonic_scale" title="Pentatonic scale">pentatonic</a>, with characteristically long intervals between some notes. As with many other aspects of Ethiopian culture and tradition, tastes in music and lyrics are strongly linked with those in neighbouring Eritrea, Somalia, Djibouti, and Sudan.<sup id="cite_ref-Abdullahi_396-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Abdullahi-396">&#91;394&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Tekle_397-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Tekle-397">&#91;395&#93;</a></sup> Traditional singing in Ethiopia presents diverse styles of <a href="/wiki/Polyphony" title="Polyphony">polyphony</a>, (<a href="/wiki/Heterophony" title="Heterophony">heterophony</a>, <a href="/wiki/Drone_(music)" class="mw-redirect" title="Drone (music)">drone</a>, imitation, and <a href="/wiki/Counterpoint" title="Counterpoint">counterpoint</a>). Traditionally, lyricism in Ethiopian song writing is strongly associated with views of patriotism or national pride, romance, friendship, and a unique type of memoire known as <i><a href="/wiki/Tizita" title="Tizita">tizita</a></i>.
</p><p>Saint <a href="/wiki/Yared" title="Yared">Yared</a>, a 6th-century Aksumite composer, is widely regarded as the forerunner of traditional music of Eritrea and Ethiopia, creating liturgical music of the Ethiopian and <a href="/wiki/Eritrean_Orthodox_Tewahedo_Church" title="Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church">Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church</a>. He also composed <i><a href="/wiki/Zema" class="mw-redirect" title="Zema">Zema</a></i>, subdivided into three chants: Ge'ez, Ezel and Araray. Yared life thought to have been "failure and success" where his was poor performance in education. Yared then fired from the school and went to his uncle birthplace Murade Qal. There his saw caterpillar endeavours to reach a tree's peak. He epitomized to his real life and returned to the school with good spirit, later became prominent to political sphere. During the remaining of his lifetime, he was a friend of Aksumite Emperor Gebre Meskel and the exiled <a href="/wiki/Nine_Saints" title="Nine Saints">Nine Saints</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-398" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-398">&#91;396&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Modern music traced back to the reign of Emperor Haile Selassie, where 40 Armenian orphans called <a href="/wiki/Arba_Lijoch" class="mw-redirect" title="Arba Lijoch">Arba Lijoch</a> arrived from <a href="/wiki/Jerusalem" title="Jerusalem">Jerusalem</a> to Addis Ababa. By 1924, the band was almost established as orchestral; but after World War II, several similar bands emerged such as Imperial Bodyguard Band, Army Band, and Police Band.<sup id="cite_ref-399" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-399">&#91;397&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In the 1960s and 1970s, traditional infused modern Ethiopian music was revived in what is known as the "<a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_Golden_Age_of_music" title="Ethiopian Golden Age of music">Golden Age</a>". Several notable musical artists emerged thereafter, for example, <a href="/wiki/Tilahun_Gessesse" title="Tilahun Gessesse">Tilahun Gessesse</a>, <a href="/wiki/Alemayehu_Eshete" title="Alemayehu Eshete">Alemayehu Eshete</a>, <a href="/wiki/Bizunesh_Bekele" title="Bizunesh Bekele">Bizunesh Bekele</a>, <a href="/wiki/Muluken_Melesse" title="Muluken Melesse">Muluken Melesse</a> and <a href="/wiki/Mahmoud_Ahmed" title="Mahmoud Ahmed">Mahmoud Ahmed</a>. It also employed tradition style called <i>tizita</i>. During the Derg regime, these artists were prohibited to perform in the country and often forced into exile in North America and Europe, mixing with jazz and funk influences. For example, Roha Band, <a href="/wiki/Walias_Band" title="Walias Band">Walias Band</a>, and Ethio Stars. By this time, <a href="/wiki/Neway_Debebe" title="Neway Debebe">Neway Debebe</a> was critical of the Derg government.<sup id="cite_ref-:9_380-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:9-380">&#91;378&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Modern music became developed shortly in the 1990s and 2000s. In this period, the most popular artists were <a href="/wiki/Aster_Aweke" title="Aster Aweke">Aster Aweke</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gigi_(singer)" title="Gigi (singer)">Gigi</a> and <a href="/wiki/Teddy_Afro" title="Teddy Afro">Teddy Afro</a>. Ethiopian music further modernized in the next decade, employing electronic type and more popular. DJ <a href="/wiki/Rophnan" title="Rophnan">Rophnan</a> was renowned for pioneering EDM after releasing his debut album <i>Reflection</i> in 2018.<sup id="cite_ref-:9_380-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:9-380">&#91;378&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Cinema">Cinema</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=52" title="Edit section: Cinema">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Cinema_of_Ethiopia" title="Cinema of Ethiopia">Cinema of Ethiopia</a></div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:142px;max-width:142px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:140px;max-width:140px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:199px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Ruth_Negga_by_Gage_Skidmore_3.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Ruth_Negga_by_Gage_Skidmore_3.jpg/138px-Ruth_Negga_by_Gage_Skidmore_3.jpg" decoding="async" width="138" height="200" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Ruth_Negga_by_Gage_Skidmore_3.jpg/207px-Ruth_Negga_by_Gage_Skidmore_3.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Ruth_Negga_by_Gage_Skidmore_3.jpg/276px-Ruth_Negga_by_Gage_Skidmore_3.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1712" data-file-height="2480" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption"><a href="/wiki/Ruth_Negga" title="Ruth Negga">Ruth Negga</a> is an Ethiopian-born actress</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>The first cinema was introduced in 1898, three years after the first world film was projected. Cinematic artifacts ascribed by Italian minister <a href="/w/index.php?title=Federico_Ciccodicola&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Federico Ciccodicola (page does not exist)">Federico Ciccodicola</a><span class="noprint" style="font-size:85%; font-style: normal;">&#160;&#91;<a href="https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Ciccodicola" class="extiw" title="it:Federico Ciccodicola">it</a>&#93;</span> which then offered to Emperor Menelik II. The early 20th century appearance with spectacle was around 1909 and embraced by documentary or biographical films. <i>Au de Menilek</i> was the first film directed by Charles Martel. The first 16mm black-and-white film dedicated to coronation of Emperor <a href="/wiki/Zewditu" title="Zewditu">Zewditu</a>, then coronation of Emperor Haile Selassie was filmed. The 1990s saw international booming of Ethiopian films. The most influential people in this era were <a href="/wiki/Haile_Gerima" title="Haile Gerima">Haile Gerima</a>,&#160;<a href="/wiki/Salem_Mekuria" title="Salem Mekuria">Salem Mekuria</a>, Yemane Demissie, and&#160;<a href="/wiki/Teshome_Gabriel" title="Teshome Gabriel">Teshome Gabriel</a>. Films began modernized in the 2000s and implemented <a href="/wiki/Amharic" title="Amharic">Amharic</a> language. The most internationally grossed films are <i><a href="/wiki/Selanchi" title="Selanchi">Selanchi</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Difret" title="Difret">Difret</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Lamb_(2015_Ethiopian_film)" title="Lamb (2015 Ethiopian film)">Lamb</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Prince_of_Love" class="mw-redirect" title="Prince of Love">Prince of Love</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Lambadina" title="Lambadina">Lambadina</a></i>. The modern era saw several reoccurring actors including <a href="/wiki/Selam_Tesfaye" title="Selam Tesfaye">Selam Tesfaye</a>, <a href="/wiki/Fryat_Yemane" title="Fryat Yemane">Fryat Yemane</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hanan_Tarik" title="Hanan Tarik">Hanan Tarik</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mahder_Assefa" title="Mahder Assefa">Mahder Assefa</a>, <a href="/wiki/Amleset_Muchie" title="Amleset Muchie">Amleset Muchie</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ruth_Negga" title="Ruth Negga">Ruth Negga</a>.
</p><p>One of the most prestigious film award is <a href="/wiki/Gumma_Film_Awards" title="Gumma Film Awards">Gumma Film Awards</a> held in Addis Ababa. The award, which was started in 2014, broadcast on live television in some stations.<sup id="cite_ref-400" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-400">&#91;398&#93;</a></sup> Festivals including <a href="/wiki/Addis_International_Film_Festival" title="Addis International Film Festival">Addis International Film Festival</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Ethiopian_International_Film_Festival" title="Ethiopian International Film Festival">Ethiopian International Film Festival</a> showcase amateur and professional filmmakers works; the latter being voted by judges. They were established in 2007<sup id="cite_ref-401" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-401">&#91;399&#93;</a></sup> and 2005 respectively.<sup id="cite_ref-402" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-402">&#91;400&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Sport">Sport</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit&amp;section=53" title="Edit section: Sport">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Sport_in_Ethiopia" title="Sport in Ethiopia">Sport in Ethiopia</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_17082009.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_17082009.JPG/220px-Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_17082009.JPG" decoding="async" width="220" height="152" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_17082009.JPG/330px-Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_17082009.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_17082009.JPG/440px-Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_17082009.JPG 2x" data-file-width="640" data-file-height="442" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele" title="Kenenisa Bekele">Kenenisa Bekele</a> at the <a href="/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics" title="2009 World Championships in Athletics">2009 World Championships in Athletics</a> in <a href="/wiki/Berlin" title="Berlin">Berlin</a>, <a href="/wiki/Germany" title="Germany">Germany</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The main sports in Ethiopia are <a href="/wiki/Track_and_field" title="Track and field">track and field</a> (particularly <a href="/wiki/Long_distance_running" class="mw-redirect" title="Long distance running">long distance running</a>) and football. Ethiopian athletes have won many <a href="/wiki/Olympic_Games" title="Olympic Games">Olympic</a> gold medals in track and field, most of them in long distance running.<sup id="cite_ref-403" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-403">&#91;401&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Abebe_Bikila" title="Abebe Bikila">Abebe Bikila</a> became the first athlete from a <a href="/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa" title="Sub-Saharan Africa">Sub-Saharan</a> country to win an Olympic gold medal when he won the Marathon at the 1960 Rome Olympic Games in a world record time of 2:15:16.<sup id="cite_ref-404" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-404">&#91;402&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-405" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-405">&#91;403&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie" title="Haile Gebrselassie">Haile Gebrselassie</a>, <a href="/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele" title="Kenenisa Bekele">Kenenisa Bekele</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Tirunesh_Dibaba" title="Tirunesh Dibaba">Tirunesh Dibaba</a> are all world-renowned long distance runners, each with multiple Olympic and <a href="/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships" title="World Athletics Championships">World Championship</a> gold medals. <a href="/wiki/Letesenbet_Gidey" title="Letesenbet Gidey">Letesenbet Gidey</a> holds the world records in both the women's 5,000 metre and 10,000 metre run. Other notable Ethiopian runners are <a href="/wiki/Mamo_Wolde" title="Mamo Wolde">Mamo Wolde</a>, <a href="/wiki/Miruts_Yifter" title="Miruts Yifter">Miruts Yifter</a>, <a href="/wiki/Derartu_Tulu" title="Derartu Tulu">Derartu Tulu</a>, <a href="/wiki/Meseret_Defar" title="Meseret Defar">Meseret Defar</a>, <a href="/wiki/Birhane_Adere" class="mw-redirect" title="Birhane Adere">Birhane Adere</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tiki_Gelana" title="Tiki Gelana">Tiki Gelana</a>, <a href="/wiki/Genzebe_Dibaba" title="Genzebe Dibaba">Genzebe Dibaba</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tariku_Bekele" title="Tariku Bekele">Tariku Bekele</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gelete_Burka" title="Gelete Burka">Gelete Burka</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Yomif_Kejelcha" title="Yomif Kejelcha">Yomif Kejelcha</a>.
</p><p>As of 2012<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup> and going into 2013, the current national <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia_national_football_team" title="Ethiopia national football team">Ethiopian national football team</a> (nicknamed the Walayia Antelopes) made history by qualifying for the <a href="/wiki/2012_Africa_Cup_of_Nations" title="2012 Africa Cup of Nations">2012 Africa Cup of Nations</a> and reached the last 10 African football teams in the last stage of <a href="/wiki/2014_FIFA_World_Cup_qualification_(CAF)" title="2014 FIFA World Cup qualification (CAF)">qualification for the 2014 FIFA World Cup</a>. Noted players include captain <a href="/wiki/Adane_Girma" title="Adane Girma">Adane Girma</a> and top scorer <a href="/wiki/Saladin_Said" title="Saladin Said">Saladin Said</a>.
</p><p>Ethiopia has Sub-Saharan Africa's longest basketball tradition as it established a <a href="/wiki/Ethiopia_national_basketball_team" class="mw-redirect" title="Ethiopia national basketball team">national basketball team</a> in 1949.
</p>
